parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296's amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no separate campaign statement.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, Navy nuclear reactor operator veteran and commercial HVAC technician, running on ending corporate election spending, progressive taxation, universal health care, and the Climate Commitment Act.
highlights: Pledges to pass SB 6358 to end corporate election spending in Washington [S1]
Calls for a progressive tax structure and universal health care [S2]
Will defend the Climate Commitment Act against raids on its funding [S1][S2]

taxes.basis: Calls for a progressive tax structure to end Washington's status as the second-most-regressive tax state.

housing.basis: Proposes state preemption to cut red tape on housing construction, a supply-side approach.

climate.basis: Pledges in his pamphlet and on his site to defend the Climate Commitment Act and modernize the grid.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected experience, running against the House Minority Leader.

local-control.basis: Supports state preemption of local red tape on housing construction.

reform.basis: His signature issue is SB 6358, which would bar corporate, union, and nonprofit election spending.

healthcare.basis: Supports universal health care as 'more effective than the private insurance market.'

social.basis: Endorsed by Washington State Stonewall Democrats; no stated position on LGBTQ+ or reproductive policy.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat between two Democrats: former Shoreline mayor Keith Scully and former FTC antitrust attorney Danica Noble, both dual-endorsed by the 32nd District Democrats and WEA-PAC.

candidates.summary: Shoreline councilmember and former mayor, attorney and former prosecutor, running on housing, climate, progressive tax reform paired with spending restraint, and limited AI regulation.
highlights: Calls the millionaires tax "the start, not the end" of tax reform and says Olympia needs to rein in spending [S3]
Would maintain the Climate Commitment Act and push toward 100% sustainable energy [S3]
Endorsed by the Seattle Times, The Stranger and Washington Conservation Action [S4]

taxes.basis: Supports the millionaires tax and progressive restructuring, but frames it as replacing regressive taxes rather than layering new ones and pairs it with spending restraint.

spending.basis: Says Olympia must rein in spending and earlier proposed a small across-the-board cut except education.

housing.basis: Mixes subsidies, tax credits and land trusts with streamlined permitting and support for state density mandates.

safety.basis: Cites bringing mental health professionals into the field in Shoreline; serves on the Regional Crisis Response Agency board.

climate.basis: Would maintain the Climate Commitment Act and push to 100% sustainable energy; former Futurewise legal director with conservation endorsements.

experience.basis: Ten years on the Shoreline council including as mayor, but no state legislative record.

immigration.basis: Supports banning masked law enforcement and defending state laws against federal overreach.

tech.basis: Favors limited, responsible AI regulation: disclosure, no AI in schools or with children, data centers only with clean energy.

local-control.basis: Says the state 'has taken important steps to mandate needed density' (state standards) and also wants 'more local freedom for districts to raise funds' (local control). Explicit statements point both ways.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and former FTC antitrust attorney running on tech and AI guardrails, competition enforcement to lower prices, and school funding.
highlights: About 20 years at the FTC, including the antitrust case against Meta [S1][S4]
Would strengthen antitrust enforcement, ban surveillance pricing, and bar insurers from using AI to deny coverage [S3]
Endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates [S1][S6]

tech.basis: Campaign centers on guardrails for AI and tech targeting kids and workers, surveillance-pricing bans and limits on student data.

spending.basis: Calls for fully funding schools and investing in public hospitals while pledging to spend wisely with real accountability.

housing.basis: Pairs faster permitting and more supply at every income level with stronger renter protections.

experience.basis: First-time candidate offering federal enforcement expertise rather than an elected record.

healthcare.basis: Proposes stronger state insurance regulation and public-hospital investment within the existing system; no universal-coverage proposal.

immigration.basis: Opposes federal deportations of refugees and supports state help for refugees.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no statement of her own on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic Rep. Edwin Obras, appointed in 2024 and elected in 2025, faces Republican newcomer Chris Martinez, who runs on lower taxes, repealing the Climate Commitment Act, and parental rights in schools.

candidates.summary: Incumbent since December 2024 and former Seattle Human Services division director, running on affordability, worker protections and immigrant rights.
highlights: Six bills signed in his first biennium, including background checks and rideshare regulation [S2]
Has pushed for rent-increase caps and voted for 2025 rent stabilization [S2][S7]
Voted for ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million) and sponsored ESHB 1296 [S4][S6]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no campaign statements on taxes found.

spending.basis: Cites securing over $30 million in state investment for the district, including housing and health.

housing.basis: Pushes rent-increase caps and limits on investor home buying, and voted for rent stabilization.

experience.basis: Under two years in office but with six enacted bills and a whip post, against a political newcomer.

immigration.basis: Pamphlet pledges to keep fighting for immigrant rights, without specifics.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no statement of his own on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

parental-rights.basis: Original sponsor of, and yes vote on, ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list.

candidates.summary: Republican precinct committee officer and blue-collar worker making his first run, on lower taxes, smaller government, repeal of the Climate Commitment Act and parental rights.
highlights: Lists "HB 6346 (Unconstitutional Income Tax)" among bills he opposes and wants lower B&O taxes [S2]
Would reduce or eliminate the Climate Commitment Act [S2]
Says parents have the right to know and guide what their children learn [S2]

taxes.basis: Opposes the new income tax, wants lower B&O taxes, and pledges to abolish energy taxes.

spending.basis: Would cut wasteful spending and reduce the size of state government.

housing.basis: Would cut regulations on home builders to make housing more affordable.

safety.basis: Runs on law and order, more officers, and holding criminals accountable.

climate.basis: Would reduce or eliminate the Climate Commitment Act and abolish energy taxes.

experience.basis: No elected office beyond appointed PCO; pitches himself as a blue-collar outsider.

parental-rights.basis: Says parents have the right to know and guide what children learn and opposes instruction without parental knowledge or consent.

social.basis: Campaigns on traditional family values; no specific statement on sports eligibility, gender-affirming care or abortion.

contests.office_does: One of 98 Washington State Representatives, serving two-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 37th District (southeast Seattle, Skyway and part of Renton).
contests.race_blurb: House Education Committee chair Sharon Tomiko Santos, the state's longest-serving House member, trails first-time candidate Kelabe Tewolde after a 51.5% to 47.9% primary; both are Democrats. The sharpest policy split is rent stabilization, which Santos voted against and Tewolde supports.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 1999 and chair of the House Education Committee; voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax and against the 2025 rent-increase cap.
highlights: Only Seattle-area legislator to vote against the 2025 rent-increase cap, citing harm to small landlords [S6][S7][S8]
Voted for ESSB 6346, the millionaires' tax I-645 would repeal [S9]
As Education chair, signed the committee's do-pass report on HB 1296 (2025 parental-rights amendments) and voted for it on the floor [S10][S11]
Opposes a universal school cellphone ban, preferring local school-board decisions [S5]

taxes.basis: Voted for the millionaires' tax and campaigns on 'tax fairness for working families'; founding member of the Washington Tax Fairness Coalition.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent-increase cap, saying rent control 'has not stemmed the cost of housing,' while supporting more supply and affordable housing near transit.

safety.basis: Campaign site emphasizes community-led violence prevention and behavioral-health response services.

experience.basis: In the House since 1999 and chair of the Education Committee; the state's longest-serving House member.

local-control.basis: Opposes a universal school cellphone ban, preferring that local school boards decide.

immigration.basis: Founding board member of Hate Free Zone (OneAmerica) and an NCSL immigration task force; site cites protecting immigrant communities.

parental-rights.basis: As Education chair signed the do-pass report on HB 1296 and voted for final passage; the bill narrowed I-2081's curriculum, records and medical-notification rights.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, Rainier Scholars leadership director and Seattle Planning Commissioner, running on generational change, rent stabilization and early education; won the primary.
highlights: Supports rent stabilization and says he would have voted for the 2025 rent-increase cap [S5][S7]
Priorities: housing affordability, childcare, interest limits on medical debt, early interventions for kids [S1]
Supports a statewide school cellphone ban [S5]
Endorsed by Gov. Bob Ferguson, Executive Girmay Zahilay, Superintendent Chris Reykdal, the WEA and The Seattle Times [S4][S6]

housing.basis: Prioritizes a real rent-stabilization cap and criticizes the incumbent's vote against the 2025 cap; anti-displacement focus.

spending.basis: Wants to fully fund early education and criticizes education cuts paired with forgone estate-tax revenue.

safety.basis: Campaign site calls for 'safety built on community investment,' including gun-violence prevention.

experience.basis: First-time candidate running explicitly on 'generation change' against a 27-year incumbent.

local-control.basis: Supports a statewide school cellphone ban, where the incumbent prefers local school-board discretion.

taxes.basis: Criticized the Legislature for giving up about $270M in estate-tax revenue while cutting education ('that doesn't make sense'). Endorsed by Tech 4 Taxes and Fuse Washington. He has no stated position on the millionaires' tax, so +1 rather than +2.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 41st District (Mercer Island, Newcastle and parts of Bellevue, Issaquah, Renton and Sammamish), voting on state law, budgets and taxes for two-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Janice Zahn, appointed in 2025 and a former Bellevue councilmember, faces Republican Elle Nguyen, who opposes a state income tax and the 2026 state housing-siting mandate. Zahn took 72% in the August primary.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2025 and former Bellevue councilmember (2017-2025); Port of Seattle chief engineer running on affordability, infrastructure investment and fiscal responsibility.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million (ESSB 6346), the tax I-645 would repeal [S8]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization (EHB 1217) and the 2026 supportive-housing siting law (ESHB 2266) [S9][S10]
Says Washington must 'accelerate investments in clean energy and community resilience' to meet 2030 climate goals [S4]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), the parents' rights amendments I-1 would undo; no public position found on the three initiatives [S7]

taxes.basis: Voted yea on ESSB 6346, the 9.9% tax on household income over $1 million; no further stated tax agenda.

spending.basis: Pairs 'delivering investments in housing, education, childcare, and transportation' with 'fiscal responsibility' and 'accountability' on budget challenges: genuinely mixed.

housing.basis: Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and for ESHB 2266 requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters.

climate.basis: Says the state must accelerate clean-energy investment to meet 2030 climate goals; endorsed by Conservation Action.

experience.basis: Sitting legislator since 2025 with eight prior years on the Bellevue council: an established record, though short legislative tenure.

local-control.basis: Voted for ESHB 2266, which requires cities to allow transitional and supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

social.basis: Pamphlet endorsement list includes Planned Parenthood; no direct statement on gender or reproductive policy.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; single vote, no statement.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger from Mercer Island, a real estate investor and community advocate without prior elected office, running on fiscal discipline, public safety and local control.
highlights: Opposes a state income tax and says 'Olympia has been fiscally irresponsible' [S4]
'Adamantly opposes' ESHB 2266: 'Olympia should not substitute statewide mandates for the judgment of local communities' [S4]
Site lists 'Supporting law enforcement, holding criminals accountable' [S3]
States a commitment to 'parental rights' without specifics; no public position found on the three initiatives [S4]

taxes.basis: Opposes a state income tax and lists 'protecting taxpayers from unnecessary tax increases'.

spending.basis: Repeated calls for fiscal discipline, stopping wasteful spending and balancing the budget; says Olympia has been fiscally irresponsible.

safety.basis: Site lists supporting law enforcement and holding criminals accountable; no detailed enforcement agenda.

experience.basis: No elected office held; prior unsuccessful school-board and legislative runs.

local-control.basis: Adamantly opposes ESHB 2266 as a statewide mandate overriding 'the judgment of local communities'; commits to 'meaningful local control'.

parental-rights.basis: Repeatedly names 'parental rights' as a commitment, but no specific position on notification, curricula or opt-outs.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 43rd District (central Seattle), voting on state law, budgets and taxes for two-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: Nicole Macri, in office since 2017 with a housing and homelessness record, faces first-time candidate Alby Clendennin, a UW resident director who emphasizes corporate influence in politics and AI regulation. Only Macri has stated positions on the statewide initiatives (no on all).

candidates.summary: Incumbent since 2017 and DESC deputy director; record centered on rent stabilization and supportive housing, with explicit positions on abortion access, gender-affirming care and the statewide initiatives.
highlights: 'I'm voting no on all statewide initiatives' (I-645, I-1, I-638) [S1]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and was an original sponsor of ESHB 2266, requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters [S8][S10]
Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million [S7]
Commits to 'fully funding access to abortion' and a 'sanctuary state for gender-affirming care' [S3]

taxes.basis: Voted for the millionaires tax and opposes I-645's repeal of it; also cites cutting small business taxes.

spending.basis: Cites tax revenue funding schools and childcare, funding supportive housing and fully funding abortion access.

housing.basis: Led on rent stabilization ('prevent rent gouging') and sponsored the supportive-housing siting law; DESC supportive-housing career.

climate.basis: 'Aggressively tackling climate change by modernizing our energy grid, cutting building emissions'.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2017 with enacted housing legislation.

local-control.basis: Original sponsor of ESHB 2266, a state requirement that cities allow supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

immigration.basis: Cites work to protect immigrant neighbors from 'hateful federal overreach'.

healthcare.basis: Frames healthcare as making care and insurance affordable and accessible within the current system; no single-payer statement.

social.basis: Explicit commitments to expand and fund abortion access and keep Washington a sanctuary for gender-affirming care; opposes I-638.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025) and says she is voting no on all statewide initiatives, including I-1.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and UW resident director who describes himself as a pragmatic progressive Democrat focused on reducing corporate influence in politics and regulating AI.
highlights: Priorities: 'reducing corporate influence in politics' and 'regulating artificial intelligence to prevent unfair pricing' [S1]
Calls for strengthening public services and 'a government that prioritizes people over profit' [S1]
No campaign website and no reported contributions as of mid-September 2026 [S1][S4]
No public position found on the three initiatives [S1]

experience.basis: No elected or government experience; first run for office.

reform.basis: Names reducing corporate influence in politics as a top priority; no specific reform proposals.

tech.basis: Wants to regulate AI to prevent unfair pricing.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 45th District (Kirkland, Redmond, Woodinville, Sammamish, Duvall), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Roger Goodman, in the House since 2007 and chair of the Community Safety Committee, faces Republican JoAnn Tolentino, a retired music teacher and compliance professional making her first legislative run. Goodman took 72.87% in the August primary.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2007 and chair of the House Community Safety Committee; attorney and former director of the state Sentencing Guidelines Commission.
highlights: Cites laws on crime survivors, drug and mental health services, and police accountability and training [S1]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million that I-645 would repeal [S6]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296, the 2025 parental-rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S5]
Pledges to champion K-12 funding, affordable housing investments, climate action and reproductive rights [S1]

experience.basis: House member since 2007 and chair of the Community Safety Committee, citing an enacted record.

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax; his statement stresses tax relief for working people and small businesses rather than new revenue.

spending.basis: Cites free school meals and childcare funding and pledges K-12 and affordable-housing investment.

safety.basis: Record and platform center on police accountability reform and expanded drug and mental health services, alongside crime-survivor protections.

climate.basis: Pledges to champion climate action; primary-era campaign material cited carbon-cap legislation.

housing.basis: Pledges continued affordable-housing investments; no deregulation or rent-policy statement.

social.basis: Single explicit pledge to champion reproductive rights.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

immigration.basis: Campaign site criticizes 'masked ICE agents' who 'snatch people out of their vehicles and off the streets' and says this has eroded trust in local law enforcement: one clear statement toward constraining ICE tactics.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger from Woodinville, a retired music teacher and compliance-software professional and five-year precinct committee officer, running as "not a politician."
highlights: Says "parents, not politicians, should guide their children's education and healthcare" [S3]
Supports voter ID, paper ballots and bipartisan election oversight [S1][S3]
Would fight regulations driving up housing costs and streamline permitting and zoning [S1][S3]
Backs fossil fuels, nuclear and hydro to keep energy bills low [S3]

experience.basis: No public office beyond precinct committee officer; presents herself as "not a politician."

parental-rights.basis: Repeated statements: "empower parents"; parents "should guide their children's education and healthcare"; involve parents and reject CRT and gender-ideology content in classrooms.

local-control.basis: Calls to "restore local control" in schools, a single statement.

housing.basis: Would fight regulations driving up housing costs and streamline permitting and zoning to build more homes.

climate.basis: Champions affordable energy and supports fossil fuels, nuclear and hydro "to keep bills low."

safety.basis: "Full support for our law enforcement" paired with "treatment, not just punishment" and recovery programs.

spending.basis: "Audit every dollar and pass balanced budgets"; waste and fraud and fiscal accountability are recurring themes.

immigration.basis: Supports legal immigration, the rule of law and border security, with "humane processing."

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 46th District in northeast Seattle, serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: seven-term incumbent Gerry Pollet, who led the primary with about 52%, and former federal prosecutor Will Dreher, who placed second with about 31% and has outraised him. AI regulation, housing and Pollet's long tenure frame the race.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative (in the House since 2011), chair of the Joint Legislative Audit and Review Committee, public-health faculty member and Hanford cleanup advocate.
highlights: Says he championed the millionaires' and capital gains taxes; voted yes on ESSB 6346 [S1][S11]
Calls himself 'a strong voice against the attacks on trans kids' and helped expand Medicaid coverage of gender-affirming care [S4]
Proposes taxing AI and data-center storage with Oregon legislators; says 10% annual rent increases are too high [S4][S9]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), the parents' rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S10]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and says he championed the millionaires' and capital gains taxes.

spending.basis: Frames new revenue as funding schools, healthcare, childcare and free college; his audit work targets tax breaks rather than spending restraint.

housing.basis: Backs density, but says 10% annual rent increases are too high and argues government must build housing for each income segment.

climate.basis: Says he worked to end fossil-fuel electricity and push life-cycle methane accounting; no stated carbon-pricing position.

experience.basis: In the House since 2011, JLARC chair and Appropriations member.

immigration.basis: Says he passed ICE mask bans and protected undocumented students from federal data sharing.

social.basis: Funded abortion access, opposes 'attacks on trans kids', helped expand Medicaid gender-affirming care coverage.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

tech.basis: Lists regulating AI and data centers and proposes an AI/data-center tax, with less emphasis than his opponent.

candidates.summary: Former federal prosecutor and Kagan clerk, now a plaintiffs' attorney, running his first campaign on aggressive AI and tech regulation.
highlights: Says he is 'the only candidate promising to aggressively regulate tech'; platform would regulate or stop new data centers [S1][S4]
Supports the No Hate in Washington State campaign 'to defeat Initiatives 1 and 638' [S4]
'I support the Millionaire's Income Tax, and I will fight any attempts to repeal it' [S4]
Pairs permitting reform and density with rent stabilization; proposes a North Seattle sex-trafficking task force [S4][S8]

taxes.basis: Supports the millionaires' income tax and pledges to fight repeal; proposes AI and corporate profits taxes.

spending.basis: Pamphlet plans to "fully fund schools"; platform adds aggressive transit investment, funded gun-violence reduction programs, a sex-trafficking task force, and emergency funding for LGBTQ+ newcomer organizations.

housing.basis: Permitting reform and density on one side, rent stabilization and supportive housing on the other.

safety.basis: Deterrence and a trafficking enforcement task force paired with non-police crisis response and evidence-based violence programs.

climate.basis: Would block diversion of Climate Commitment Act funds and stop or regulate new data centers to preserve climate progress.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected or legislative experience.

immigration.basis: Would divest public funds from private detention facilities and provide healthcare regardless of immigration status.

social.basis: Supports defeating I-638 and emergency funding for LGBTQ+ newcomer organizations.

parental-rights.basis: Supports defeating I-1; his only parental-notification proposal concerns reading-assessment results.

tech.basis: Aggressive AI, data-center and social-media regulation is the centerpiece of his campaign.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 47th District (Kent, Auburn and Covington area of South King County), serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Eight-year Democratic incumbent Debra Entenman faces Libertarian housing developer Cobi Clark, who is endorsed by the 47th District Republicans. Clark would repeal the 2026 income tax and the 2025 parental-rights amendments; Entenman voted for both.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2018 and former congressional district director. Running on her public safety funding and college student support bills and on the safety net.
highlights: Prime sponsor of HB 2015 (2025), which her pamphlet says secured $100 million for public safety [S1][S2]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S4]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025); her platform supports district-set curricula and comprehensive sex education, plus parental opt-outs from specific lessons [S3][S5]
Platform calls for independent investigations of police use of force and for social workers alongside officers [S3]
Endorsed by Washington Conservation Action, King County Democrats and The Urbanist [S9][S10][S11]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million; no separate campaign statement on taxes.

spending.basis: Runs on strengthening safety-net programs (rental assistance, eviction prevention, childcare, healthcare) and investment in frontline responders.

housing.basis: Platform commits to rental assistance, eviction prevention and housing stability services.

safety.basis: Mixed: sponsored new public safety funding (HB 2015) while backing independent use-of-force investigations and social workers in safety response.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 and backs district-set curricula and comprehensive sex education, but her platform also supports parental opt-outs from specific lessons.

tech.basis: Platform calls for laws requiring companies to disclose and give consumers control over the personal data they collect.

experience.basis: In the seat since 2018, with four committee assignments and signed bills (HB 2015, HB 1559).

candidates.summary: Libertarian housing developer and construction project manager from Auburn, endorsed by the 47th District Republicans. Running on housing deregulation, opposition to the income tax, and civil liberties.
highlights: Would 'Repeal the state income tax contemplated under SB 6346' [S3]
Would 'Repeal HB 1296 which undermined the voter approved parents rights initiative 2081' [S3]
Would cut permitting delays and limit building codes to safety, based on his developer experience [S1][S7]
Would end qualified immunity, criminalize masked arrests, and ban Flock cameras [S3][S9]
Proposes multi-winner ranked-choice voting and advisory votes on new taxes [S4]

taxes.basis: Opposes any state income tax in the pamphlet and on his site, and would repeal the 2026 income tax in SB 6346.

spending.basis: 'Washington doesn't have a revenue problem. It has a spending problem'; would rein in spending, cut waste and tie spending to revenue sources.

housing.basis: Supply-side deregulation from developer experience: faster permits, building codes limited to safety, fewer regulations.

climate.basis: Puts affordable, 'abundant' energy and stopping 'policies that punish commuters' first, while also backing nuclear and geothermal investment; does not name carbon pricing.

parental-rights.basis: Would repeal ESHB 1296 to restore the I-2081 parental-rights law, and says schools should 'respect the role of parents in education decisions.'

reform.basis: Proposes multi-winner ranked-choice voting, restoring advisory votes on new taxes, and 50-year sunsets for legislation.

experience.basis: No elected office (lost a 2025 Auburn council race); runs on private-sector development experience.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 48th District (parts of Redmond, Bellevue and Kirkland plus the Points communities and Medina), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Democrat Osman Salahuddin, appointed in 2025 and elected that November, faces Republican Jeffery Poppe, a retired CPA campaigning on no new taxes, fraud audits and individual-only contributions.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative appointed in January 2025 and elected in November 2025; former Redmond City Councilmember and Fred Hutch cancer researcher.
highlights: Passed 2025 bills on behavioral-health co-response teams and paid sick leave for immigration proceedings [S4]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S8]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296, the 2025 parental-rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S7]
Endorsed by Gov. Ferguson, the State Labor Council, teachers, nurses and Planned Parenthood Alliance [S1]

experience.basis: About two sessions in the House after a 2025 appointment and election, plus prior Redmond council service.

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax and describes the 2025 budget's "equitable revenue measures."

safety.basis: Passed a co-response bill meant to "reduce reliance on law enforcement" and says safety means "prioritizing prevention"; also passed a sentencing aggravator for rape resulting in pregnancy.

immigration.basis: Sponsored the enacted paid-sick-leave law for immigration proceedings and cites immigrant-protection bills.

climate.basis: Calls for a just transition to clean energy with environmental justice in emissions reduction.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger; retired CPA and financial systems consultant and former San Diego Taxpayers Association director, running on no new taxes and fraud audits.
highlights: "No more new taxes! Washington has an outrageous spending problem, not an income problem" [S1]
Pledges to spearhead fraud audits and publish spending and performance metrics [S1][S3]
Will accept only individual contributions, no PAC or union money [S1][S3]

experience.basis: No prior elected public office; runs on a private-sector auditing career.

taxes.basis: Repeated pledge to reject any new taxes; says the state has a spending problem, not an income problem.

spending.basis: Platform built on fraud audits, efficiency and spending transparency.

reform.basis: Repeated pledge to accept only individual contributions and refuse PAC and union money; no other structural-reform positions.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, covering school funding, the tax structure, housing rules, behavioral-health funding, transportation projects, and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Appointed Democratic incumbent Zach Hall faces Republican Michelle Bennett, Mercer Island's police chief, after a close primary (44.5% to 43.0% in the King County count). The seat is on the ballot as both a short term and a full two-year term.

candidates.summary: Appointed in June 2025 and seeking election in his own right; Vice Chair of the House Environment & Energy Committee and a former Issaquah City Councilmember.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million [S4]
Frames public safety around first responders, gun-violence prevention, and behavioral-health interventions [S2]
Commits to cutting greenhouse gas emissions and moving away from fossil fuels faster [S2]

taxes.basis: Recorded yea on House final passage of the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no further public statement on revenue found.

spending.basis: Calls for more school funding, protecting essential services, and investment in infrastructure, childcare and healthcare access.

housing.basis: Housing platform centers on supply and reforms that make it easier to finance and build homes faster; no tenant-protection or social-housing position stated.

safety.basis: Describes safety as first-responder support, gun-violence prevention, and behavioral-health and substance-use interventions that meet people where they are.

climate.basis: Commits to reducing emissions and transitioning away from fossil fuels faster; endorsed by WA Conservation Action and Sierra Club.

experience.basis: Appointed incumbent with one legislative session plus six years on a city council; a short record rather than long tenure.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and the WA State Stonewall Democrats; no direct statement found.

candidates.summary: Mercer Island police chief and former chief in Maple Valley and Sammamish, running for office for the first time on tax restraint and public safety.
highlights: Says Olympia passed "the largest tax increase in state history" and that police lack clear tools [S1]
Says state housing and zoning mandates do not work for every community [S2]
Endorsed by the King County Republican Party [S8]

taxes.basis: Opposes an income tax, criticizes recent tax increases in her pamphlet, and cites the new income tax as a reason for running.

spending.basis: Pledges to ensure state spending delivers measurable results, an accountability frame.

safety.basis: Police-chief candidate who says police lack tools to protect victims and wants drugs made illegal again, paired with pretrial diversion.

experience.basis: First run for office, though she brings a long law-enforcement executive career rather than a legislative record.

local-control.basis: Said Olympia dictating a city's housing zoning or affordable housing 'simply doesn't work for every community.'

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent Shelley Kloba, in the House since 2017, faces Republican Cliff Moon, a construction-business owner who edged Democrat Jenne Alderks for the second primary slot. Kloba defends the 2026 Millionaires Tax and her AI and privacy record; Moon runs on property-tax relief, police funding and curriculum transparency.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2017 and Vice-Chair of the House Technology, Economic Development, and Veterans Committee, focused on data privacy, AI guardrails and tax-code changes.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and calls it the start of correcting an upside-down tax code [S2][S5]
Prime sponsor of the People's Privacy Act (HB 1671) and a data-broker registry bill [S8]
Original sponsor of HB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list [S7]

taxes.basis: Voted for the Millionaires Tax and defends it and the capital gains tax as correcting an upside-down tax code, pledging further 'fair tax' bills.

spending.basis: Platform emphasizes fully funding K-12, behavioral-health access and renewable-energy investment rather than audits or restraint.

safety.basis: Highlights crisis-responder teams and crisis treatment centers law enforcement can use instead of jail or the ER.

climate.basis: Supports reducing dependence on fossil fuels, renewable-energy investment and green jobs in pamphlet and website; endorsed by Sierra Club.

experience.basis: Nine years in the House, committee vice-chair, bills enacted; opponent has never held office beyond PCO.

healthcare.basis: Says health care is 'a right, not a privilege', should never be tied to employment, and calls for 'getting rid of the middleman'; no explicit single-payer proposal.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and Washington Stonewall Democrats; no statement of her own beyond protecting civil rights.

parental-rights.basis: Original sponsor of and yes vote on ESHB 1296, which modified and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parental-rights list.

tech.basis: Record centers data-privacy and AI regulation: People's Privacy Act, data-broker registry bill, AI consumer-harm work; says AI should not exploit people for profit.

candidates.summary: Republican construction-business owner and Precinct Committee Officer running on property-tax relief, police funding, spending audits and curriculum transparency.
highlights: Supports property-tax caps and senior exemptions and lower B&O taxes for small operators [S2]
Supports fully funding police, with crisis response as 'a complement to — not replacement for' police [S2]
Opposes 'one-size-fits-all mandates from Olympia' on housing [S2]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet and website center tax relief: property-tax caps, lower B&O taxes and resisting tax increases.

spending.basis: Says the state should spend wisely and audit programs that aren't delivering results.

safety.basis: Runs on fully funding police and accountability in the courts, while also backing mental-health crisis response as a complement.

housing.basis: Supports removing barriers to housing production and local control over development; no public-housing or tenant-protection proposals.

local-control.basis: Explicitly opposes one-size-fits-all mandates from Olympia and wants local communities to shape their own development.

climate.basis: Wants environmental policies that do not destroy jobs or make energy unaffordable; no stated climate-policy commitments.

experience.basis: No elected office beyond Precinct Committee Officer; runs on a business background against a nine-year incumbent.

parental-rights.basis: Says parents should raise their children and supports 'parental involvement, transparency in curriculum'; no specific notification or opt-out proposal.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, covering school funding, the tax structure, housing rules, and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Five-term Republican Mike Steele, the capital-budget ranking member, faces Democrat Maggie Adams, an IATSE union representative from Snoqualmie. Steele led the primary 41.1% to 33.9%; Adams led the King County portion.

candidates.summary: Incumbent since 2017, Capital Budget ranking member and Lake Chelan Chamber director, running on small-business, budget and infrastructure priorities.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 (2026) and ESHB 1296 (2025) [S5][S6]
Says taxes, fees and regulation make housing less affordable [S12]
Endorsed by the State Labor Council and WEA-PAC as well as AWB and the King County GOP [S3][S13][S14][S15]

taxes.basis: Voted against the 2026 income tax, campaigns on lowering tax burdens, and has said the state has a spending problem rather than a revenue problem.

spending.basis: Emphasizes balanced budgets and making sure every education dollar delivers results; describes a spending problem.

housing.basis: Said affordable housing cannot be made more affordable by more taxes, fees or unfavorable regulation.

safety.basis: Reported to oppose decriminalization; endorsed by the Fraternal Order of Police.

climate.basis: Opposes policies that would significantly raise transportation and energy costs; no direct climate statement.

experience.basis: Ten years in office with budget-committee seniority and past caucus leadership.

healthcare.basis: Wants to expand affordable options through transparency, choice and cost containment within the current system.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296 twice; his caucus site backs school choice and 'empowering parents.'

candidates.summary: IATSE Local 887 business representative from Snoqualmie, a first-time candidate running on healthcare access, workers' rights and water protection.
highlights: Calls healthcare "a fundamental human right" and wants comprehensive access statewide [S2]
Has said she supports a millionaire's tax [S7]
Supports term limits and lowering the voting age to 16 for state and local elections [S2]

taxes.basis: Has said she supports a millionaire's tax and higher taxes on high-grossing businesses; pamphlet lists tax fairness.

spending.basis: Wants better pay and facilities for educators and statewide healthcare access.

housing.basis: Would regulate vacation rentals and mandate affordable units in new construction.

safety.basis: Emphasizes community policing and de-escalation.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with union leadership but no public office.

reform.basis: Supports constitutional term limits for elected offices and federal judges and voting at 16.

healthcare.basis: Calls healthcare a human right and wants comprehensive access everywhere, without naming single-payer.

tech.basis: Wants communities and farmers to have priority for water over incoming data centers.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, including school funding, taxes, housing, and criminal statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Kristine Reeves, chair of the House Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee, faces Paul McDaniel (prefers Independent Party), a former appointed Federal Way councilmember. Reeves voted against the 2026 income tax on earnings over $1 million, which narrows the tax contrast.

candidates.summary: Incumbent state representative (2017-2019 and since 2023) who chairs the House Agriculture and Natural Resources Committee and founded the Veterans & Military Families Caucus.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million [S3]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025) and ESSB 5599 (2023) [S4][S6]
Cites passing laws on homeless students, senior food access, wildfire risk, and $100 million for local public safety [S1]

taxes.basis: Mixed: voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, but cites helping pass college aid funded by large companies.

spending.basis: Runs on program delivery ($100M public safety, food access, paid family leave, childcare) rather than restraint.

safety.basis: Pairs first-responder resources and public-safety funding with community policing and mental-health officer programs.

healthcare.basis: Calls health care a right but backs the state public option to make insurers compete, rather than single-payer.

experience.basis: Multi-term incumbent and committee chair, against a challenger with no legislative experience.

social.basis: Voted for ESSB 5599 on youth access to gender-affirming and reproductive care; no further statements found.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which amended the Initiative 2081 parental-rights list; no separate statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Former appointed Federal Way City Councilmember, Marine Corps veteran, and technology consultant, running on lower taxes, public safety, housing supply, and protecting girls' sports.
highlights: Will oppose any state personal income tax and supports eliminating the sales tax on services [S3]
Pledges to 'protect girls' sports' [S1]
Listed as 'BEST CHOICE' by the King County Republican Party [S11]

taxes.basis: Pledges to reduce taxes, oppose a state personal income tax for anyone, and eliminate the sales tax on services.

spending.basis: Calls for eliminating wasteful spending and 'spending smarter' before asking taxpayers for more.

housing.basis: Emphasizes increasing supply, middle housing, ADUs, and streamlined permitting.

safety.basis: Explicitly pairs law-enforcement support with expanded addiction and mental-health treatment: 'not tougher... not softer... smarter.'

experience.basis: Former appointed city councilmember with no legislative record, running against a multi-term incumbent.

social.basis: Pledges to 'protect girls' sports' in his pamphlet statement; no further detail.

parental-rights.basis: Says parents deserve meaningful involvement and supports transparency about academic progress and more educational choice.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, including school funding, taxes, housing, and criminal statutes.
contests.race_blurb: First-term Republican Joshua Penner, a former Orting mayor, faces Democrat John Bielka, a civil engineer and public works director. Both run on fiscal accountability, and Bielka says he will not back tax increases until spending is prioritized.

candidates.summary: First-term state representative, former eight-year Orting mayor, and Marine Iraq War veteran, running on oversight of state agencies and lowering living costs.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million) and ESHB 1296 (2025) [S4][S5]
Opposed SB 6309, which he says lets Sound Transit sidestep local zoning [S2]
Cites saving Buckley's Rainier School and funding the White River and Fairfax bridge repairs [S1]

taxes.basis: Voted against the 2026 income tax and pledges to lower living costs; no broader tax-cut platform stated.

spending.basis: Runs on 'data-driven oversight' and demanding accountability and return on investment from state agencies.

local-control.basis: Opposed letting Sound Transit sidestep local zoning, and offered amendments to shield local governments from Attorney General demands.

experience.basis: First-term legislator with eight years as mayor and six on the city council, against a first-time candidate.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296's amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no separate campaign statement.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, civil engineer and public works director with 30+ years in infrastructure and budgets, running on practical results, housing supply, and budget discipline.
highlights: Will not support increased taxes until the Legislature prioritizes its spending [S3]
Supports ADUs, duplexes, townhomes, and predictable permitting to add housing [S3]
Supports the Second Amendment and responsible gun ownership [S2]

taxes.basis: Says he will not support tax increases until the Legislature prioritizes spending, quoting 'a spending problem, not a revenue problem.'

spending.basis: Calls for measuring results and ending programs that fail to deliver, while prioritizing maintenance of existing infrastructure.

housing.basis: Emphasizes more housing types and faster, predictable permitting.

safety.basis: Supports officer recruitment and holding repeat offenders accountable, alongside stronger crisis-response systems.

experience.basis: First-time candidate ('First time public servant'), running against an incumbent.

healthcare.basis: Supports wider access, price transparency, and fewer surprise bills within the existing system; no universal-coverage proposal.

social.basis: Endorsed by Washington State Stonewall Democrats; no stated position on LGBTQ+ or reproductive policy.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Lauren Davis, known for behavioral-health legislation, faces fellow Democrat Imraan Siddiqi, executive director of CAIR-Washington, who runs on immigrant protection and affordability. The local party dual-endorsed both.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2019 whose record centers on addiction and behavioral-health policy, including Ricky's Law and the Recovery Navigator Program.
highlights: Passed Ricky's Law and created the Recovery Navigator Program and the Lynnwood Crisis Care Center [S1]
Voted for ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million) and was an original sponsor of ESHB 1296 [S5][S7]
Says she is "completely pro-choice" and has championed health care for immigrants and protections against ICE [S1]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no campaign statements on taxes found.

spending.basis: Calls for game-changing investments in education and treatment on demand.

housing.basis: Voted for rent stabilization and prioritizes supportive and affordable housing.

safety.basis: Record combines involuntary addiction treatment (Ricky's Law) with diversion and treatment programs; endorsed by police guilds and progressive groups.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2019 with a substantial enacted behavioral-health record.

immigration.basis: Says she has championed health care for immigrants and protections against ICE.

social.basis: States she is completely pro-choice; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates.

parental-rights.basis: Original sponsor of, and yes vote on, ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and executive director of CAIR-Washington running on immigrant protection, affordability, and taxing the wealthiest.
highlights: Executive director of CAIR-Washington and one of the original plaintiffs against the Muslim ban [S1]
Would fund legal defense for immigrants and keep state institutions from facilitating federal enforcement [S3]
Calls for progressive revenue so the wealthiest pay their fair share [S3]

taxes.basis: States he will support progressive revenue to make the wealthiest pay their fair share.

spending.basis: Wants to invest in affordability and expand access to services.

housing.basis: Pairs more housing near transit with stronger renter protections and anti-displacement measures.

experience.basis: No elected experience; civil-rights organizer challenging an eight-year incumbent.

immigration.basis: Immigrant protection is a core plank: legal defense funding, due process, and no state facilitation of federal enforcement.

social.basis: Pledges to fight harmful legislation aimed at LGBTQIA+ and other communities; endorsed by Stonewall Democrats.

tech.basis: Supports strong privacy protections so state data systems 'cannot be weaponized against communities'. Data privacy is a pole_b element.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, serving a two-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Thirteen-year Democratic incumbent Mia Su-Ling Gregerson, vice-chair of House Appropriations, faces first-time Republican candidate Yuri Marinchik, who took the second primary slot by 600 votes.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2013, former SeaTac mayor and Appropriations vice-chair, running on state programs she helped deliver such as free school meals and right to repair.
highlights: Cites free school meals for every student, emergency food aid and free transit for kids [S1]
Sponsored the 2025 Right to Repair Act for consumer electronics [S11]
Voted for ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million), ESHB 1296 and rent stabilization [S3][S4][S5]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; no campaign statements on taxes found.

spending.basis: Runs entirely on expanded state programs: universal free school meals, emergency food aid and free youth transit.

housing.basis: Voted for rent stabilization in 2025; no campaign housing statement found.

experience.basis: In the House since 2013, Appropriations vice-chair, former SeaTac mayor, with enacted bills.

tech.basis: Sponsored the Right to Repair Act, which requires electronics makers to provide parts and tools and restricts parts pairing.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no statement of her own on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, the 2025 amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: First-time Republican candidate and small-business owner running against career politicians on lower costs, no new taxes, and public safety.
highlights: Says new taxes will not make things better and the state spends more than it earns [S2]
Calls for lower housing and energy costs and stronger public safety [S1]
Signed the U.S. Term Limits pledge on congressional term limits [S6]

taxes.basis: States new taxes will not make things better; cites car-tab and RTA tax grievances.

spending.basis: Says the state faces a shortfall and is spending more than it earns.

safety.basis: Calls for stronger public safety and cites property crime and break-ins, without stating enforcement or prevention policies.

experience.basis: No elected experience; runs explicitly against career politicians.

reform.basis: Signed a congressional term-limits pledge and frames his run against career politicians.

contests.office_does: One of 98 Washington State Representatives, serving two-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 34th District (West Seattle, Vashon Island, White Center and part of Burien).
contests.race_blurb: House Majority Leader Joe Fitzgibbon, a 16-year incumbent with a climate and tax record, faces first-time candidate Mary Anito, an operations engineer running on fiscal responsibility combined with public investment; both prefer the Democratic Party. Fitzgibbon took 74.5% in the primary.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2010 and House Majority Leader since 2022; led passage of the Climate Commitment Act and Clean Fuel Standard and championed the 2026 millionaires' tax.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 9.9% tax on income over $1 million, and publicly opposes I-645, which would repeal it [S7][S9]
Led passage of the Climate Commitment Act and Clean Fuel Standard; pledges to protect and strengthen the CCA [S1][S3]
Co-sponsored HB 1296 (2025), the parental-rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S5][S6]
Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limit (EHB 1217) [S8]

taxes.basis: Voted for and says he led passage of the millionaires' tax, and publicly opposes I-645's repeal of it.

spending.basis: Cites secured investments in education, healthcare and transit and warns repeal would force 'devastating cuts to education'; also credits himself with stabilizing the budget.

climate.basis: Led passage of the Climate Commitment Act and Clean Fuel Standard and pledges to protect and strengthen the CCA.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limit and pledges renter and anti-displacement protections, alongside support for building more housing near transit.

experience.basis: Sixteen-year incumbent and House Majority Leader with an enacted climate and tax record.

social.basis: Campaign site commits to protecting reproductive freedom and healthcare access; no documented position on gender-identity issues.

parental-rights.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for ESHB 1296, which replaced I-2081's curriculum-examination right and eliminated some medical-service notifications in favor of student-privacy provisions.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and operations engineer (REI, Wayfair, Caterpillar) and small-business owner, running on fiscal responsibility alongside public investment in schools and healthcare.
highlights: Argues 'fiscal responsibility and strong public investment are not mutually exclusive' [S1]
Supports fully funding schools and fixing the levy and equalization structure [S3]
Supports universal-healthcare efforts such as the Washington Health Trust and restoring abortion-access funding [S3]

spending.basis: Explicitly pairs budget balancing and 'fiscal responsibility' with fully funding schools, infrastructure and healthcare.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with a private-sector operations background challenging a 16-year incumbent leader.

healthcare.basis: Supports 'efforts toward universal healthcare, such as The Washington Health Trust' while also emphasizing restoring Medicaid funding.

social.basis: Pledges access to reproductive healthcare including restoring funding for abortion access; no documented position on gender-identity issues.

housing.basis: Campaign site supports building and preserving affordable housing and preventing evictions. That leans toward tenant protection and public investment, and she states no deregulation or market-supply position.

contests.office_does: One of 98 Washington State Representatives, serving two-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 37th District (southeast Seattle, Skyway and part of Renton).
contests.race_blurb: Open seat: Lavender Rights Project director Jaelynn Scott, a Democrat with a detailed progressive platform and endorsements from Bernie Sanders to the House Speaker, faces Independent college student Evon McCorkle. Scott took 88.3% in the primary.

candidates.summary: Executive Director of the Lavender Rights Project and self-described Democratic Socialist; would be Washington's first openly transgender legislator.
highlights: Says she redirected $16 million from jails into supportive housing [S1][S6]
Platform: wealth, capital-gains, corporate and high-earner taxes; a 5% rent-increase cap and social housing [S4]
Supports universal healthcare and defends abortion and gender-affirming care [S1][S4]
Community-based crisis response, independent police oversight and ending qualified immunity [S4]

taxes.basis: Calls for 'taxing the rich': corporate income, capital gains, wealth and high-earner payroll taxes.

spending.basis: Platform calls for universal childcare, universal healthcare, social housing and fully funded schools.

housing.basis: 'Housing is a human right, not a commodity': 5% rent cap, social housing, public and cooperative ownership, TOPA/COPA.

safety.basis: Community-based crisis response, independent police oversight, ending qualified immunity; redirected jail funding to housing.

experience.basis: No prior elected office, but a seven-year nonprofit executive with an organizational record.

immigration.basis: Platform: 'build a real sanctuary for Washington state.'

healthcare.basis: Supports universal healthcare with 'no deductibles, no debt' and the Washington Health Trust.

social.basis: Platform defends abortion and gender-affirming care; leads an organization serving Black trans communities.

tech.basis: Calls for ending mass surveillance and regulating and taxing data-center energy and water use.

candidates.summary: College student studying mathematics and physics and a first-time Independent candidate running on education, housing, healthcare and representation for working-class residents.
highlights: Says he is 'not backed by powerful insiders or political machines' [S1]
Priorities: education funding, housing affordability, affordable healthcare, 'fair tax reform' with financial responsibility [S4]
Has raised $700 and lists no endorsements [S3][S7]

experience.basis: College student and first-time candidate with no prior elected office.

reform.basis: Runs explicitly against 'powerful insiders or political machines' and on restoring trust in government, without specific reform proposals.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 41st District (Mercer Island, Newcastle and parts of Bellevue, Issaquah, Renton and Sammamish), voting on state law, budgets and taxes for two-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: House Deputy Majority Leader My-Linh Thai, in office since 2019, faces Independent Michael Rosen, a Mercer Island attorney running on fiscal discipline and refusing special-interest money. Thai took 66% in the August primary.

candidates.summary: Incumbent since 2019 and House Deputy Majority Leader; a pharmacist and former Bellevue School Board president focused on healthcare access, behavioral health, climate and civil rights.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million (ESSB 6346), which I-645 would repeal [S8]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization (EHB 1217) and the 2026 supportive-housing siting law (ESHB 2266) [S9][S10]
Top priorities: affordable care, behavioral health and 'meaningful action on climate change' [S1]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025); no public position found on the three initiatives [S7]

taxes.basis: Voted yea on ESSB 6346; also cites expanding tax credits and eliminating sales tax on essentials.

spending.basis: Cites securing local project funding and expanding behavioral health, housing and shelter funding.

housing.basis: Voted for rent stabilization and ESHB 2266; cites securing housing and shelter funding.

climate.basis: Lists climate action as a top priority; endorsed by Sierra Club and Washington Conservation Action.

experience.basis: In the House since 2019, now Deputy Majority Leader with eight committee assignments.

local-control.basis: Voted for ESHB 2266, a state requirement that cities allow supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

immigration.basis: Says she has 'fought to defend immigrant families and workers'; endorsed by CAIR Action.

healthcare.basis: Frames healthcare as 'protecting access to affordable and high-quality care' within the current system; no single-payer statement.

social.basis: Endorsed by WA Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and WA Stonewall Democrats; no direct statement on these policies.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; single vote.

candidates.summary: Independent challenger, a Mercer Island attorney, investor and licensed nutritionist without prior elected office, running on fiscal discipline and refusing special-interest money.
highlights: 'Olympia keeps spending more and delivering less'; says state spending 'more than doubled in two decades' [S1]
Calls for 'real fiscal discipline — demanding results from every dollar we spend before asking taxpayers for more' [S3]
'I take no money from special interests'; says he is bound to neither party [S3]
No public position found on the three initiatives [S1][S3]

taxes.basis: Criticizes rising taxes and Olympia 'asking families for more'; no position on specific taxes.

spending.basis: Fiscal discipline is the core of both his pamphlet statement and his general-election profile.

safety.basis: Says people with addiction or mental illness need 'real treatment and recovery, not simply a roof without adequate support': indirect skepticism of housing-first.

experience.basis: No elected experience; first run for office as an independent.

reform.basis: Says he takes no money from special interests and is bound to neither party.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 45th District (Kirkland, Redmond, Woodinville, Sammamish, Duvall), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat after Rep. Larry Springer's retirement. Redmond City Councilmember Vanessa Kritzer, who took 62.75% in the primary, faces Republican John P Gibbons, who filed no pamphlet statement or biography and reports no fundraising.

candidates.summary: Redmond City Councilmember since 2020 and former Council President; executive director of the Washington Association of Land Trusts.
highlights: Supports progressive revenue, including recent taxes on high earners, and is open to an income tax [S5]
Raised Redmond's inclusionary-zoning requirements and created a renter-protections code chapter [S5]
Says "the state should set the floor" on housing, with cities choosing how to meet it [S5]
Lists support for reproductive rights and LGBTQIA+ protections [S3]

taxes.basis: Calls the tax code deeply regressive, supports taxing high earners and is open to an income tax; cites Redmond's head tax.

spending.basis: Would fully fund education, restore childcare and early-learning cuts, and use progressive revenue for sustained investment.

housing.basis: Record on inclusionary zoning, supportive housing and renter protections; supports state rent stabilization, alongside supply-oriented planning.

climate.basis: Calls climate action a moral imperative; record includes Redmond's sustainability plan, net-zero strategy and CCA-funded electric fire engines.

experience.basis: Six-plus years on the Redmond council including Council President; no state legislative record.

local-control.basis: "The state should set the floor" on housing production and affordability, with local flexibility on implementation.

social.basis: Lists standing up for reproductive rights and passing policies affirming LGBTQIA+ rights; supports stronger state anti-discrimination protections.

candidates.summary: Republican candidate who submitted no statement, biography or photo to the voters' pamphlet and lists no campaign website.
highlights: No pamphlet statement or biography submitted [S1]
No PDC financial reports on file as of September 17 [S3]

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 46th District in northeast Seattle, serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Darya Farivar, who won about 89% of the primary vote, faces independent first-time candidate Rodney 'Star' Thornley, who has reported no fundraising.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative, King County ADA and disability-equity specialist, and the first Middle Eastern woman elected to the Legislature.
highlights: Passed legislation stopping stores from blocking new grocers and pharmacies, and legislation expanding the caregiver workforce [S1][S4][S5]
Campaign site backs a wealth tax and calls rent stabilization 'the most important legislation' on housing [S6]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346 (2026) and ESHB 1296 (2025) [S7][S8]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and her campaign site supports a wealth tax.

housing.basis: Calls rent stabilization the most important housing legislation, alongside support for missing-middle housing.

safety.basis: Police-accountability coalition board member; cites behavioral-health response teams and AG police-misconduct investigations.

climate.basis: Supports transit expansion to 'tackle the climate crisis'; no carbon-pricing position.

healthcare.basis: Vision includes 'universal coverage, prioritizing patients over profits', mechanism unspecified.

social.basis: Supports the reproductive-care Shield Law; endorsed by Pro-Choice Washington.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

experience.basis: Sitting legislator with committee leadership and enacted bills; tenure length not documented in the dossier.

candidates.summary: Independent first-time candidate with decades in the Lake Washington Education Association and sports officiating, running against party-line politics.
highlights: Proposes a voluntary state registration credential for undocumented residents, with limits on transfers to ICE [S1][S4]
Proposes a 50% assessment on political contributions to fund voter information [S4]
Would cut B&O taxes on small businesses and says the capital gains tax should be 'reconsidered by voters' [S4]

taxes.basis: Would reduce the B&O tax on small businesses and put the capital gains tax back to voters.

spending.basis: Calls for fiscal accountability and 'a government that listens to citizens before it spends their money'.

housing.basis: Permitting streamlining and preserving single-family zoning, alongside rent caps in mixed-income housing and landlord incentives.

safety.basis: Wants misdemeanors enforced and repeat offenders prosecuted, paired with treatment and housing.

local-control.basis: Would modify HB 1110's state multifamily zoning mandate and give school districts more authority over graduation standards.

reform.basis: Runs as an independent against party-line politics and proposes a 50% assessment on political contributions.

immigration.basis: Supports a state credential for qualifying undocumented residents and a warrant requirement for ICE transfers, excluding new arrivals and people with felonies.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected experience.

tech.basis: Platform says Flock surveillance cameras raise 'legitimate privacy concerns' and need clear access rules: a single clear statement for data-privacy guardrails on surveillance tech (pole_b), without a broader regulatory agenda.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 47th District (Kent, Auburn, Covington and Maple Valley area of South King County), serving a two-year term writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: A rematch of 2024: Democratic incumbent and House Speaker Pro Tempore Chris Stearns faces Republican Ted Cooke, a software tester and longtime party officer. They differ on taxes, parental rights, gender policy, climate and density.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative and House Speaker Pro Tempore; a Navajo attorney, former Auburn City Councilmember and former Washington State Gambling Commission chair.
highlights: Calls reproductive and gender-affirming care 'a human right' the Legislature must protect [S3]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S5]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), the parental-rights amendments I-1 would undo [S6]
Sponsored a clean energy infrastructure bill (HB 1461) signed into law [S2]
Endorsed by Gov. Ferguson, Rep. Adam Smith, the mayors of Auburn, Kent and Covington, and Washington Conservation Action [S1]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million; no separate campaign statement on taxes.

spending.basis: Runs on delivered investment in affordable housing and behavioral health, and pledges to 'fight for investments in families' including universal childcare.

housing.basis: Cites expanding affordable housing as a result and priority; served on the King County Affordable Housing Commission.

climate.basis: Sponsored clean energy infrastructure legislation and is endorsed by Washington Conservation Action; no stated carbon-pricing position.

social.basis: Repeatedly calls reproductive and gender-affirming care a human right, calls Dobbs 'unconscionable', and cites recognition by Pro-Choice Washington.

parental-rights.basis: Single record item: voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

tech.basis: Sponsored HB 1221 on data privacy and security, which passed the Senate.

experience.basis: Sitting House Speaker Pro Tempore and committee vice chair with bills signed into law; former city councilmember.

candidates.summary: Republican software tester and team lead from Covington, a precinct committee officer since 2009 and former King County GOP 2nd Vice Chair. He lost this seat to Stearns in 2024.
highlights: Would freeze new taxes, eliminate taxes on income, property and fuel, and audit every state office [S1]
Would 'restore full parental rights in education' and post school curricula online for parental review [S1][S4]
Pledges to 'uphold the biological definition of gender' [S1]
Would end cap-and-trade and lower or eliminate the gas tax [S4]
Prefers 'starter homes with yards over high-density apartments forced on us by Olympia' [S1]

taxes.basis: Would freeze all new taxes and eliminate income, property and fuel taxes, and wants the capital gains tax eliminated.

spending.basis: Would audit every state office and program, cut waste, and stop increases in government spending.

housing.basis: Would ease the Growth Management Act, streamline permitting and cut taxes to spur building, while opposing state-driven high-density apartments.

safety.basis: Public safety first; would let police act on reasonable suspicion rather than probable cause and keep 'anti-police' members off use-of-force review boards.

climate.basis: Would end cap-and-trade (the Climate Commitment Act's mechanism) and eliminate fuel taxes to cut energy costs.

local-control.basis: Opposes 'high-density apartments forced on us by Olympia', would ease the Growth Management Act, and would end legislative commissions.

social.basis: Pledges to 'uphold the biological definition of gender'; a single repeated pamphlet line, with no other gender or reproductive policy detail.

parental-rights.basis: Would 'restore full parental rights in education', give parents 'oversight of children and education', and post all curricula online for parental review.

experience.basis: Has never held public office; party officer and 2024 challenger.

contests.office_does: One of two Washington State Representatives for the 48th District (parts of Redmond, Bellevue and Kirkland plus the Points communities and Medina), serving two-year terms writing state law and budgets.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: incumbent Amy Walen, who voted against the 2026 millionaires' tax, and Redmond City Councilmember Jessica Forsythe, backed by the district and county Democrats and the State Labor Council. Forsythe finished 17 votes ahead in the primary.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2019, chair of Consumer Protection & Business, and former Kirkland mayor; describes herself as a "pragmatic governing Democrat who works across the aisle."
highlights: Voted no on ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax, calling it unconstitutional and "not progressive enough" while backing a high-earners income tax in another form [S3][S4]
Prime sponsor of bills enabling commercial-to-housing conversions and limiting historic designations [S3]
Says reproductive options and gender-affirming care "are health care" [S3]
Cites banning ICE agents from wearing masks and sponsoring a bill removing citizenship requirements from most professional licenses [S1][S3]

experience.basis: Seven-year legislator and committee chair with an enacted bill record, plus ten years in Kirkland city government.

taxes.basis: Voted against the millionaires' tax and proposed returning most of its revenue through a sales-tax cut, but says she supports a high-earners income tax and a corporate income tax in place of B&O.

spending.basis: Stresses balanced budgets, the credit downgrade and homelessness-authority oversight, while proposing robust childcare funding and "borrow now" infrastructure investment.

housing.basis: Record emphasizes supply and deregulation (conversions, historic-designation limits, occupancy limits), alongside financing tools for public housing authorities.

local-control.basis: Says she carried cities' concerns on missing-middle policy; The Urbanist reports she voted against statewide middle-housing reform.

safety.basis: Combines police-guild endorsement and support for law enforcement training with gun restrictions, police accountability and crisis-response services.

climate.basis: Voted for the Climate Commitment Act and supports low-carbon fuel standards, alongside an all-sources clean-energy list including nuclear and hydrogen.

immigration.basis: Supported the ICE mask ban and limits on ICE entering schools and hospitals without a warrant; sponsored HB 1889 opening professional licenses to non-citizens.

social.basis: Explicit written support for abortion rights and gender-affirming care as insured health care and for self-determined gender identity; cites backfilling Planned Parenthood funding.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296 and says schools have "an essential role" in comprehensive sexual health education and in protecting children "from unhealthy or abusive families."

candidates.summary: Redmond City Councilmember since 2020 and former Council President; small business owner, SEIU member and former Emerge WA executive director.
highlights: Won tenant protections and $7.5M for housing and human services on the Redmond council [S1]
Co-wrote Redmond's Climate Emergency Declaration [S3]
Pledges to fight for the 2SLGBTQIA+ community, immigrant rights and reproductive freedom [S4]
Endorsed by the 48th and King County Democrats, the State Labor Council and former Gov. Inslee [S1][S5]

experience.basis: Six years of municipal office but no state legislative record, challenging a seven-year incumbent.

housing.basis: Emphasizes deeply affordable housing and renter protections, with a call for more housing at all affordability levels.

climate.basis: Co-wrote a climate emergency declaration and net-zero plan; wants to shift debate from upfront costs to the costs of climate change.

safety.basis: Chaired Redmond's alternative crisis response subcommittee and added mental health professionals to the crisis response team.

spending.basis: Calls K-12 underfunded and wants to fully fund education and reduce reliance on local levies.

immigration.basis: Says she fought for immigrant communities and will fight for immigrant rights.

social.basis: Pledges to fight for the 2SLGBTQIA+ community and reproductive freedom; cites safeguarding reproductive rights.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital, and transportation budgets, covering school funding, the tax structure, housing rules, and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: A 2024 rematch: Democratic incumbent Lisa Callan, Capital Budget vice chair since 2019, against Republican Patrick Peacock, an Army veteran and King County GOP vice chair. Callan won the King County primary count 57.7% to 42.3%.

candidates.summary: Incumbent since 2019 and Vice Chair of the House Capital Budget Committee; former Issaquah School Board director and Boeing engineer.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and wants a tax code that "doesn't squeeze working people" [S1][S3]
Pledges to "defend reproductive freedom" [S1]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), the law I-1 would undo [S4]
