taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and campaigns for a tax code that does not squeeze working people.

spending.basis: Campaigns on school funding, youth mental health, childcare and workforce housing investment.

housing.basis: Calls for workforce housing and is endorsed by the Housing Alliance; mechanism not specified.

climate.basis: Pledges to protect forests and clean air; endorsed by Sierra Club and Washington Conservation Action.

experience.basis: In office since 2019 with budget-committee leadership.

social.basis: States she will defend reproductive freedom and is endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no LGBTQ+ or sports position found.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parent and guardian rights list.

candidates.summary: Army counter-intelligence veteran, Boeing security specialist and King County GOP vice chair, running again on no state income tax and lower fuel taxes.
highlights: "No state income tax. Roll back fuel taxes" [S2]
Would cut red tape blocking new home construction [S2]
Endorsed by the 5th LD and King County Republicans [S1]

taxes.basis: Opposes a state income tax in both the pamphlet and on his site and wants fuel taxes rolled back.

housing.basis: Housing plan is to cut the red tape blocking new construction.

safety.basis: Back officers, hold repeat offenders accountable, restore safe streets.

climate.basis: Wants fuel taxes rolled back on cost grounds; no direct climate-policy statement.

experience.basis: Calls himself not a career politician and has not held public office, though he is a county party officer.

parental-rights.basis: Asks schools to respect parents as partners in their kids' education; no notification or opt-out specifics.

contests.office_does: The State Senator is the 30th District's single member of the Washington Senate, voting on state law and budgets and confirming gubernatorial appointments.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Claire Wilson, a former Federal Way School Board director, faces first-time Republican candidate Michael Rutland, a retired Air Force senior master sergeant. The race splits on taxes, school policy, and local control.

candidates.summary: Incumbent state senator and former Federal Way School Board director whose record centers on early learning, childcare, and K-12 funding.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and says millionaires should pay their fair share to fund education [S3][S8]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (the 2025 amendments I-1 would undo) and co-sponsored SB 5599 (2023) on youth shelters and protected health care [S9][S11]
Endorsed by WEA-PAC, SEIU 775, and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates [S15][S16][S17]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 9.9% tax on income over $1 million and says she will support legislation making millionaires pay their fair share to fund schools.

spending.basis: Runs on landmark childcare and early-learning investments and says education is still critically underfunded.

housing.basis: Cites delivering public resources for affordable housing for low-income families and people leaving homelessness.

safety.basis: Pairs votes for police pay raises and training with funding for drug treatment and recovery.

climate.basis: Describes the clean-energy transition as an opportunity and supports transit to reduce air pollution; no specific carbon-policy position.

experience.basis: Sitting senator and former eight-year school board director, against a first-time candidate.

social.basis: Co-sponsored SB 5599 on youth access to gender-affirming and reproductive care, sponsored the LGBTQ Commission, and campaigns on reproductive rights.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 and sponsored district-selected comprehensive sexuality education, while describing her work as empowering parents' voice.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, retired Air Force senior master sergeant and former Boeing manager, running on cost of living, opposition to new income taxes, and local control.
highlights: Pledges to oppose new income taxes and demand budgeting instead of higher taxes [S1]
Calls for protecting local decision-making and reducing one-size-fits-all state mandates [S3]
Endorsed by the King County Republican Party and former 30th LD Senator Mark Miloscia [S4][S6]

taxes.basis: Repeatedly pledges to oppose new income taxes and calls for budgeting instead of higher taxes.

spending.basis: Calls for responsible budgeting and a government that lives within its means.

safety.basis: Supports law enforcement and addressing repeat offenses, while also listing prevention and intervention programs.

local-control.basis: Lists protecting local decision-making and reducing one-size-fits-all mandates as a priority.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected experience, running against a sitting senator.

parental-rights.basis: Says every parent deserves a voice and emphasizes parental involvement and keeping Olympia's 'political agendas' out of schools; no specific notification or opt-out proposal.

climate.basis: Pamphlet pledges to repeal policies 'driving up fuel and grocery prices' [S1]. Pole_a names repealing or paring back fuel-cost climate policy, and this is a single clear statement.

contests.office_does: The State Senator is the 31st District's single member of the Washington Senate, voting on state law and budgets and confirming gubernatorial appointments.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Republican Phil Fortunato, a senator since 2017, faces first-time Democratic candidate Tamara Stramel, a PTA and school-bond organizer. The race splits on spending, taxes, and school and family policy.

candidates.summary: Senator since 2017 and earlier a state representative, running on spending restraint, Second Amendment rights, and parental rights.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million), ESHB 1296 (2025), and ESSB 5599 (2023) [S4][S5][S7]
Proposes zero-based budgeting and funding transportation without raising taxes [S3]
Endorsed by the Association of Washington Business and the King County Republican Party [S12][S13]

taxes.basis: Voted against the 2026 income tax and says families are being crushed by rising taxes; proposes funding transportation without new taxes.

spending.basis: Blames excessive spending and program growth, and proposes zero-based budgets and rolling back budget increases.

housing.basis: Blames regulations, fees, and land-use rules for a 'self-imposed housing crisis' and proposes opening up the state to build all kinds of housing.

safety.basis: Says sidewalk camping cannot be allowed and that people should be removed from the streets into treatment, alongside transitional housing.

local-control.basis: Proposes letting school districts waive costly state mandates.

experience.basis: Senator since 2017 with earlier House service, against a first-time candidate.

social.basis: Voted against ESSB 5599 on youth access to gender-affirming and reproductive care; no further statements found.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296's amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list and campaigns on defending parental rights.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, Democratic precinct officer, and PTA and school-bond organizer from near Lake Tapps, running on infrastructure, school funding, and cost of living.
highlights: Wants the district prioritized in the transportation budget, including Fairfax Bridge funding [S1][S3]
Would change the school funding model and expand free school meals to all schools [S3]
Would support laws prohibiting surveillance and surge pricing [S3]

spending.basis: Says schools are asked to do more with less and calls for expanding free school meals and infrastructure investment.

experience.basis: First-time candidate whose only office is precinct committee officer, running against a long-serving senator.

tech.basis: Supports laws prohibiting surveillance and surge pricing that exploit customers.

social.basis: Endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no stated position on reproductive or LGBTQ+ policy.

contests.office_does: A State Senator writes and votes on Washington state law, the state budgets and tax policy, and confirms gubernatorial appointments, serving a four-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democratic legislators face off: Rep. Cindy Ryu, who calls incumbent Sen. Jesse Salomon too moderate, against Salomon. Both voted for the new tax on income over $1 million; they split on whether to extend it to lower incomes.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2011 and chair of the House technology committee, challenging the incumbent senator from the left on taxes and housing.
highlights: Said in an October KUOW debate she would extend the new income tax to household incomes near $250,000, at a lower rate [S5]
Voted for ESSB 6346 (2026 income tax over $1 million) and for 2025 rent stabilization [S9][S11]
Endorsed by the 32nd District Democrats and WEA-PAC [S13][S14]

taxes.basis: Voted for the $1 million income tax and says she would extend it to households near $250,000; pamphlet asks the wealthiest to pay their share.

spending.basis: Platform centers on investing in public schools, early learning, childcare and transportation; no audit or restraint language.

housing.basis: Voted for rent stabilization and lists rent caps, homebuyer programs and social/mixed-income housing, alongside speeding construction.

climate.basis: Lists advancing renewable energy and green jobs and safeguarding the environment.

experience.basis: Sixteen years in the House, committee chair, with bills signed into law.

tech.basis: Backs AI regulation and a state privacy law, opposes data-center subsidies, and passed a 2025 law on AI-forged likenesses.

social.basis: Calls herself a proud advocate of protecting reproductive rights, decisions for patients and doctors.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, the 2025 amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Two-term incumbent state senator and Local Government Committee chair who supports the millionaires tax but opposes extending it, and pledges to audit spending.
highlights: Pulled SB 6346 (millionaires tax) from Senate Rules and voted for it, but calls a $250,000 threshold "incredibly out of touch" [S6][S7]
Pamphlet pledges to audit spending and expand senior property-tax relief [S1]
Endorsed by the Seattle Times (per his site), AWB and the Snohomish County Sheriff [S4][S14]

taxes.basis: Voted for and backs the $1 million income tax, but rejects extending it and says more revenue should have gone to tax relief rather than the operating budget.

spending.basis: Pamphlet says government must be more responsible with tax dollars and pledges to audit spending.

housing.basis: Wrote permitting and supply bills and also voted for rent stabilization; a genuine mix of both poles.

safety.basis: Describes a balanced enforcement-and-treatment approach, criticizing the Blake overcorrection while backing treatment, housing and officer decertification.

climate.basis: Says he sponsored the Climate Commitment Act and supported a fracking ban and clean-energy investment.

experience.basis: Incumbent senator since 2019 and committee chair with bills passed each session.

immigration.basis: Cites banning ICE face masks and co-sponsoring judicial-warrant and audit-notice protections.

healthcare.basis: Health priorities are price accountability and oversight within the existing system; no universal-coverage proposal.

social.basis: Says he is 100% pro-choice, sponsored SB 5400 shielding providers, and supports a constitutional right to reproductive care.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, the 2025 amendments to the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

tech.basis: Cites leading the fight to block AI-powered rent-setting schemes.

contests.office_does: One of 49 Washington State Senators, serving four-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 36th District (Ballard, Magnolia, Queen Anne and the Greenwood area of northwest Seattle).
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Noel Frame, a co-sponsor of the 2026 millionaires' tax and the Legislature's lead wealth-tax sponsor, faces Republican party officer Jillian England, whose top priority is repealing that tax. Frame took 87.7% in the primary.

candidates.summary: State Senator since 2023 after seven years as the district's State Representative; Vice Chair of Finance on Ways & Means and a leading advocate of progressive tax restructuring.
highlights: Co-sponsored and voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 millionaires' tax that I-645 would repeal [S5][S6]
Prime sponsor of wealth-tax bills since 2021 [S2][S4]
Cites expansion of the Working Families Tax Credit and senior property-tax exemption [S1]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025 parental-rights amendments) and EHB 1217 (2025 rent-increase limit) [S7][S8]

taxes.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for the millionaires' tax, sponsors wealth-tax bills, and calls for the wealthiest to pay their fair share.

spending.basis: Frames new revenue as funding schools, healthcare, human services and early learning, with expanded credits and assistance programs.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limit and cites 'historic investments in affordable housing.'

experience.basis: Ten years in the Legislature with finance leadership in both chambers and an enacted tax record.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which narrowed I-2081's parental notification and records rights; no public statements on the topic.

candidates.summary: Republican challenger, longtime precinct committee officer and 36th District Republican vice chair with a career in computer science and health-care operations; running to repeal the millionaires' tax and the Climate Commitment Act.
highlights: Top priority is repealing the 9.9% 'Millionaires Tax'; also targets the sales and B&O taxes [S1][S3]
Would repeal the Climate Commitment Act and accelerate nuclear and natural gas [S1][S3]
Calls for clearing encampments and for 'exit' programs rather than housing alone [S1][S3]
Campaign posts say she will oppose policies that weaken 'parental rights over minor children' and describe sex as binary [S4]

taxes.basis: Top priority is repealing the millionaires' tax; also targets the sales and B&O taxes.

spending.basis: Calls for cutting 'fraud and wasteful spending' and says 'government force cannot create prosperity, safety, or abundance.'

safety.basis: Calls for clearing encampments, restoring public safety, and funding exit programs; frames homelessness around addiction and 'open tolerance.'

climate.basis: Would repeal the Climate Commitment Act on cost grounds and expand nuclear and natural gas.

experience.basis: No elected office beyond party precinct officer; runs on private-sector experience.

tech.basis: Calls Seattle's data-center moratorium 'Luddite symbolism' and wants to capture AI infrastructure growth.

social.basis: Campaign post calls sex 'binary' and gender-affirming interventions for minors 'elective and irreversible interventions that sterilize.'

parental-rights.basis: Says she will oppose any policy that 'weakens parental rights over minor children,' criticizes shelter notification going to DCYF instead of parents, and says schools should 'educate students rather than indoctrinate them.'

contests.office_does: One of 49 Washington State Senators, serving four-year terms writing state law and the state budget for the 37th District (southeast Seattle, Skyway and part of Renton).
contests.race_blurb: Open seat between two Democrats: Rep. Chipalo Street, who voted for the millionaires' tax and rent stabilization and has broad labor and party backing, and first-time candidate Tatiana Brown, an environmental-justice organizer who refuses corporate and PAC money. Street took 73.8% in the primary.

candidates.summary: State Representative since 2023 and Microsoft technologist, running for the open Senate seat with endorsements from the outgoing senator, the House Speaker, labor unions and the King County Democrats.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax and campaigns on it [S1][S6]
Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limit and cites zoning reform to increase home building [S1][S8]
Cites banning ICE agents from wearing masks and stopping Flock camera surveillance; supports barring ICE from courthouses [S1][S5]
Cites restoring abortion funding; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Advocates Washington and Pro-Choice Washington [S1][S4]

taxes.basis: Voted for and champions the millionaires' tax, calling it 'a one in one hundred year bill.'

spending.basis: Cites $131 million in district capital investments and says the millionaires' tax funds education and healthcare access.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limit and cites 'tenant protections like rent stabilization,' alongside zoning reform to increase home building.

safety.basis: Says 'investment in our communities is the only sustainable path to real public safety' and partners with police-accountability groups; also cites an assault weapons ban.

experience.basis: Sitting legislator since 2023 with an enacted record, but a short tenure compared with long-serving incumbents.

immigration.basis: Cites banning masked ICE agents and maintaining food assistance for immigrants; supports barring ICE from courthouses and a state CDL for immigrants.

social.basis: Cites restoring abortion funding and is endorsed by Planned Parenthood Advocates Washington and Pro-Choice Washington; no documented gender-identity position.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which narrowed I-2081's parental notification and records rights; no public statements on the topic.

reform.basis: Pamphlet statement runs on "unmatched endorsements from labor and environmental advocates"; site lists an extensive party, labor and officeholder coalition.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate, co-chair of the Washington Environmental Justice Council and collaborative-governance strategist, running on progressive revenue, climate justice and community assemblies without corporate or PAC money.
highlights: Rejects corporate, PAC, fossil-fuel and 'war profiteer' donations; small-donor funded [S3]
Wants government-funded community assemblies so 'the people most impacted by public policy should help create it' [S1]
Calls for a statewide moratorium on new hyperscale AI data centers and making data centers pay for their energy use [S4]
Would formally refuse ICE cooperation and champion SB 5906 to 'ICE-proof' schools [S4][S5]

taxes.basis: Wants the wealthiest to pay their fair share; proposes new progressive revenue, closing the data-center sales-tax exemption and a higher top real-estate excise tax bracket.

spending.basis: Pledges to direct investments into the district and fully fund school counselors and social workers, and to defend college grants.

climate.basis: Co-chairs the Environmental Justice Council implementing the HEAL Act, helped shape CCA advocacy, and runs on climate justice.

experience.basis: First run for elected office; community-organizer profile against a sitting legislator.

reform.basis: Refuses corporate and PAC money and campaigns on government-funded community assemblies.

immigration.basis: Would formally refuse ICE cooperation, decommission the Tacoma detention center and pass the SAFE Act to 'ICE-proof' schools.

tech.basis: Calls for a statewide moratorium on new hyperscale AI data centers and for developers to pay for their energy use.

housing.basis: Names affordable housing and anti-displacement as top priorities ('House our community and combat displacement'). She gives no market-supply or deregulation framing.

contests.office_does: One of 49 Washington State Senators, serving a four-year term writing state law, budgets and taxes for the 43rd District (Capitol Hill, University District, Wallingford, Fremont, Eastlake and downtown Seattle).
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, prime sponsor of the 2026 millionaires tax that I-645 would repeal, faces labor communicator Hannah Sabio-Howell, who runs to his left and refuses corporate PAC money. KUOW reports Pedersen took about 66% in the primary to her 23%.

candidates.summary: Senate Majority Leader, in the Legislature since 2007 and general counsel at McKinstry; prime sponsor of the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million.
highlights: Led passage of the Millionaires Tax and a capital gains tax, paired with tax cuts for working families [S1][S11]
Cites banning masked ICE agents and limiting camera surveillance for immigration enforcement [S1]
Leads on marriage equality, LGBTQ+ civil rights and transgender privacy protections; cites abortion rights [S1]
Says he worked to 'defend the Climate Commitment Act' and backed $100 million for police hiring and training [S4]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025); defended the millionaires tax against the repeal effort [S10][S7]

taxes.basis: Prime sponsor of the millionaires tax and the capital gains tax, but paired with tax cuts, with openness to estate-tax rollback and opposition to a payroll-tax fund.

spending.basis: Commits to 'amply funding schools' and cites $1.4 billion more for school districts and $770 million for housing.

housing.basis: Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and cites housing funding, alongside laws streamlining housing construction.

safety.basis: Supported a $100 million police hiring and training investment, alongside license-revocation reform for misconduct.

climate.basis: Says he worked to defend the Climate Commitment Act; cites climate action among accomplishments.

experience.basis: In the Legislature since 2007, Senate Majority Leader, with an enacted signature tax law.

local-control.basis: Voted for ESHB 2266, a state requirement that cities allow supportive housing and shelters in specified zones.

reform.basis: Frames his approach as coalition-building; accepts institutional and union backing and holds a large fundraising lead, against a no-corporate-PAC opponent.

immigration.basis: Cites enacted bans on masked ICE agents and on camera surveillance for immigration enforcement.

social.basis: Long record leading on marriage equality, LGBTQ+ civil rights and transgender privacy; cites abortion rights and Planned Parenthood funding.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yea on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; no statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Former Working Washington communications director and legislative staffer, making a first run for office; wants new corporate and payroll taxes, universal pre-K and non-police crisis response, and refuses corporate PAC money.
highlights: Calls the millionaires tax 'a super important first step'; wants a corporate income tax and a payroll-based Well Washington Fund [S4][S5][S6]
Proposes social workers on non-violent emergency calls and alternatives to incarceration [S4]
'The only campaign in this race not taking corporate PAC money' [S1]
Would restrict AI and surveillance use by law enforcement, 'including the expansion of data centers' [S4]
No public position found on the three initiatives [S3][S4][S5]

taxes.basis: Wants a corporate income tax, a payroll-based fund and reversal of tax cuts for the ultra-wealthy, beyond the millionaires tax.

spending.basis: Proposes universal pre-K, a home-care cash benefit, restored childcare enrollment and social housing investment.

housing.basis: Social housing investment and a tighter rent cap, paired with statewide supply deregulation ('ending apartment bans', cutting red tape).

safety.basis: Non-police responders for non-violent calls, community programs as alternatives to incarceration, restoring use-of-force standards.

experience.basis: No elected office; runs against 'career politicians who protect the status quo'.

local-control.basis: Wants to end apartment bans statewide and build housing 'everywhere', plus a tighter statewide rent cap.

reform.basis: Refuses corporate PAC money, frames the race against corporate deal-making, and supports even-year local elections.

immigration.basis: Would shield data from immigration enforcement, strip incentives from ICE contractors and bar hiring former ICE officers.

healthcare.basis: Supports the state backstopping federal cuts and taking steps toward universal healthcare.

social.basis: Serves on the Pro-Choice Washington PAC board 'to advance reproductive justice'; organized with queer rights organizations.

tech.basis: Would regulate and restrict AI and surveillance use by law enforcement, including the expansion of data centers.

contests.office_does: One of 49 Washington State Senators, serving a four-year term writing state law and budgets for the 46th District in northeast Seattle.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Javier Valdez, a Senate committee chair, faces Republican Sandra Stephens, a retired nurse in her first campaign. Valdez won about 91% of the primary vote.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Senator and chair of the Senate State Government, Tribal Affairs and Elections Committee; in the Legislature since 2017, first in the House.
highlights: Prime sponsor of SB 5855 (2026), banning face-concealing masks for law enforcement including ICE agents; final Senate approval March 9, 2026 [S6]
Voted yes on ESSB 6346 (2026), the tax on household income over $1 million that I-645 would repeal [S9]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), the parents' rights amendments that I-1 would undo [S8]
Says he helped backfill Planned Parenthood funding and supported a cap on rent increases [S1]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346, the millionaires' income tax, and campaigns on having voted to tax millionaires and the very wealthy.

spending.basis: Frames new revenue as paying for free school lunches, small-business tax relief and healthcare investments.

housing.basis: Cites a cap on rent increases alongside zoning reform for more affordable housing.

immigration.basis: Prime sponsor of SB 5855 banning masked ICE and police officers; says he barred federal camera surveillance of immigrants.

social.basis: Says he helped backfill state Planned Parenthood funding after federal cuts; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates.

parental-rights.basis: Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parents' rights law; single vote, no campaign statement on the topic.

experience.basis: In the Legislature since 2017, Senate committee chair, with an enacted record.

candidates.summary: Retired registered nurse and first-time candidate endorsed by the King County Republican Party; her statement centers on alleged corruption and the pro-life position.
highlights: States a belief in 'the sacredness of life'; two terms in the National Association of Pro-Life Nurses (1988-1992) [S1]
Attributes rising taxes and declining services to 'theft of taxpayers funds through unaudited nonprofits' [S1]
Says the King County Republican Party platform represents her policies [S1]

social.basis: States belief in 'the sacredness of life' and served in a pro-life nurses' association.

spending.basis: Centers her statement on unaudited nonprofit funding and misuse of taxpayer money, an audit-first framing.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no public-office record; background is nursing and volunteering.

contests.office_does: One of 49 Washington State Senators, serving a four-year term writing state law and budgets for the 47th District (Kent, Auburn and Covington area of South King County).
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Democrat Claudia Kauffman faces Republican Covington City Councilmember Kristina Soltys. Both talk about affordability and public safety; they split on income taxes, housing policy tools, and state versus local control.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Senator since 2022, who also held the seat from 2007 to 2011; former Muckleshoot Tribe intergovernmental affairs liaison. Running on affordability, housing supply with renter protections, and the safety net.
highlights: Voted yes on ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on household income over $1 million that I-645 would repeal [S5]
Platform says the bottom 20% pay 'SEVEN times more of their income in taxes than billionaires' and proposes cutting property and sales taxes [S4]
Wants more housing supply and protection for renters from 'predatory price gouging' [S1]
Voted yes on ESHB 1296 (2025), the parental-rights amendments I-1 would undo [S6]
Endorsed by Gov. Ferguson, the mayors of Auburn, Covington and Kent, the State Labor Council and Washington Conservation Action [S1][S3][S11]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 millionaires' tax (ESSB 6346) and argues the tax code burdens the poor far more than billionaires, proposing lower sales and property taxes instead.

spending.basis: Emphasizes expanded childcare, a 'robust' safety net and capital investments, without a stated program to expand public spending broadly.

housing.basis: Pairs housing supply with renter protections against 'predatory price gouging' and middle-income housing.

parental-rights.basis: Single record item: voted yes on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

experience.basis: Two Senate stints (2007-2011, 2022-present), committee leadership, and a 2026 legislative record.

candidates.summary: Covington City Councilmember since 2019 and former diagnostic medical sonographer who immigrated from Ukraine as a child. Running against the income tax and recent tax increases, and for permitting reform and police funding.
highlights: Opposes a state income tax ('Washington voters have rejected an income tax ten times') and says Olympia has 'a spending problem' [S4]
Said in July of the income tax repeal effort that an income tax 'doesn't belong here' [S5]
Favors permitting reform and market incentives; says state government should empower local communities rather than impose mandates [S4]
On the council: funded an additional police officer and started a community resource officer program for residents in crisis [S1]
Has raised more than the incumbent: $208.9K in contributions [S6]

taxes.basis: Repeated opposition to an income tax and to recent B&O and gas tax increases; calls the state's problem one of spending, not revenue.

spending.basis: 'Spending problem' framing and demand for budget results, while also backing funding for police and transportation.

housing.basis: Relies on permitting reform and market incentives over state mandates; no tenant-protection or public-housing proposals.

local-control.basis: 'Local communities know their neighborhoods. State government should empower them'; opposes top-down mandates, stated for housing.

safety.basis: Prioritizes fully funded police and more officers, paired with treatment resources and a community resource officer program.

experience.basis: Seven years on a city council but new to the Legislature, running against a long-serving incumbent.

contests.office_does: A U.S. Representative writes and votes on federal law and spending, oversees the executive branch, and serves constituents for a two-year term; the 2nd District covers part of Snohomish County and all of Skagit, Whatcom, Island and San Juan counties.
contests.race_blurb: Thirteen-term Democratic incumbent Rick Larsen, the lead Democrat on the Transportation & Infrastructure Committee, faces first-time Republican candidate Edwin H. Feller. The race contrasts Larsen's ICE-accountability, climate and abortion-rights positions with Feller's lower-tax, enforcement-first and sex-based Title IX platform.

candidates.summary: Thirteen-term incumbent and lead Democrat on the House Transportation & Infrastructure Committee, running on lowering costs, health care access, ICE accountability, abortion rights and infrastructure funding.
highlights: Will not vote for full-year DHS and ICE funding without oversight; voted against the Laken Riley Act [S2][S7]
Calls health care a right and backs universal coverage, with a record of ACA and Medicare cost measures [S2]
Voted for the Inflation Reduction Act and calls climate mitigation a top priority [S2][S8]
Supports the Women's Health Protection Act and cites a 100% voting record on choice [S2]
Voted for the 2024 Israel and Ukraine security supplementals [S9][S10]

taxes.basis: Supports scrapping the cap on income subject to Social Security taxes and voted against the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act; no broader wealth-tax position stated.

spending.basis: Backs expanded child care, a $17 minimum wage, Medicare hearing benefits and infrastructure investment; voted for the Inflation Reduction Act.

safety.basis: On fentanyl pairs 'addiction is a disease' and prevention/recovery funding with strengthening law enforcement against traffickers.

climate.basis: Says mitigating climate change must be a top priority, supports clean energy, and voted for the Inflation Reduction Act.

experience.basis: Thirteenth-term incumbent and lead Democrat on Transportation & Infrastructure, facing a first-time candidate.

immigration.basis: Conditions DHS/ICE funding on oversight, wants ICE body cameras and visible ID, supports ending family detention and private detention, and voted against the Laken Riley Act.

healthcare.basis: States universal coverage as a goal but his record and proposals work through ACA and Medicare; no single-payer proposal.

social.basis: Supports suspending the filibuster to pass the Women's Health Protection Act, cites a 100% pro-choice record, endorsed by Planned Parenthood Action Fund and Stonewall Democrats.

tech.basis: Calls for 'strong guardrails' on data centers so their power and water costs are not passed to ratepayers.

defense.basis: Voted for the 2024 Israel and Ukraine security supplementals while opposing 'reckless foreign wars.'

reform.basis: S2: has voted for legislation to 'end partisan gerrymandering, require disclosure of dark money, expand opportunities to vote' (dark-money disclosure is a named pole-B item).

candidates.summary: First-time Republican candidate and retired HVAC professional from Whatcom County, running on lower taxes, smaller government, enforcement-first immigration and public safety, energy deregulation and sex-based Title IX eligibility.
highlights: Blames the affordability crisis on high taxes and a government grown too large; supports balanced budgets [S1]
Proposes ending sanctuary policies, designating cartels as terrorist organizations and merit-based immigration [S2]
Would dismantle environmental mandates and repeal federal carbon taxes while expanding nuclear and hydro [S2]
Supports defining sex in Title IX as biological sex and a federal ban on irreversible medical procedures for minors [S2]

taxes.basis: Says the affordability crisis comes from taxes being too high and proposes repealing federal carbon taxes.

spending.basis: Supports balanced budgets, says government has grown too large, and lists fiscal responsibility as a priority.

safety.basis: Supports robust law enforcement and a federal Safe Streets mandate tying grants to local cooperation and ending sanctuary policies.

climate.basis: Proposes dismantling 'radical environmental mandates', repealing federal carbon taxes and expanding nuclear and hydro capacity.

experience.basis: Has never held public office and runs explicitly against a long-serving incumbent.

immigration.basis: Supports secure borders, ending sanctuary policies and a merit-based system that ends chain migration.

social.basis: Supports codifying Title IX 'sex' as biological sex in athletics and a federal ban on irreversible medical procedures for minors.

contests.office_does: A Court of Appeals judge hears appeals from superior courts; Division 1, District 2 judges are elected by Snohomish County voters to six-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Linda Coburn, on the Court of Appeals since 2021, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Court of Appeals judge since 2021 and former Edmonds Municipal Court judge and Snohomish County public defender, running unopposed.
highlights: Court of Appeals judge since 2021; Edmonds Municipal Court judge until 2021 [S1]
Former Snohomish County public defender and law clerk at the Court of Appeals and Snohomish County Superior Court [S1]
Member of the Supreme Court's Minority and Justice Commission; Judicial College faculty [S1]

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent Clyde Shavers, a Navy veteran and attorney who has voted against the recent state tax increases, faces Republican Stanwood councilmember Robert (Chili) Hicks, a retired Navy Master Chief. They differ most on parental rights in schools, spending and abortion.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative and Vice Chair of House Education, a Naval Academy graduate and Yale-trained attorney from Whidbey Island who campaigns on lowering costs and not raising taxes.
highlights: Voted no on the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, the 2025 gas-tax package, the services sales tax and the B&O increases [S7][S9][S10][S11]
"I do not support raising taxes" [S3]
Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limits (EHB 1217) and against the 2025 clean fuel standard bill [S12][S13]
Says he is "100 percent pro-choice"; voted for ESHB 1296, the parental-rights amendments I-1 would repeal [S3][S8]

taxes.basis: Voted against the income tax over $1M, the gas-tax package, the services sales tax and B&O increases, and states he does not support raising taxes.

spending.basis: Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget twice; no stated spending philosophy.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limits, and favors incentives for nonprofit affordable-housing development.

climate.basis: Backs a clean-energy economy and fusion research, but voted against the 2025 clean fuel standard bill and the gas-tax package.

safety.basis: General pledge to support law enforcement with resources and tools; no enforcement or prevention specifics.

experience.basis: Sitting representative and Education Committee vice chair, facing a first-term city councilmember.

social.basis: Repeatedly states he is "100 percent pro-choice"; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no record on gender or sports policy.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which amended and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parents' rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Stanwood City Councilmember (elected 2024) and retired Navy Master Chief running on lower taxes, spending audits, enforcement-first public safety and parental rights.
highlights: Proposes lowering the sales tax, repealing the estate tax and stopping new taxes and fees [S3]
Calls for independent audits, public review of every major budget and performance-based funding [S3]
Would restore the original parents' bill of rights, require schools to post curricula and notify parents before non-emergency health services [S2][S3]
Supports police pursuits and a crackdown on fentanyl dealers, with treatment for those ready [S3]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet and platform pledge to lower taxes, cut the sales tax, repeal the estate tax and stop new taxes and fees.

spending.basis: Centers fiscal discipline, independent audits, public budget review and performance-based funding.

safety.basis: Platform centers police pursuits, full police funding, accountability for judges and prosecutors and a drug-dealer crackdown; treatment is secondary.

experience.basis: Local elected experience (Stanwood council since 2024) but no state legislative record, challenging an incumbent.

parental-rights.basis: Would restore the original parents' bill of rights, require curriculum posting, and require parent notice before non-emergency health services.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, including ferry funding, school funding, tax structure and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Four-term Democratic incumbent Dave Paul, chair of House Postsecondary Education & Workforce, faces Republican Tim Hazelo, a Navy veteran and contractor from Oak Harbor. They split on the income tax over $1 million, electric ferries and state spending.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative seeking a fifth term, a Skagit Valley College administrator who chairs the House Postsecondary Education & Workforce Committee.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 gas-tax package; voted against the 2025 services sales tax and B&O increases [S5][S7][S8][S9]
Says he is "fighting to fix our upside-down tax code" [S1]
Prioritizes funding three more electric ferries; voted for the 2025 clean fuel standard bill [S15][S11]
States he is pro-choice; voted for ESHB 1296 [S1][S6]

taxes.basis: Voted for the income tax over $1M and the gas-tax package and backs fixing the 'upside-down tax code', but voted against the 2025 services sales tax and B&O increases.

spending.basis: Voted for the 2025-27 operating budget; no stated spending philosophy beyond protecting college grant funding.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 rent-increase limits and names affordable housing a priority.

climate.basis: Voted for the 2025 clean fuel standard bill and prioritizes electric-ferry funding; endorsed by Sierra Club.

experience.basis: Seeking a fifth term, committee chair, with enacted bills; opponent has never held public office.

social.basis: Pamphlet states he is pro-choice; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates; no record on gender or sports policy.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which amended and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parents' rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Republican Navy veteran, contractor and truck driver from Oak Harbor and former Island County Republican chair, running against income taxes and electric ferries and for spending audits.
highlights: "No income taxes on Washington State residents!" [S3]
Calls for audits and transparency of every dollar spent [S3]
Opposes electric ferries as less dependable and costlier; favors diesel-electric boats [S6]
Would end cashless bail and cut housing regulations [S1]

taxes.basis: Platform opposes any income tax; Herald reports he opposes the millionaires' tax and any tax not approved by voters.

spending.basis: Calls for audits of every dollar, blames unsustainable spending for taxes, and questions social-program spending.

housing.basis: Would cut red tape and regulations he says drive up housing costs; no other housing proposals.

safety.basis: Would end cashless bail and 'catch and release'; no broader public-safety program.

climate.basis: Opposes the state's electric ferries in favor of diesel-electric on cost and reliability grounds.

experience.basis: No elected public office beyond precinct committee officer, challenging a four-term incumbent.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the state budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing and land-use rules for cities, and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: incumbent Strom Peterson, House Housing chair who also sits on the Snohomish County Council, faces Mukilteo Council President Jason Moon, who pledges to give up his city seat. The race contrasts Peterson's state housing mandates and Millionaire's Tax vote with Moon's calls for local control over density and protecting taxpayers.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative and House Housing Committee chair, also a Snohomish County Councilmember and Edmonds small-business owner, whose record centers rent stabilization, supportive-housing siting and gun-safety laws.
highlights: Chairs the House Housing Committee; co-sponsored 2025 rent stabilization (EHB 1217) [S1][S7]
Prime sponsor of ESHB 2266 (2026), requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters [S8][S11]
Co-sponsored and voted for the 2026 Millionaire's Tax [S2][S5]
Campaigns on reproductive freedom and gun-safety laws [S1][S2][S3]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and says he was 'proud to cosponsor and vote for the Millionaire's Tax' to fix an 'upside-down' tax code.

spending.basis: Cites nearly a billion dollars for the Housing Trust Fund and investments in behavioral health, transportation and workforce training.

housing.basis: Co-sponsored rent stabilization (7% plus CPI cap), prime-sponsored supportive-housing siting and highlights Housing Trust Fund investment, alongside supply bills.

safety.basis: Emphasizes gun-safety laws and expanded treatment and behavioral-health services rather than enforcement measures.

climate.basis: Voted for the 2025 clean fuels bill; endorsed by Conservation Action and serves on a coal-opposition board; no carbon-pricing statement.

experience.basis: Sitting House committee chair and county councilmember, former Edmonds council president.

local-control.basis: Prime sponsor of a 2026 law requiring local governments to allow supportive housing and shelters in residential areas; cites state middle-housing legislation.

social.basis: Repeated statements defending abortion rights and pledging to fight for LGBTQ neighbors; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates.

parental-rights.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for ESHB 1296, which amended and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Mukilteo City Council President and business partner running as a Democrat on local control of housing density, protecting taxpayers, law-enforcement staffing and full-time representation.
highlights: Says 'state mandated density threatens the character of our communities' and local governments need more control [S1][S2]
Pledges to protect taxpayers from higher taxes: 'It's not a Revenue problem, it's a spending problem' [S2]
Will resign from the Mukilteo City Council if elected; criticizes the incumbent's two offices [S1][S2]

taxes.basis: Pledges leadership 'that protects taxpayers from higher taxes' and says the state has a spending, not revenue, problem.

spending.basis: Calls for balanced, accountable budgeting while protecting essential services.

local-control.basis: Pamphlet and site both oppose state-mandated density and 'top-down' housing mandates and call for more local control.

safety.basis: Says low law-enforcement staffing 'has to change,' while also calling addiction and homelessness system failures.

experience.basis: City council president running on 'fresh perspectives' against a long-serving legislator; has local but not state office.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the state budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent Lillian Ortiz-Self, House Majority Caucus Chair and a school counselor, faces Libertarian Bruce Guthrie, a retired executive and teacher. Ortiz-Self voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; repealing that tax is Guthrie's top issue.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative and House Majority Caucus Chair, an Everett School District counselor, campaigning on education, behavioral health, child care, immigrant protections and reproductive rights.
highlights: House Majority Caucus Chair; sits on Education and Children, Youth and Families [S1]
Voted for ESSB 6346 and ESSB 5813's capital gains and estate tax changes [S5][S7]
Says she introduced bills on private detention oversight and notice of federal employment-document requests [S2]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list [S6]

taxes.basis: Recorded votes for ESSB 6346 (tax on income over $1 million) and ESSB 5813 (more progressive capital gains and estate taxes).

spending.basis: Says the state needs leadership 'ready and willing to invest in Washington' to backfill federal cuts to services.

housing.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for EHB 1217 rent and fee limits and voted for ESHB 2266 supportive-housing siting.

safety.basis: Pairs expanding behavioral health care and gun violence prevention with 'strengthening and diversifying law enforcement.'

climate.basis: Cites climate action and clean-economy infrastructure and voted for the 2025 clean fuels bill; no carbon-pricing statement.

experience.basis: Long-serving representative and eight-year House Majority Caucus Chair.

local-control.basis: Voted for ESHB 2266, which sets state rules requiring cities to allow supportive housing and shelters.

immigration.basis: Says states must be 'the first line of defense' and that she introduced detention-oversight and ICE-notice bills to protect immigrants.

social.basis: Campaign site states abortion protection is something she has 'long fought for' and must keep fighting for.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which amended and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Libertarian candidate in his seventh campaign, a retired sales and marketing executive and teacher from Edmonds, whose top issue is repealing the state income tax.
highlights: Top issue: 'Oppose/Repeal State Income Tax'; also cut gas taxes and state spending [S1][S2]
Would arrest shoplifters and bike thieves and stop 'subsidizing' homelessness [S2]
Supports barring 'genetic males' from girls' sports in grades 9 and up, school vouchers and legislative term limits [S2]

taxes.basis: Repeatedly calls for repealing the state income tax and cutting gas and other state taxes.

spending.basis: Pamphlet and site both call for cutting record-level state spending.

housing.basis: Blames high rents on property taxes and land over-regulation that limits supply.

safety.basis: Proposes reducing homelessness by arresting shoplifters and bike thieves and ending subsidies.

climate.basis: Opposes the gas tax and says the Climate Commitment Act and cap-and-invest have raised gas prices without helping the environment.

immigration.basis: Would help ICE deport people convicted of crimes but not cooperate in deporting others: a mixed position.

reform.basis: Supports term limits of four terms for legislators.

social.basis: Supports barring 'genetic males' from competing against girls in grades 9 and above.

experience.basis: Has never held elected office; seventh Libertarian campaign.

contests.office_does: A State Senator writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, and the Senate confirms the governor's appointments.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent Marko Liias, in the Senate since 2014 and chair of its Transportation Committee, faces Republican Riaz Khan, a former Mukilteo councilmember. Liias has voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and other progressive tax bills; Khan campaigns on lower taxes, spending restraint and parental rights.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Senator since 2014 and chair of the Senate Transportation Committee, a former state representative and Mukilteo councilmember whose record includes clean-fuels laws, progressive tax votes and student cellphone limits.
highlights: Chairs Senate Transportation; in the Legislature since 2008 [S1]
Voted for ESSB 6346, the 9.9% tax on income over $1 million, and ESSB 5813's capital gains and estate tax changes [S5][S7]
Lists clean fuels, building-emissions and greenhouse-gas tracking laws among his achievements [S3]
Prime sponsor of SB 5346, restricting student cellphone use in public schools [S11]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025), which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list [S6]

taxes.basis: Recorded votes for ESSB 6346 (tax on income over $1 million) and ESSB 5813 (more progressive capital gains and estate taxes), two independent tax votes.

spending.basis: Campaigns on transportation infrastructure jobs and lists school-funding and transportation packages as achievements; no stated restraint agenda.

housing.basis: Cites winning resources for affordable units and voted for EHB 1217 rent and fee limits, alongside calls for more housing near transit.

climate.basis: Lists the Low Carbon Fuel Standard, building-emissions standards and GHG tracking as achievements and voted for the 2025 clean fuels bill.

experience.basis: Senator since 2014, representative 2008-2014, current committee chair and former Majority Floor Leader.

local-control.basis: Says he has demanded more housing near light rail and voted for ESHB 2266's state rules on siting supportive housing and shelters.

tech.basis: Sponsored student cellphone restrictions and says he is working to tax large social media platforms and search engines to fund local news.

immigration.basis: Pamphlet cites advocacy for immigrant neighbors and protecting families from 'dangerous federal policies'; no specific bill cited.

social.basis: Pamphlet cites his advocacy for LGBTQ+ neighbors; no specific policy on gender or reproductive issues cited.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which amended and narrowed parts of the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: Boeing employee and former Mukilteo City Councilmember (2019-2023) running on lower taxes, reduced spending, public safety and parental rights.
highlights: Former Mukilteo City Councilmember and Boeing SPEEA council representative [S1]
Lists 'Lower Taxes' and reducing unnecessary government spending as priorities [S1][S2]
Names protecting parental rights as a priority, without specific proposals [S1][S2]

taxes.basis: Lists lower taxes as a top priority and says Washington's future depends on protecting taxpayers; stated generally, without specific tax proposals.

spending.basis: Supports responsible budgeting and reducing unnecessary government spending, without naming cuts.

experience.basis: One term on a city council and no state office, challenging a twelve-year senator.

parental-rights.basis: Names preserving parental rights as a priority in pamphlet and site, without detail on notification or opt-outs.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent Julio Cortes, seeking a third term, faces Army veteran and nurse Jeff Kelly of the centrist Cascade Party after a primary in which Cortes took about half the vote. Both put affordability first; they differ on the 2026 millionaires tax, rent limits and how to approach public safety.

candidates.summary: Two-term incumbent and City of Everett economic-development manager whose record includes votes for the millionaires tax, rent-increase limits and juvenile diversion standards.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and co-signed a session report celebrating it [S6][S7]
Co-sponsored and voted for the 2025 limit on annual rent increases, while also backing faster permitting [S9][S10][S11]
Cites standardizing juvenile diversion programs and wants more funding for diversion and reentry support [S1][S11]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025 parental-rights amendments) [S8]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 9.9% tax on income over $1 million, co-signed a report calling it historic, promoted it in interviews and would consider lifting the 1% property-tax growth cap.

spending.basis: Defends programs such as early learning and child care but says the state should not fund programs it cannot sustain and should cut low-impact ones: genuinely mixed.

housing.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for the 2025 rent-increase cap, while also calling for cutting red tape and faster permitting to add supply.

safety.basis: Cites standardizing juvenile diversion and wants to shift money from jailing youth and adults to support systems and social-worker programs; also wants police hiring that reflects communities.

climate.basis: Said the state should be more aggressive at targeting major polluters and investing in green technology; single interview statement.

healthcare.basis: Reported by the Herald as among sponsors of a 2025 Washington Health Trust (universal coverage) bill that died in committee; no statement of his own on single-payer.

immigration.basis: Co-signed a session report expressing concern about ICE actions and listing passed bills restricting masked officers and immigration enforcement's use of license plate readers.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2022 seeking a third term, against a first-time candidate; a shorter tenure than a senior legislator.

social.basis: Pamphlet pledges to keep fighting for reproductive rights and lists a Planned Parenthood endorsement; no LGBTQ+ or sports statement.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which modified the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

candidates.summary: First-time Cascade Party candidate, an Army combat medic, registered nurse and north Everett neighborhood chair, running on affordability, law-enforcement funding and spending review.
highlights: Would 'fully fund law enforcement' and treat addiction without 'enabling' it [S1][S2]
Wants lower taxes and a smaller state gas tax, and a fairer 'proportional' tax plan [S1][S2][S4]
Would run cost-benefit reviews of state programs and expects spending cuts [S4]
Favors builder-friendly housing policy and faster permits [S2][S4]

taxes.basis: Lists lowering taxes and a gas-tax cut as priorities, but also calls the system regressive and promises an undefined fairer plan, so not maximal.

spending.basis: Says the Legislature must cut spending and would run cost-benefit analysis of programs, while warning against cavalier cuts.

housing.basis: Would increase housing through builder-friendly policies and streamlined permits; no tenant-protection position.

safety.basis: Would fully fund law enforcement and retail-theft units and treat addiction 'not enable it', while also funding behavioral health services.

climate.basis: Calls for reducing the state gas tax burden at the pump; no position on carbon pricing or clean energy.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected office, from a new third party, running on outsider 'accountability'.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Democratic incumbent Mary Fosse is the only candidate for this seat.

candidates.summary: Incumbent Democratic State Representative and House Deputy Majority Floor Leader, a former Everett City Councilmember, running unopposed.
highlights: State Representative and Deputy Majority Floor Leader; previously on the Everett City Council [S1]
Lists lowering the cost of living, affordable housing, childcare and healthcare access as priorities [S1]
Endorsed by Sen. June Robinson, Sheriff Johnson, SnoCo Democrats, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and the Washington State Labor Council [S1]

contests.office_does: A State Senator writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, and confirms the governor's appointments, for a four-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic incumbent June Robinson, chair of the Senate budget committee, faces first-time Republican candidate Brad Bender; Robinson took about two thirds of the primary vote. The race contrasts Robinson's sponsorship of the 2026 tax on income over $1 million with Bender's call for a low-tax state.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Senator and chair of Senate Ways & Means, in the Legislature since 2013, a public-health professional whose record centers the state budget, tax reform, housing and health care.
highlights: Chairs the Senate Ways & Means (budget) Committee; in the House 2013-2020 and the Senate since 2020 [S5]
Co-sponsored and voted for SB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and prime-sponsored the 2021 capital gains tax [S6][S7][S8]
Pledges to safeguard reproductive rights and defend immigrant and LGBTQ+ neighbors [S1]
Voted for ESHB 1296 (2025 parental-rights amendments) and EHB 1217 (rent increase limits) [S9][S10]

taxes.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for the 9.9% tax on income over $1 million, prime-sponsored the 2021 capital gains tax, and calls asking millionaires to pay a fair share her tax-reform achievement.

spending.basis: Cites record investments in housing, behavioral health, child care and health care and ties tax reform to sustaining public investment; as budget chair she also manages constraints, so not maximal.

housing.basis: Voted for the 2025 cap on residential rent increases, cites record investments in affordable housing and is a former housing consortium director.

immigration.basis: Pamphlet pledges to defend immigrant neighbors; no specific enforcement or sanctuary measures named.

experience.basis: In the Legislature since 2013 and chair of Senate Ways & Means; opponent has never held office.

social.basis: Pledges to safeguard reproductive rights and defend LGBTQ+ neighbors, calls reproductive care a human right, will protect abortion access and objects to attacks on care for transgender people.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296, which modified the I-2081 parental-rights list, and says she helped pass the state's comprehensive sex-education law; no statement on notification or opt-outs.

candidates.summary: First-time Republican candidate, an electrician and small-business owner running on making Washington a low-tax, affordable state.
highlights: Wants Washington to be 'a reasonable, economical, and low-tax state' [S1]
Says Democrats in Olympia raise taxes to cover their own spending [S1]
No prior elected office; over thirty years in the electrical field [S1]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet statement centers lowering taxes and a 'low-tax state'; a single source.

spending.basis: Criticizes state spending as the driver of tax increases; no specific cuts or audits proposed.

experience.basis: States he has no previous elected experience and offers a 'blue-collar voice' against a long-serving incumbent.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering taxes, school funding, housing rules, health policy and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two-term Republican incumbent Sam Low, ranking Republican on House Housing, faces Democrat Kathryn Lewandowsky, a registered nurse and first-time candidate. The race contrasts Low's opposition to the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and his supply-side housing record with Lewandowsky's single-payer health care and tenant-protection platform.

candidates.summary: Registered nurse and former hospital union steward running for office for the first time on single-payer health care, housing as a human right and a pause on data-center growth.
highlights: Supports a universal, publicly accountable single-payer health care system; board officer of Whole Washington and One Payer States [S1][S2]
Calls housing a human right and backs tenant protections and more affordable housing [S1][S2]
Says data-center expansion must stop until privacy and cost protections are law [S3]
Endorsed by Snohomish County Democrats and Washington State Stonewall Democrats [S1][S4]

healthcare.basis: Platform calls for a universal single-payer system; she holds board roles in two single-payer advocacy organizations.

housing.basis: Calls housing a human right, not a speculative investment, and supports expanding affordable housing and protecting tenants from predatory practices.

tech.basis: Says data-center growth must stop until laws protect privacy and make corporations bear the costs, and opposes shifting data-center power costs onto families.

climate.basis: Supports accelerating the clean-energy transition and calls climate stability a right; no stated position on carbon pricing.

experience.basis: Has never held public office; running against a two-term incumbent.

social.basis: Endorsed by Washington State Stonewall Democrats; no statement of her own on LGBTQ+ or reproductive policy.

candidates.summary: Two-term Republican incumbent and former Snohomish County councilmember, ranking Republican on House Housing, running on tax relief, transportation, housing supply and public safety.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and joined the 24-hour House floor fight against it [S2][S3][S4]
Says Washington 'does not have a revenue problem. It has a spending problem' [S3]
Prime sponsor of EHB 1345, allowing detached ADUs outside urban growth areas, signed in 2026 [S3][S10]
Voted against 2025 rent-increase limits (EHB 1217) and the clean-fuels expansion (2SHB 1409) [S7][S8]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346 and ESSB 5814, publicly opposed the income tax and pledges tax relief; multiple independent sources.

spending.basis: Calls the 2026 supplemental budget unsustainable, opposed using pension surplus to ease budget pressure, and says the state has a spending problem.

housing.basis: Blames regulation and permitting for housing costs, sponsored rural ADU legalization, and voted against 2025 rent-increase limits.

climate.basis: Criticizes CCA and fuel taxes as driving costs and wants CCA revenue for roads; voted no on the 2025 clean-fuels expansion.

safety.basis: Lists prioritizing public safety and law-enforcement endorsements; sponsored benefits for families of fallen officers; no detailed enforcement proposals.

experience.basis: Two-term incumbent and committee ranking member, three terms on the county council, 12 bills enacted in 2025-2026.

parental-rights.basis: Voted no on ESHB 1296, which amended the I-2081 parental-rights list; no campaign statement on the topic.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering taxes, school funding, housing rules, health policy and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat left by retiring Republican Rep. Carolyn Eslick. Democrat Ida Keeley, a former juvenile court and child-welfare administrator, faces Republican Steve Ewing, a former Lake Stevens councilmember running on low taxes, balanced budgets and public safety.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate and former juvenile court and DCYF administrator running on affordability, school and special-education funding, and public safety that combines accountability with prevention.
highlights: More than 25 years in court, child-welfare and juvenile-justice administration; founding member of Dawson Place [S1][S3]
Supports staffed, trained law enforcement alongside behavioral-health, treatment and youth-intervention investments [S2]
Supports a pause on new high-capacity data centers and enforceable AI standards [S2]
Pledges to fully fund public schools and special education [S1][S2]

safety.basis: Explicitly pairs law-enforcement staffing and accountability with prevention, treatment and youth-intervention spending.

spending.basis: Wants to expand affordable housing and childcare, protect economic-security programs and fully fund schools, while also stressing stewardship of tax dollars.

tech.basis: Supports a pause on new high-capacity data centers until safeguards exist and enforceable AI standards.

experience.basis: First-time candidate, though with a long public-administration career; opponent has six years of city council service.

candidates.summary: Former Lake Stevens councilmember (2019-2025) and Department of Corrections hearings officer running on low taxes, balanced budgets, public safety and 'normal' government.
highlights: Says he passed balanced budgets and opposed higher taxes on the city council [S1]
Calls for 'taxes that are spent wisely and kept low' [S2]
Calls statewide limits on police 'extremism'; endorsed by WACOPS [S1][S2]
Endorsed by the 39th District's Republican delegation [S1]

taxes.basis: Pamphlet and site both pledge low taxes and say he opposed higher taxes; claims are his own, with no independently reviewed votes.

spending.basis: Emphasizes balanced budgets and taxes 'spent wisely'; no specific cuts proposed.

safety.basis: Calls statewide limits on police an 'extremism' to reverse and is endorsed by WACOPS.

experience.basis: Six years on the Lake Stevens City Council plus planning, health and library boards; never served in the Legislature.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.

candidates.summary: Incumbent State Representative since 2021 and House Transportation vice chair, a Navy veteran whose record centers road safety, emergency preparedness and consumer protection.
