spending.basis: Pairs cutting duplicative technology costs with new courthouse access programs funded mainly by grants and partners.

contests.office_does: The Clark County Council adopts the county budget and property-tax levies, sets councilmanic taxes and fees, adopts the growth-management comprehensive plan and land-use rules for unincorporated areas, and decides which county propositions go to voters.
contests.race_blurb: First-term incumbent Glen Yung, who voted for the 2026 property-tax levy increase and a 0.1% housing sales tax, faces business owner Bryan Shull, who runs on a "tax-last" approach, lower fees and faster permitting, and treatment and accountability in place of housing-first strategies.

candidates.summary: First-term District 1 councilor and former banker and remodeling-business owner who runs on homelessness, housing affordability and public-safety investments.
highlights: Voted for the 1% general-fund levy increase in the 2026 county budget [S5]
Voted for the 0.1% sales tax for affordable housing and behavioral health: "we are experiencing a housing crisis" [S6]
Secured funding for a 120-bed shelter with integrated addiction and mental-health treatment [S1]
Backs "a balanced approach that addresses both crime and the root causes behind it" [S4]
Voted with the full council to put the Proposition 12 jail bond and Proposition 13 levy lid lift on the ballot [S8]

taxes.basis: Voted for the 2026 1% levy increases with banked capacity and for the 0.1% councilmanic housing sales tax, citing rising service costs and the housing crisis.

spending.basis: Pushes investment in shelter, treatment and housing now, while also citing a county-manager performance review and responsible budgeting.

housing.basis: Pairs public funding (housing sales tax) and mobile-home-park protections with supply measures (middle housing, faster permitting).

safety.basis: Explicitly balances law-enforcement investment and body cameras with treatment-linked shelter and root-cause approaches.

experience.basis: First-term incumbent running on his council record.

candidates.summary: Vancouver brewery and small-business owner and renewable-energy engineer, president of the Uptown Village Association, running for office for the first time.
highlights: Supports a "tax-last" approach: responsible budgeting before asking taxpayers to pay more [S1]
"We must address out of control spending" [S2]
Would cut permit fees and wait times and address fees and land-use rules that raise housing costs [S2]
Would replace housing-first and harm-reduction strategies with more treatment and accountability [S2]

taxes.basis: Repeatedly calls tax increases a burden and taxes a last resort after budget reprioritization, without pledging no new taxes.

spending.basis: Calls for addressing "out of control spending" and reprioritizing funds to core services before new revenue.

housing.basis: Housing plan centers on lower fees, streamlined permitting and land-use changes.

safety.basis: Supports law enforcement and wants treatment and accountability in place of housing-first and harm reduction.

climate.basis: Renewable-energy engineer who backs clean energy but frames it around affordability and reliability.

experience.basis: Political newcomer with business and nonprofit leadership but no public office.

contests.office_does: The Clark County Council adopts the county budget and property-tax levies, sets councilmanic taxes and fees, adopts the growth-management comprehensive plan and land-use rules for unincorporated areas, and decides which county propositions go to voters.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Michelle Belkot, who cast the lone votes against the 2026 levy increase and the housing sales tax, faces teacher John Zingale, who says the county should use its allowed 1% levy increase and invest in roads, parks, housing and social services.

candidates.summary: First-term District 2 councilor, a military veteran and former federal procurement official who runs on no new taxes, opposition to annexation and light-rail tolls, and law-enforcement funding.
highlights: Only council vote against the 1% general-fund levy increase in the 2026 budget [S4]
Lone vote against the 0.1% housing sales tax, citing no spending plan [S5]
Prioritizes law enforcement, fire and infrastructure "before expanding programs or increasing spending" [S1]
Opposes light-rail taxes and tolls and Vancouver annexation of District 2 [S2]
Moved the resolution placing the Proposition 12 jail bond on the ballot [S6]

taxes.basis: Recorded no votes on the 2026 levy increase and the housing sales tax, and a "No New Taxes" platform.

spending.basis: Core services before program growth and demands a tracking and spending plan before new revenue, while backing public-safety funding.

housing.basis: Opposes impact fees and new development fees and voted against the housing sales tax, though she voted to extend the mobile-home-park moratorium.

safety.basis: Repeatedly puts law-enforcement funding first and says she stands with local, state and federal law enforcement.

experience.basis: First-term incumbent in office since 2023 running on her council record.

candidates.summary: Middle-school history teacher, 2026 Southwest Washington Teacher of the Year and teachers' union representative, running for office for the first time.
highlights: Says skipping the allowed 1% property-tax increase contributed to the deficit and "we do need to find ways to increase revenue" [S3]
Names roads, parks, public safety and housing as spending priorities and would explore a metropolitan park district [S3]
Favors building "up, not out" with a mix of housing sizes [S3]
Endorsed by Councilors Sue Marshall and Wil Fuentes, Sen. Adrian Cortes and Vancouver Mayor Anne McEnerny-Ogle [S4]

taxes.basis: Supports using the 1% annual levy increase and finding new revenue to avoid service cuts.

spending.basis: Calls for investing in social services, infrastructure and parks and warns budget cuts threaten essential services.

safety.basis: Wants a holistic, affordability-centered approach to homelessness and more behavioral-health capacity rather than a drug-use framing.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with no elected public office; teacher and union representative.

contests.office_does: The Clark County Council adopts the county budget and property-tax levies, sets councilmanic taxes and fees, adopts the growth-management comprehensive plan and land-use rules for unincorporated areas, and decides which county propositions go to voters.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat left by Council Chair Sue Marshall. Battle Ground councilor and former mayor Troy McCoy faces Charter Review Commissioner Peter Silliman; both stress public safety and caution on taxes, but split on a charter amendment requiring a council supermajority for taxes and on growth regulation.

candidates.summary: Battle Ground city councilor, former mayor and former school board president, and a small-business owner, who stresses managed growth, jail capacity and collaboration.
highlights: "I don't think there's a lot of room for tax increases"; opposes the tax-supermajority charter amendment as too high a bar [S9]
As mayor, voted with the unanimous Battle Ground council for a 0.1% public-safety sales tax to add police officers [S8]
Calls current jail capacity unacceptable and wants outside funding pursued before taxpayers [S3]
Opposes industrial development on farmland and in rural Brush Prairie [S3]
Endorsed by The Columbian and Council Chair Sue Marshall [S11][S6]

taxes.basis: Cautions against tax increases and wants outside funding first, but voted as mayor for a councilmanic police sales tax and opposes a tax supermajority.

safety.basis: Emphasizes police staffing, equipment and jail capacity within what he calls a holistic approach.

experience.basis: School board, city council and mayoral record; runs on "proven and effective leadership."

candidates.summary: Elected Charter Review Commissioner, former county council policy analyst and communications consultant, and a Republican precinct committee officer, running on tax restraint, budget accountability and law enforcement.
highlights: Criticizes the council's maximum levy increases and sales tax; supports requiring four of five councilors to raise taxes [S5][S17]
Chairs the committees for Charter Amendments 20 (budget transparency) and 27 (performance audits), which he sponsored; opposes Charter Amendment 22 [S11][S12][S13]
Would revisit county GMA restrictions beyond state law and limit permitting timelines [S3]
Co-sponsored a charter amendment to require deputy staffing; "citizens must elect unapologetically pro law enforcement representatives" [S9][S6]

taxes.basis: "Protection from tax increases" platform, criticism of maximum levy and sales-tax increases, and support for a council tax supermajority.

spending.basis: Authored the performance-audit and budget-transparency amendments and pledges to find non-essential services to cut.

housing.basis: Attributes high home costs to GMA, impact fees, zoning, permitting and building codes and would roll back county requirements beyond state law.

safety.basis: Co-sponsored a charter mandate for deputy staffing and calls for "unapologetically pro law enforcement" officials.

experience.basis: Cites county-office and charter-commission experience to "hit the ground running" while campaigning on "Leading for a Change"; has not held a governing seat.

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Kristen L. Parcher is the only candidate for Department 1.

candidates.summary: District Court judge in Department 1 since 2018 and a court commissioner from 2011 to 2018; the only candidate.
highlights: Department 1 judge since 2018; District Court commissioner 2011-2018 [S1]
Former indigent defense attorney with Vancouver Defenders and family law attorney [S1]

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Chad E. Sleight is the only candidate for Department 2.

candidates.summary: District Court judge since March 2017 (appointed by the County Council, re-elected 2018 and 2022) and a former city prosecutor; the only candidate.
highlights: Appointed to the bench by the Clark County Council in 2017; re-elected 2018 and 2022 [S1]
Prosecutor for Battle Ground, Ridgefield and La Center 2009-2017; pro tem judge 2013-2017 [S1]

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge James B. Smith is the only candidate for Department 3.

candidates.summary: District Court judge since 2021 (appointed, elected 2022), assistant presiding judge overseeing Veterans Therapeutic Court, and a former deputy prosecutor; the only candidate.
highlights: Appointed in 2021, elected 2022; assistant presiding judge [S1]
Oversees the Veterans Therapeutic Court program [S1]
Sixteen years as a deputy prosecutor in Cowlitz and Clark counties [S1]

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Leslie A. Lopez is the only candidate for Department 4, on the ballot for both the short and the full four-year term.

candidates.summary: District Court judge since 2025, after serving as court commissioner and chief civil deputy prosecutor; on the ballot for the short and full four-year term. The only candidate.
highlights: District Court judge since 2025; commissioner 2024-2025 [S1]
Chief Civil Deputy in the Clark County Prosecutor's Office 2021-2024 [S1]
On the ballot for both the short and the full four-year term [S2]

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Megan D. Peyton is the only candidate for Department 5, on the ballot for both the short and the full four-year term.

candidates.summary: Appointed by the Clark County Council and on the District Court bench since January 2026, after a career in indigent defense; on the ballot for the short and full term. The only candidate.
highlights: Appointed by the County Council; on the bench since January 2026 [S1]
Indigent defense attorney in Clark County from 2007 [S1]
On the ballot for both the short and the full four-year term [S2]

contests.office_does: District Court judges hear misdemeanor and gross misdemeanor criminal cases, traffic infractions, civil suits up to $100,000, small claims, protection orders and felony first appearances for Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Abigail E. Bartlett is the only candidate for Department 6.

candidates.summary: District Court judge since 2021, previously a court commissioner and senior deputy prosecutor; presides over Treatment Alternative Court and DUI Court. The only candidate.
highlights: District Court judge since 2021; commissioner 2017-2021 [S1]
Senior deputy prosecutor 2006-2017 [S1]
Presides over Treatment Alternative Court and DUI Court [S1]

contests.office_does: The prosecuting attorney runs the Clark County Prosecuting Attorney's Office, which charges and prosecutes felonies countywide and misdemeanors in unincorporated areas, and is the county government's civil lawyer.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Senior Deputy Prosecutor Laurel Smith is the only candidate for this open office.

candidates.summary: Senior deputy prosecutor in the Clark County Prosecuting Attorney's Office since 2012, supervising domestic violence and child abuse units; the only candidate.
highlights: Clark County deputy prosecutor since 2012, supervising specialized units including domestic violence and child abuse [S1]
Judge pro tempore in Clark County District Court since 2022 [S1]
Pledges to hold offenders accountable while using 'smart, evidence-based approaches' [S1]

contests.office_does: The sheriff runs the Clark County Sheriff's Office, which patrols unincorporated Clark County, investigates crimes, serves civil process and warrants, and operates the county jail.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: incumbent Sheriff John Horch, elected in 2022, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Incumbent Clark County Sheriff seeking a second term; previously the office's enforcement chief and drug task force commander. The only candidate.
highlights: Sheriff for the past four years; formerly enforcement chief, drug task force commander and FBI organized-crime task force member [S1]
Cites added patrol and investigations staffing, a body-worn camera program and a regional police academy [S1]
Says increasing deputy staffing remains his top priority; the office is among the lowest-funded in the state by officer-to-citizen ratio [S1]

contests.office_does: The treasurer collects property taxes for the county and its taxing districts, invests public funds, and manages the county investment pool and debt.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: incumbent Treasurer Alishia Topper, in office since 2019, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Clark County Treasurer since 2019 and a former Vancouver city councilmember; the only candidate.
highlights: Treasurer since 2019; Vancouver City Council 2014-2018 [S1]
Says the county investment pool exceeds $1 billion and allocated a record $47 million in interest last year [S1]
Reports clean financial and performance audits with no findings [S1]

contests.office_does: The U.S. Representative for Washington's 3rd District votes on federal law, taxes, spending and oversight for Southwest Washington, including Clark County.
contests.race_blurb: Two-term Democrat Marie Gluesenkamp Perez, who often votes across party lines, faces state Senate Republican Leader John Braun in a toss-up district; they finished within 0.2 points of each other in the initial primary count, and a late-September poll had them within the margin of error. They differ most on taxes, abortion, energy and money in politics, with closer overlap on border enforcement and defense.

candidates.summary: Republican state Senate leader from the 20th District, retired Navy captain and Chehalis manufacturer, running on lower taxes, border security and domestic energy.
highlights: Voted against the 2026 state tax on income over $1 million, the 2025 state tax package and the 2021 capital gains tax [S6][S7][S9]
Pledges to cut waste and lower taxes; says Olympia has "an unsustainable spending problem" [S16]
Would complete border barriers, hire more agents and tighten asylum rules [S2]
Described as a consistent anti-abortion vote in the state Senate; supports sex-based eligibility in women's sports [S15]
Endorsed by President Trump, Speaker Mike Johnson and Majority Leader Steve Scalise [S14]

taxes.basis: Voted against the 2026 income tax over $1M, the 2025 tax package and the 2021 capital gains tax, and pledges to lower federal taxes.

spending.basis: Repeatedly pledges to cut waste and unnecessary spending and says a spending problem cannot be solved with new revenue.

safety.basis: 'Compassion with consequences': shut down open-air drug markets and back camping bans, paired with funding detox and mental-health beds.

climate.basis: All-of-the-above energy platform including oil and gas, and voted twice against the 2021 Climate Commitment Act.

immigration.basis: Campaign centred on border barriers, more agents, tighter asylum rules and cartel interdiction; Trump's endorsement cited his border advocacy.

defense.basis: Supports 'a lethal, modern force' and rebuilding the defense industrial base, and faults his opponent on defense funding.

social.basis: Consistent anti-abortion Senate record, says he hopes to change the state's abortion law someday, and backs sex-based eligibility in women's sports.

reform.basis: Describes governing as coalition-building within the system and takes leadership PAC money; no PAC, stock-trading or term-limit reform position found.

experience.basis: Thirteen years in the state Senate, Senate Republican Leader since 2020, former Ways and Means chair.

candidates.summary: Two-term Democratic congresswoman and auto-shop co-owner from Skamania County who often crosses party lines on enforcement, energy and defense votes.
highlights: Voted against the 2025 federal tax and spending law (H.R. 1) [S5][S6]
Voted for the Laken Riley Act, the SAVE Act and the 2026 Homeland Security appropriations, each with few other Democrats [S7][S8][S9]
Pro-choice; voted against federal women's sports bills but for barring Medicaid funding of gender transition for minors [S2][S12][S17]
Voted for both recent NDAAs and for War Powers limits on the Iran war [S20][S21][S23]
Refuses corporate PAC money and introduced congressional stock-trading ban and pay-freeze bills [S1]

taxes.basis: Voted against the 2025 federal tax cuts but backs an expanded Child Tax Credit and a family-farm capital gains exemption, and has taken no stand on the state income tax.

spending.basis: Says the budget must be balanced and backs a fiscal commission and a 3%-of-GDP deficit cap, though she voted against the 2025 rescissions bill.

safety.basis: Calls for stricter punishment for drug sale and possession alongside treatment, and voted for two Republican crime bills most Democrats opposed.

climate.basis: Says climate change is man-made and backs efficiency rebates, but voted with Republicans against California's clean-car waiver and for oil, gas and LNG bills.

immigration.basis: Voted for the Laken Riley Act, SAVE Act and 2026 DHS appropriations, but against H.R. 2 (2023) and the Deporting Fraudsters Act.

healthcare.basis: Would protect Medicare and Medicaid, cut out middlemen and speed generic drugs; no single-payer position found.

defense.basis: Voted for the FY2026 and FY2027 NDAAs and Ukraine aid, while voting for War Powers resolutions to end U.S. hostilities with Iran.

social.basis: Pro-choice and voted against federal sports-eligibility and gender-care criminalization bills, but voted to bar Medicaid funding of gender transition for minors.

reform.basis: Refuses corporate PAC money, introduced stock-trading ban and pay-freeze bills, and is endorsed by End Citizens United.

experience.basis: Two-term incumbent on the House Appropriations Committee who presents herself as independent of her party.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two-term Republican Rep. Kevin Waters, a former Port of Skamania commissioner, faces Democrat Ben Christly, a Navy veteran and flight nurse on the county charter review commission. Waters has voted against the 2025 and 2026 tax bills and the operating budget; Christly campaigns on school funding and asking large corporations to pay more.

candidates.summary: Navy veteran, flight nurse and former small-business owner who sits on the elected Clark County Charter Review Commission, running on school funding, early learning, housing and health-care access.
highlights: Says working families and small businesses carry too much of the tax burden while "billion-dollar corporations" avoid theirs [S2]
Wants to fully fund public schools and expand preschool, pre-kindergarten and trade programs [S2]
Elected Clark County Charter Review Commissioner; first run for the Legislature [S5][S1]
Endorsed by the Washington Education Association PAC, the state labor council, Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and Pro-Choice Washington [S4]

taxes.basis: Calls for a 'fair and responsible tax structure' in which large corporations pay more and working families less; no position on the income tax over $1 million.

spending.basis: Defines responsible budgeting as investing in schools, health care and economic opportunity, including fully funding schools and expanding early learning.

social.basis: No direct statement; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and Pro-Choice Washington.

experience.basis: First legislative run; his only office is an elected seat on the county charter review commission, against a two-term incumbent.

candidates.summary: Two-term Republican incumbent from Stevenson, executive director of the Skamania Economic Development Council and founder of Backwoods Brewing, running on infrastructure, schools and public safety.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 and the 2025 capital gains, excise and B&O tax bills [S3][S5][S6][S7]
Offered an amendment to expire the 2025 services taxes on July 1, 2026; it failed 42-53 [S4]
Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget and says the state has "a results problem" [S8][S15]
Voted against rent-increase limits, the clean fuels expansion and ESHB 1296's changes to the parental-rights law [S9][S10][S11]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346 and three 2025 revenue bills, sponsored an amendment to expire the 2025 services taxes, and his campaign site promises tax cuts.

spending.basis: Voted twice against the 2025-27 operating budget and criticized spending past $80 billion, while also faulting the majority's education cuts.

housing.basis: Voted against limits on rent and fee increases (EHB 1217); pamphlet backs 'practical solutions' to expand affordable housing.

safety.basis: Supports law enforcement; campaign site calls for fully funding police and giving them tools for the fentanyl crisis.

climate.basis: Voted against the 2025 clean fuels program bill (2SHB 1409) on House passage and final passage.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296, which changed the parental rights enacted by Initiative 2081; no position on I-1 found.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2023 and Port of Skamania commissioner 2010-2019; challenger has not held legislative office.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: First-term Republican Rep. David Stuebe, also mayor of Washougal, won the seat by under 900 votes in 2024 and faces Democrat Diana H. Perez, a Vancouver city councilor and retired Forest Service manager. Stuebe campaigns on no new taxes and spending limits; Perez pairs state housing investment with permitting reform and backs the clean-energy transition with cost caveats.

candidates.summary: Vancouver city councilor since 2022 and former state parks and housing finance commissioner, with 30-plus years in Forest Service natural-resource management, running on housing costs, infrastructure, schools and public safety.
highlights: Would increase state investment in affordable housing while cutting permitting delays and regulatory barriers [S3]
Cast the only council vote against Vancouver's 0.1% public-safety sales tax, citing the cumulative tax burden [S8]
Says climate change is real and the energy transition must not jeopardize grid reliability or raise utility costs [S3]
Recommended by The Columbian's editorial board [S6]

spending.basis: Pledges 'living within our budgetary means' and fiscal responsibility alongside more state investment in housing, schools and infrastructure.

housing.basis: Combines more state investment in affordable housing and homelessness prevention with reducing permitting delays and regulatory barriers.

safety.basis: Wants adequate law-enforcement staffing alongside prevention, behavioral health and victim support: 'both immediate response and long-term prevention.'

climate.basis: Calls the clean-energy transition essential but says it must not jeopardize grid reliability or raise utility costs.

experience.basis: No legislative tenure, but a sitting city councilor since 2022 and former state commissioner, running against a first-term legislator.

candidates.summary: First-term Republican incumbent, mayor of Washougal and retired Marine Corps colonel, running on lowering costs, public safety and holding state government accountable.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 and the 2025 revenue bills; says "I voted no on a state income tax" [S3][S5][S6][S7][S1]
Offered an amendment to cut the state sales tax from 6.5% to 5%; it failed 43-52 [S4]
Calls for no new taxes, a two-thirds vote to raise them and tying budget growth to inflation and population [S15]
His bill HB 2531, on ambulance Medicaid funding, was signed in 2026 [S16]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346 and three 2025 revenue bills, sponsored a sales-tax cut amendment and calls for no new taxes and a two-thirds vote to raise them.

spending.basis: Says the state has 'a spending problem,' wants budget growth tied to inflation and population, programs without returns cut, and voted against the 2025-27 budget.

housing.basis: Voted against limits on rent and fee increases (EHB 1217) and faults the majority for no regulatory relief to speed housing construction.

safety.basis: Counts blocking shorter sentences for serious crimes and limits on local camping-law enforcement as wins; pamphlet commits to strengthening public safety.

climate.basis: Voted against the clean fuels program bill (2SHB 1409) and counts blocking a data-center energy tax and a wildfire utility surcharge as wins.

healthcare.basis: Wants Medicaid access and 2025 Medicaid funding restored and more support for rural hospitals within the current system; sponsored an ambulance Medicaid bill.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296, which changed the parental rights enacted by Initiative 2081; no position on I-1 found.

experience.basis: First-term legislator and sitting Washougal mayor, running against a city councilor without legislative tenure.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two-term Republican Rep. Stephanie McClintock, a former Battle Ground School Board member, faces Democrat Randi L. Knott, a first-time candidate with a public-policy career; they split most clearly on the tax on income over $1 million, which McClintock voted against and Knott supports.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate with more than 25 years of public-policy work, a former Brush Prairie bed-and-breakfast and horse-ranch owner, and a disability advocate, running on affordability, special-education funding and health care.
highlights: Says the ultra-wealthy need to be taxed and called the millionaire tax bill "drafted very well" [S6]
Calls for fully funded special education and infrastructure investments that keep pace with growth [S3]
Says health care is a human right and supports universal health-care solutions [S3]
Serves on the Clark County Developmental Disabilities Advisory Board; has not held elected office [S1][S4]

taxes.basis: Says the ultra-wealthy need to be taxed to fund schools and praises the millionaire tax bill; pamphlet opposes policies that protect the wealthy and big corporations.

spending.basis: Calls for fully funded special education, infrastructure investment and restored Medicaid funding, framed as 'economically progressive policies that are fiscally responsible.'

healthcare.basis: Calls health care a human right and supports 'universal healthcare solutions that reduce cost and complexity', without naming a single-payer system.

experience.basis: First-time candidate running against a two-term incumbent, though with a long public-policy career and board appointments.

candidates.summary: Two-term Republican incumbent, ranking member on House Consumer Protection and Business and former Battle Ground School Board member, running on lower taxes, law enforcement and K-12 accountability.
highlights: Voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 B&O and transportation revenue bills [S5][S6][S7]
Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget and the 2026 supplemental budget [S8][S9]
Campaigns on law-enforcement funding, restoring police pursuit and sex-offender registration bills [S1][S2][S13]
Co-sponsored HB 1699 on sex-separated girls' school sports and voted against ESHB 1296, which amended the 2024 parents' rights law [S11][S14]
Endorsed by The Columbian editorial board [S16]

taxes.basis: Voted against ESSB 6346, ESHB 2081 and ESSB 5801, co-sponsored bills repealing 2025 tax increases, and says she opposes the income tax.

spending.basis: Voted against both operating budgets and pledges to oppose 'reckless spending' and demand accountability, while naming special education and Medicaid as budget priorities.

housing.basis: Voted against EHB 1217, the 2025 limit on residential rent and fee increases.

safety.basis: Calls for fully funding law enforcement and restoring police pursuit; prime-sponsored sex-offender registration bills and co-sponsored encampment-removal funding.

social.basis: Co-sponsored HB 1699, letting schools bar biologically male students from girls' sports; no recorded position on abortion or gender-affirming care.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296, which amended the parents' rights enacted by I-2081, and describes herself as a champion of parental involvement as a school director.

tech.basis: Says AI is better handled federally and that differing state regulations create challenges for businesses.

experience.basis: Two-term incumbent, ranking committee member and former school director with an enacted prime-sponsored bill (SHB 1121).

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: First-term Republican Rep. John Ley faces Democrat Deken Letinich, a Laborers union political director, in a race shaped by the Interstate 5 Bridge replacement, which Ley opposes as planned and Letinich supports, and by the tax on income over $1 million, which Ley urges voters to repeal.

candidates.summary: Assistant political and legislative director for the Washington/Northern Idaho District Council of Laborers and former construction laborer, running on affordability, childcare, school funding and building the I-5 Bridge.
highlights: Supports taxing income above $1 million and opposes lowering the threshold [S6]
Pamphlet: "It's time to build the bridge, build more housing and build more childcare facilities" [S1]
Wants smaller class sizes, more school counselors and expanded Pre-K and ECEAP [S3]
States he is pro-choice [S1]
Endorsed by The Columbian editorial board and a slate of building-trades unions [S8][S4]

taxes.basis: Supports the tax on income over $1 million and wants the 'extremely wealthy' to pay their fair share, while opposing a lower threshold.

spending.basis: Calls for more education funding, smaller classes, more school staff, expanded Pre-K and ECEAP, and new infrastructure funding.

safety.basis: Cites a 'clear need for necessary and appropriate funding' for police, firefighters and emergency medical professionals.

healthcare.basis: Proposes clinic funding, workforce training and tougher drug-price negotiations within the existing system; no single-payer position.

social.basis: Pamphlet states 'I'm Pro-Choice'; no position found on sports eligibility or gender-affirming care.

tech.basis: Says the state should require reinvestment in communities where data centers use local resources.

experience.basis: Has not held elected office; challenging a first-term incumbent after a career as a union organizer.

candidates.summary: First-term Republican incumbent, retired Delta Air Lines captain and Air Force veteran, and former Clark County Today reporter, running against the income tax, tolls and light rail on the I-5 Bridge, and state spending growth.
highlights: Voted against the tax on income over $1 million and urges a yes vote on I-645 to repeal it [S7][S4]
Proposes capping state budget growth to household income and population and auditing state programs [S3]
Opposes tolls, light rail and the current I-5 Bridge replacement plan [S1][S19]
Co-sponsored bills restricting gender-transition care for minors and allowing sex-based eligibility in girls' sports [S16][S17]
Campaigns to "restore parental control over children's education" and voted against ESHB 1296 [S1][S13]

taxes.basis: Voted against ESSB 6346 and ESHB 2081, urges a yes vote on I-645, and pledges to 'End state income tax' and exempt $250,000 of home value from property tax.

spending.basis: Proposes capping budget growth and auditing programs, says the state has 'a spending problem', and voted against both operating budgets.

housing.basis: Would modify the Growth Management Act to allow smaller parcels, ties affordability to property-tax cuts, and voted against the 2025 rent-increase limit.

safety.basis: Pledges to fund more police and stop 'catch and release'; supports the three-strikes law and jail for drug dealers.

climate.basis: Would end the carbon tax, backed the 2024 initiatives to repeal it and to stop natural-gas restrictions, and co-sponsored HB 1324 on transportation funding and the CCA.

local-control.basis: Criticizes the Growth Management Act as a barrier to development and wants it modified to allow smaller acreages.

reform.basis: Pamphlet pledges to 'Support citizen initiatives'; his platform highlights initiatives he backed that became law.

social.basis: Co-sponsored HB 1038 (prohibiting puberty blockers, cross-sex hormones and transition surgery for minors) and HB 1699 (sex-based eligibility in girls' school sports).

parental-rights.basis: Campaigns to restore parental control over education, backed the 2024 parents' bill of rights, voted against ESHB 1296 and co-sponsored education savings accounts.

tech.basis: Says the state should decide to meet data centers' power and resource demands to gain jobs, citing Quincy.

experience.basis: First-term incumbent (since 2025) on three House committees and the Joint Oregon-Washington Legislative Action Committee.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Peter Abbarno of Chehalis, a Centralia attorney and House Republican Caucus chair, seeks a fourth term against Democrat Andy Zahn, a Toutle writer and photographer in his first race. They split on taxes, data centers and AI, corporate campaign money and climate policy.

candidates.summary: State representative since 2021, former Centralia City Council member and Centralia attorney, running on tax relief, affordability and bringing capital-budget money to the district.
highlights: Voted no on the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 tax package; pledges 'meaningful tax relief' [S5][S6][S1]
Says he helped secure $81 million in 2025 capital-budget money for the district [S15]
Voted no on 2025 rent-increase limits and the clean-fuels expansion [S8][S11]
Voted no on both 2025 bills amending the parents' rights law [S9][S10]
Chairs Cascade PAC, which funds Republican candidates [S17]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346 and ESSB 5814, calls the income tax 'unconstitutional, unpopular, and unnecessary,' and campaigns on tax relief.

spending.basis: Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget and says taxpayers should spend their own money, while touting capital-budget money won for the district.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent-increase limits (EHB 1217); no other housing statements.

safety.basis: Backs more law-enforcement funding and stronger penalties for repeat offenders, opposed 2021 police-reform bills, and voted no on the 2026 officer face-covering bill.

climate.basis: Voted against the 2025 clean-fuels changes and called 2021 climate bills including cap-and-trade job-killing, while offering amendments to redirect rather than end the program.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296 and ESSB 5181, which amended the parents' rights law; lists the right 'to parent' among rights he defends.

reform.basis: Chairs Cascade PAC, which funds Republican candidates, and accepts corporate contributions.

experience.basis: House member since 2021, House Republican Caucus chair, and six years on the Centralia City Council.

immigration.basis: Voted no on House final passage of SB 5855 (2026), the law-enforcement face-covering ban; the rubric's immigration pole_b names masking bans. One recorded vote and no statement, so magnitude 1 at medium.

candidates.summary: Toutle freelance writer and photographer in his first race for office, running on rural parks, industrial hemp, passenger rail and limits on data centers, and refusing corporate contributions.
highlights: Proposes a moratorium on new data centers and limits on generative AI in the state [S5][S4]
Calls the state tax structure regressive and wants more revenue with less burden on middle and lower earners [S6]
Proposes publicly owned hourly passenger rail on the I-5 corridor with small-town stops [S7]
Supports a universal government-paid health care system [S6]
Refuses corporate campaign contributions [S9][S1]

taxes.basis: Calls the tax structure 'deeply flawed and regressive' and says reform could raise more revenue while easing the burden on middle and lower earners; names no specific tax.

spending.basis: Proposes borrowing for self-repaying public investment in parks, rail, housing and community colleges, while saying he wants a balanced budget.

housing.basis: Proposes a publicly built rent-to-own housing model and affordable housing in town centers instead of sprawl.

climate.basis: Says fossil-fuel extraction and use must cease and calls climate change urgent; prioritizes demand reduction and distributed solar.

healthcare.basis: Says paying for health care through a government universal health care system would save individuals 'an immense amount of money.'

tech.basis: Repeatedly calls for a data-center moratorium, a ban on generative AI and cryptocurrency in data centers, higher data-center utility taxes and AI-content labeling.

reform.basis: Says big-money interests must be evicted from government and has vowed to refuse all corporate contributions.

experience.basis: First bid for any elected office, with no elected experience.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Ed Orcutt of Kalama, in the House since 2002 and ranking Republican on the Finance Committee, faces Democrat Evan Jones, a Port of Longview commissioner and IBEW journeyman who says he ran over Orcutt's vote against a 2025 contractor child-labor bill. Both say the state does not need new taxes; they differ most on tenure and worker-safety enforcement.

candidates.summary: Consulting forester and 12-term state representative who leads House Republicans on tax policy, running on protecting taxpayers, natural-resource jobs and living within existing revenue.
highlights: Voted no on the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and offered three amendments to it, including sending it to voters [S5][S6][S7]
Prime sponsor of bills to repeal the 2025 tax increases and cut the state sales tax [S11]
Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget; says government must live within existing revenue [S10][S3]
Voted no on the 2025 contractor child-labor bill, rent-increase limits and both parents'-rights amendment bills [S23][S12][S13][S14]

taxes.basis: No votes on ESSB 6346 and ESSB 5814, sponsored repeal and tax-cut bills, and repeated statements that he works to prevent tax increases.

spending.basis: Voted against the 2025-27 operating budget and repeatedly says the state is overspending and must live within existing revenue.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent-increase limits (EHB 1217); no housing statements.

climate.basis: Voted against the 2025 clean-fuels program changes (2SHB 1409); no climate statements.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296 and ESSB 5181, which amended the parents' rights law; no campaign statement on the topic.

experience.basis: In the House since 2002, Finance Committee ranking member and JLARC vice chair.

candidates.summary: Port of Longview commissioner, IBEW journeyman and Army combat veteran in his first legislative race, running on permitting reform, family-wage jobs and contractor safety.
highlights: Cast the lone port vote against a contractor with a record of safety incidents and wants to close the loopholes that allowed the award [S3][S2]
Says permitting gridlock drives timber, shipping and construction jobs out of state [S1][S2]
Platform plank: 'More Taxpayers, Not More Taxes' [S2]
Pledges to defend the Second Amendment [S2][S3]

taxes.basis: Platform says 'We don't need to raise taxes' and proposes growing the tax base instead; no record.

experience.basis: Port commissioner since 2024 with regional board roles, in his first legislative race against a 25-year incumbent.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Open Vancouver seat, the first in 15 years, after Rep. Sharon Wylie ran for county auditor. Democrat Kim Harless, a two-term Vancouver City Council member endorsed by The Columbian, faces Republican Sarah Mittelman, a psychiatric nurse practitioner and former chair of the Clark County Democratic Women; they split on the tax on income over $1 million, I-638, spending and state housing-siting rules.

candidates.summary: Two-term Vancouver City Council member and nonprofit policy director who co-chaired the 2021 county charter review, running on progressive revenue, tenant protections, climate action and universal healthcare.
highlights: Would defend the tax on income over $1 million and the capital gains tax and expand taxes on concentrated wealth [S2]
Wants rent stabilization with a lower cap than the 2025 law, just-cause eviction and social housing [S2]
Urges a no vote on I-1 and I-638; defends comprehensive sex education and gender-affirming care access [S2]
Backs the Washington Health Trust for a unified system covering all residents and the SAFE Act on immigration enforcement [S2]
Endorsed by The Columbian's editorial board [S6]

taxes.basis: Platform defends the tax on income over $1 million and seeks more wealth taxes; says she passed Vancouver's first B&O tax.

spending.basis: Would direct new revenue to housing, education, healthcare and the public workforce, restore child-care funding and move toward free community college.

housing.basis: Platform centers rent stabilization, tenant protections and social housing; city record also includes supply measures (MFTE expansion, removing parking minimums).

safety.basis: Favors co-responders, civilian crisis response and civilian traffic enforcement, while her city record also includes body cameras and police and fire funding measures.

climate.basis: Would defend the Climate Commitment Act and adopt a climate superfund; championed Vancouver's carbon-neutrality framework and a bulk fossil-fuel storage moratorium.

experience.basis: Two terms on the Vancouver City Council and charter review co-chair; first run for the Legislature.

reform.basis: Supports ranked choice and proportional ranked choice voting and led the charter review effort to put RCV on the ballot.

immigration.basis: Would pass the SAFE Act limiting federal immigration enforcement in sensitive places, fund deportation legal defense and lists immigrant rights as a priority.

healthcare.basis: Would champion the Washington Health Trust for a unified system covering all residents; pamphlet lists universal healthcare.

social.basis: Would protect abortion access, gender-affirming care and the shield law, opposes I-638; endorsed by Pro-Choice Washington and Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates.

parental-rights.basis: Urges a no vote on I-1, saying it would force schools to out LGBTQIA+ students, and would defend comprehensive sex education; her council voted to oppose I-1.

tech.basis: Wants ratepayers protected from data-center infrastructure costs with energy and water transparency, and further limits on surveillance tools such as Flock cameras.

candidates.summary: Psychiatric mental health nurse practitioner with 20 years in emergency, behavioral health and homeless-outreach care, a first-time candidate and former Clark County Democratic Women chair now running as a Republican, on accountability for spending and behavioral-health outcomes.
highlights: "No blank checks without measurable outcomes"; would review programs before expanding costs [S2]
Supports I-638: "Biological males should not compete in girls sports" [S5]
Opposed HB 2266's state siting rules for supportive housing as lacking local input [S6]
Calls for more detox and stabilization capacity, involuntary treatment when clinically necessary and accountability for repeat offenders [S8][S2]
Campaign video sets out concerns about the new income tax [S3]

taxes.basis: Campaign video presents concerns about the tax on income over $1 million; pledges to protect families and small businesses from unnecessary financial burdens.

spending.basis: Repeatedly calls for measurable outcomes before new spending, including in Clark County homelessness programs.

safety.basis: Pairs expanded treatment capacity with involuntary treatment when clinically necessary and accountability for repeat offenders and traffickers.

local-control.basis: Opposed HB 2266's limits on local governments' siting authority for supportive housing; says state policy should reflect local voices.

social.basis: Supports I-638 on sex-based girls' sports while calling for opportunities for transgender students; no position found on abortion or gender-affirming care.

experience.basis: No elected experience; the Columbian describes her as a political newcomer.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: House Majority Floor Leader Monica Stonier, who has held this Vancouver seat since 2016, faces Republican Derek Thompson, a retired cosmetology instructor who lost a 2025 Vancouver City Council race. Stonier runs on a long voting and sponsorship record; Thompson's brief platform centers on the school funding formula, avoiding unnecessary taxes and efficient spending.

candidates.summary: Incumbent and House Majority Floor Leader, an Evergreen Public Schools access coach and former middle-school teacher, seeking re-election on childcare, housing, special-education funding and healthcare costs.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and defended it at an April town hall [S5][S4]
Voted for the 2025 capital gains, excise and B&O tax increases [S6][S7][S8]
Prime sponsor of the 2025 law that rewrote the Initiative 2081 parents' rights, removing some notification rights [S10]
Voted for the 2025 limits on residential rent increases [S9]
Voted for the 2023 reproductive and gender-affirming care protections [S14][S15]

taxes.basis: Yea on ESSB 6346 (2026) and on the 2025 capital gains, excise and B&O tax increases; defended the income tax at a town hall.

spending.basis: Calls for real funding for special education, childcare and housing and describes the operating budget as a contract with the people.

housing.basis: Voted for EHB 1217's limits on rent and fee increases; cites Clark County's eviction rate.

social.basis: Voted for ESHB 1469 (reproductive and gender-affirming care shield law) and ESSB 5599 (youth seeking protected health care).

parental-rights.basis: Prime sponsor of ESHB 1296, which eliminated several Initiative 2081 parental notification rights and lengthened records access to 45 days; also voted for ESSB 5181.

experience.basis: In the House since 2016 after earlier serving the 17th District; House Majority Floor Leader.

immigration.basis: Cites new protections for immigrant workers among her work; pamphlet says she stands with neighbors under federal attack.

healthcare.basis: Healthcare agenda works within the current system: required insurance coverage of infertility treatment (HB 1730) and capital funding for dental access.

candidates.summary: Retired cosmetology instructor and former Nike department supervisor, a first-time legislative candidate who lost a 2025 Vancouver City Council race, running on school funding, cost of living and efficient use of tax dollars.
highlights: Pledges to "fix school funding at the source" [S1]
Says fiscal accountability starts with protecting families from "unnecessary taxes" [S2]
Says education funding should focus on classrooms, "not bureaucracy" [S2]
Would protect legacy businesses from being sidelined by major infrastructure projects [S1]

taxes.basis: Campaign plank on protecting families from unnecessary taxes; no statement on the 2026 income tax.

spending.basis: Pledges efficient use of tax dollars and classroom spending over bureaucracy.

experience.basis: No elected experience; says he is not a career politician; lost his only prior race (2025 Vancouver council).

contests.office_does: Clark Public Utilities commissioners set rates, budgets and resource plans for the county's public electric and water utility; in the general the whole county elects the District 3 seat.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Jane Van Dyke runs on the utility's rate, conservation and reliability record; retired BPA engineer Gordon Matthews calls it well run but wants new solar resources as hydro supply tightens. No rubric axis applies to PUD races, so neither candidate is scored.

candidates.summary: Incumbent District 3 commissioner and attorney, past president of the Washington PUD Association, running on the utility's rate, conservation and customer-service record.
highlights: Says the utility had one electric rate increase in 15 years and one water rate increase in 13 years [S1]
Says conservation exceeded regional goals, avoiding costly new investments [S1]
Will advocate for power and water at nonprofit rates [S1][S2]

candidates.summary: Licensed engineer with 12 years at Georgia Power research and 32 at BPA, campaigning on new solar resources as hydro supply tightens.
highlights: Says the BPA hydro system can no longer meet the utility's full requirements [S1]
Proposes building solar with eastern Washington public utilities and redesigning community solar [S1][S2]
Endorsed by Washington Conservation Action [S1]

contests.office_does: A Court of Appeals judge reviews appeals from superior-court cases; District 2 judges are elected for six-year terms by voters in Clallam, Grays Harbor, Jefferson, Kitsap, Mason and Thurston counties.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Erik D. Price, on the Court of Appeals since 2021 and now Division II's acting chief judge, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Court of Appeals judge since 2021 and Division II's acting chief judge; previously a Thurston County Superior Court judge (2012-2021) and a civil litigator for 19 years. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Court of Appeals judge since 2021; acting chief judge of Division II [S1]
Thurston County Superior Court judge 2012-2021, including presiding judge and drug court chief judge [S1]
Unopposed on the 2022 ballot, with 98.09% of the Kitsap vote [S2]

contests.office_does: The assessor sets the market value of every taxable property in Kitsap County and runs appeals and the senior, disabled and other exemption programs; the office does not set tax rates.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Phil Cook (Prefers Republican Party), assessor since 2015, runs on office efficiency and a nationally recognized exemption workflow. Navy veteran and Redfin agent Michael Simonds (Prefers Democratic Party) says high-value properties are under-assessed relative to working-class neighborhoods and wants data-driven modernization.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Assessor since 2015, with a background in real estate, mortgage lending and property management, running on accuracy, transparency and efficiency.
highlights: Assessor since 2015; nearly 25 years in Kitsap real estate and property management [S1]
Says the office handled a 76% jump in senior/disabled exemption applications without added staff or funding [S3]
Says the exemption workflow won national recognition and became a state-recommended practice [S1][S3]
Says tax rates are set by taxing districts and levies, not the assessor [S3]

experience.basis: Three-term incumbent (since 2015) running on the office's operational record.

spending.basis: Stresses fiscal responsibility and absorbing added workload through process improvement 'without additional staff or taxpayer funding.'

candidates.summary: Navy veteran and Redfin real-estate agent who has not held office, proposing data analytics to correct neighborhood-level valuation imbalances.
highlights: Former Navy nuclear missile technician; Redfin's first Kitsap-based agent since 2017 [S1]
Says working-class neighborhoods often pay more than their share while high-value properties lag [S1]
Proposes online valuation and appeal tools and outreach on exemptions for seniors, veterans, disabled and lower-income residents [S1]

experience.basis: First-time candidate running on 'accountability, transparency, and modernization' against a 12-year incumbent.

contests.office_does: The auditor runs Kitsap County's elections and voter registration, records deeds and other documents, and keeps the county's accounts and annual financial reports.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Auditor Paul Andrews (Prefers Democratic Party), in office since 2018, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Auditor since 2018 and the county's chief election official; previously an IT professional and county data analyst for 29 years. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Elected auditor in 2018 and re-elected in 2022 with 58.54% [S2][S3]
Past president of the Washington State Association of County Auditors; serves on the state Voting Systems Review Board [S1]
Says he has prioritized transparency and cross-trained staff to do more with less [S1]

contests.office_does: The county clerk keeps Kitsap County Superior Court records and filings, helps judges, lawyers and the public through the court process, and handles jury administration and passport services.
contests.race_blurb: Two candidates who prefer the Democratic Party: incumbent David T Lewis III, a 41-year veteran of the office and clerk since 2021, faces deputy clerk Brien Kennedy, a former tech and e-commerce executive who promises a public audit, plain-language guides and monthly office hours. This is the third contested clerk race in 28 years.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Clerk since 2021 after more than four decades in the clerk's office; president of the Washington Association of County Clerks.
highlights: Appointed clerk in 2021, elected in 2022; 41+ years in the clerk's office [S1]
Cites e-filing as a modernization that improves access to justice [S1]
Endorsed by the Kitsap County Democrats and the 26th LD Democrats [S1]

experience.basis: Four decades in the office and the sitting clerk since 2021; president of the state clerks' association.

candidates.summary: Deputy clerk for about a year and former Amazon, Microsoft and e-commerce executive, running a first campaign on accountability and plain-language public service.
highlights: Pledges a full public operational audit of the clerk's office [S3][S1]
Promises plain-language guides, monthly public office hours and an annual report, with no added staff or budget [S3][S2]
Says 'Unopposed races must stop'; this is the third contested clerk race in 28 years [S2][S1]
Has been in the clerk's office just over a year after a private-sector career [S4]

experience.basis: First-time candidate who argues repeatedly for fresh eyes and outside management experience over long tenure in the office.

spending.basis: Proposes a public audit of contracts, staffing and technology spending and improvements 'without more staff or more budget'; does not call for cuts.

contests.office_does: The three-member Board of Commissioners sets Kitsap County's budget and taxes, runs county property, roads and jails, and writes county land-use, building and health rules for unincorporated areas; District 3 candidates are nominated in the district and elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Incumbent Katie Walters (Prefers Democratic Party), in office since 2023 and chair of Kitsap Transit, faces Kevin Tisdel (Prefers Republican Party), a former Seattle Public Utilities manager who has not held office. They split mainly on growth: Walters backs the county's urban-growth plans and affordable housing, while Tisdel wants the Growth Management Act and state density laws repealed. Both take office facing a projected $9.8 million county shortfall in 2027.

candidates.summary: One-term District 3 commissioner and former Leadership Kitsap director who chairs Kitsap Transit, running on managed growth, housing, behavioral health and transit.
highlights: Commissioner since 2023; helped complete the Comprehensive Plan update and the Silverdale Regional Center Plan [S4]
Voted with the 2-1 majority in 2025 to drop 14 rural residential rezone requests that conflicted with policies directing growth to urban areas [S6]
Wants more affordable and workforce housing; accepted a national award for the county's 75-bed low-barrier navigation shelter [S3][S9]
Pairs support for accountable law enforcement with investment in youth mental health and treatment [S3]
Endorsed by Kitsap mayors, the sheriff, the prosecutor, two tribes and the Kitsap County Democrats [S5]

experience.basis: One-term incumbent with a documented record (comprehensive plan, critical areas ordinance) and regional board chairs; not a long-tenure officeholder.

housing.basis: Prioritizes expanding affordable and workforce housing and a services-based response to homelessness, including the low-barrier navigation center; past chair of Housing Kitsap.

safety.basis: Says public safety and behavioral health go hand in hand: supports accountable law enforcement while investing in treatment and youth mental health to address problems 'before they become crises.'

spending.basis: Pledges investment in infrastructure, public safety and services alongside a 'fiscally responsible' approach and careful budgeting; no clear lean either way.

candidates.summary: Fourth-generation Kitsap native, former Seattle Public Utilities manager and collision-repair business owner, running on repealing the Growth Management Act and keeping Kitsap rural.
highlights: Wants the Growth Management Act repealed first, then the county and state density and builder's-remedy laws [S3]
Says Kitsap has a housing surplus and an affordability problem driven by King County commuters, not a shortage [S3]
Would end the multifamily property-tax exemption and opposes taxing working farms [S3]
Says land-use and infrastructure decisions must produce net-positive revenue for county taxpayers [S3]
Endorsed by the Washington Farm Bureau PAC [S2]

experience.basis: Has never held elected office and runs against 'photo-op projects', though he cites 14-15 years of utility administration in Seattle.

taxes.basis: Would end the multifamily tax exemption because it shifts taxes onto residents, and supports 'no farm taxation'; frames growth as a cost borne by taxpayers.

spending.basis: Wants every land-use and infrastructure decision to deliver measurable net-positive revenue, and criticizes ratepayer cost-sharing in the Silverdale sewer plan; he also proposes some new projects.

contests.office_does: A Kitsap County District Court judge hears misdemeanor and gross-misdemeanor criminal cases and traffic infractions, sets bail and holds preliminary hearings; the county's four district judges are elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: incumbent Judge Claire A. Bradley, on the bench since 2014, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County District Court judge since 2014 and presiding judge of its Behavioral Health Court; previously a deputy prosecutor for 17 years. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Judge since 2014; re-elected unopposed in 2018 and 2022 [S2][S3][S4]
Helped create and presides over the county's first mental health court [S1]
Deputy prosecutor 1997-2014, focused on crimes against children, sexual assault and domestic violence [S1]

contests.office_does: A Kitsap County District Court judge hears misdemeanor and gross-misdemeanor criminal cases and traffic infractions, sets bail and holds preliminary hearings; the county's four district judges are elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Gina M. Buskirk, a former Bremerton city prosecutor and defense attorney now on the District Court bench, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County District Court judge; previously a Bremerton city prosecutor, criminal defense attorney and municipal judge pro tem. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Former Bremerton city prosecutor and assistant city attorney, and a public defender and private defense attorney [S1]
Past president of the Kitsap County Bar Association [S1]
Says she uses technology to make the court easier to navigate [S1]

contests.office_does: A Kitsap County District Court judge hears misdemeanor and gross-misdemeanor criminal cases and traffic infractions, sets bail and holds preliminary hearings; the county's four district judges are elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Shane R. Seaman, who won Department 3 in a contested 2022 race, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County District Court judge since 2022 and assistant presiding judge; previously a Bremerton Municipal Court commissioner and 18-year trial lawyer. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Elected in 2022 with 55.11% over Stan Glisson [S2]
Assistant presiding judge; co-chair of the Council for Independent Courts [S1]
Former Bremerton Municipal Court commissioner, prosecutor and public defender [S1]

contests.office_does: A Kitsap County District Court judge hears misdemeanor and gross-misdemeanor criminal cases and traffic infractions, sets bail and holds preliminary hearings; the county's four district judges are elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Kevin P Kelly, on the bench since a 2017 appointment, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County District Court judge since a 2017 appointment; previously a county deputy prosecutor for 27 years. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Appointed in 2017; elected unopposed in 2018 and 2022 [S1][S2][S3]
Deputy prosecutor for 27 years, including chief deputy of the District/Municipal Court Division [S1]
Helped create the county's Veterans Treatment Court and Behavioral Health Court as a prosecutor [S1]

contests.office_does: The prosecuting attorney charges and tries criminal cases for the state in Kitsap County, defends lawsuits against the county, and is legal adviser to county government and school districts.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats. Incumbent Chad M. Enright, prosecutor since 2019, runs on his diversion programs, staffing record and broad institutional endorsements. Public defender and former deputy prosecutor Joe Lombardi says the office is mismanaged and pledges to refuse corporate PAC money and keep ICE out of county cases.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Prosecutor since 2019 and in the office since 2008; runs on diversion and treatment-court programs, full staffing, balanced budgets and endorsements from the county party, the deputy prosecutors' guild and the attorney general.
highlights: Created Kitsap's first pre-arrest diversion program and the North Kitsap Recovery Resource Center diversion [S3][S6]
Says violent crime, sex offenses and crimes against vulnerable people remain the priority [S5]
Plans race-blind charging and a real-time public case-data website [S1]
Reports all prosecutor positions filled and no case backlog [S1][S3]
Endorsed by Kitsap County Democrats, the DPA Guild, AG Nick Brown and former sheriffs Gese and Simpson [S4][S5]

experience.basis: Eight-year incumbent with 18 years in the office; makes experience and management record the central contrast.

safety.basis: Record of building pre-arrest diversion, recovery-center diversion and therapeutic courts, while keeping violent and sex crimes as the stated priority.

reform.basis: Campaigns on endorsements from every local Democratic elected official, the county party and allied organizations.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County public defender and former Kitsap deputy prosecutor and assistant attorney general who says the prosecutor's office is mismanaged and runs on changing its culture.
highlights: Says a 'toxic management culture' has driven experienced prosecutors out and led to erratic charging [S4]
Would personally prosecute the most serious violent cases and expand diversion for low-level offenders [S1][S2]
Pledges to keep ICE out of county cases and prosecute unlawful federal enforcement actions [S1][S2]
Refuses contributions from corporate PACs and special interests [S2]
Endorsed by the Kitsap County Central Labor Council [S3]

experience.basis: Challenger with no elected or supervisory experience who runs on changing the office ('I am not a politician'), while citing a decade of legal practice.

reform.basis: Refuses contributions from corporate PACs and special interests.

safety.basis: Would expand diversion and mental-health services for low-level offenders while prioritizing violent crime and enforcing probation.

contests.office_does: The sheriff runs the Kitsap County Sheriff's Office, the county's largest department and its chief law-enforcement agency, which patrols, investigates, makes arrests and serves court orders and warrants.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat after Sheriff John Gese resigned in June 2026. KCSO patrol chief Brandon L. Myers (Prefers Democratic Party), a 23-year insider, faces King County deputy and retired Navy officer Rick Kuss (Prefers Republican Party), who argues for change from outside the office and pledges no new taxes while the county weighs a sales-tax increase.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Sheriff's Office patrol chief with a 23-year career in the office, from Explorer Cadet to detective sergeant; endorsed by the outgoing and former sheriffs and the deputies' guild.
highlights: 23 years at KCSO; promoted to patrol chief in 2026 [S6][S7]
Founding member of the office's Crisis Intervention Team; supervised major-crime and child-abuse investigations [S1]
Says the office must be properly staffed, supported and equipped, and calls for restoring proper funding [S1][S5]
Emphasizes transparency, community trust and keeping party politics out of the office [S3]
Endorsed by Sheriff John Gese, retired Sheriff Gary Simpson, the Deputy Sheriff's Guild and the Kitsap County Democratic Committee [S2]

experience.basis: Runs on a 23-year career inside KCSO, now patrol chief, with endorsements from current and former sheriffs; not the incumbent.

spending.basis: Says the office must be properly staffed, supported and equipped, and calls for restoring proper funding for the Sheriff's Office.

candidates.summary: King County deputy sheriff and retired Navy lieutenant commander with a criminal-justice master's degree; lost the 2022 Kitsap sheriff race and now runs as an outside change candidate.
highlights: Would restore a regional drug task force and says he will not seek reelection if he does not [S3]
Pledges no new taxes, a budget review to cut waste and overtime control [S3]
Says 'Change needs to come from the outside' [S3]
Names protecting children from abuse, exploitation and drugs as his top priority [S1][S2]
Supports 'accountable diversion' with incarceration if mandatory treatment fails [S3]

experience.basis: Argues change must come from outside the office and that he is 'unburdened by its past'; has never held the office or worked at KCSO.

taxes.basis: Pledges not to seek new taxes to fix problems he attributes to wasteful spending, while calling taxation a last resort.

spending.basis: Would thoroughly review the office budget, cut waste, control overtime and redirect existing money to frontline priorities.

safety.basis: Leads with enforcement (drug task force, fentanyl traffickers, incarceration when mandatory treatment fails) alongside accountable diversion.

contests.office_does: The treasurer collects Kitsap County's money, including property taxes, pays it out on the auditor's warrants, and invests county and special-district funds.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Treasurer Pete Boissonneau (Prefers Democratic Party), in office since 2023, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Kitsap County Treasurer since 2023, previously the office's chief deputy and investment officer and a fixed-income broker. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Elected treasurer in 2022 as the only candidate; in office since 2023 [S1][S2]
Says an insured cash sweep program he set up has earned the general fund more than $2 million [S1]
Endorsed by the Kitsap County Democrats and 26th LD Democrats [S1]

contests.office_does: A KPUD commissioner sits on the three-member elected board that sets budgets and rates for Kitsap's public water, wastewater and fiber utility, for a six-year term; every county voter votes on each seat in November.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Commissioner Stacey Smith, appointed to the South Kitsap seat in 2025, is the only candidate. The same ballot carries KPUD Proposition 1 on electric authority, which her board placed there.

candidates.summary: KPUD commissioner for South Kitsap since a 2025 appointment and Kitsap County's Director of Aging and Long-Term Care; a licensed counselor. The only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Appointed KPUD commissioner in 2025; seeking the full six-year term [S1][S2][S3]
Priorities: fair public utility rates, broadband expansion, clean water and wastewater support [S1][S3]
Signed, as board secretary, the resolution placing KPUD Proposition 1 on the ballot; no personal position on it found [S4]

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding, ferries and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: three-term Rep. Tarra Simmons, who faces a $52,000 state ethics penalty she is appealing, against first-time candidate Daria Ilgen, a former tech strategist running on fiscal discipline and accountability. Simmons won the primary about 57% to 39%; they differ on new taxes, spending, policing and housing.

candidates.summary: Attorney and former nurse in the House since 2021, now Deputy Speaker Pro Tempore, known for criminal-justice, reentry and health-care legislation; the Legislative Ethics Board fined her in 2026 and she is appealing.
highlights: Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and 2025 capital gains, estate and B&O tax increases [S18][S20][S22]
Authored prior-authorization, charity-care and mental health parity laws [S6]
Voted against Initiative 2081 (2024) and co-sponsored its 2025 rewrite, HB 1296 [S26][S28]
Sponsored the ICE Out Act (HB 2641), which died in committee [S15]
Ethics board found three violations; penalty with costs is about $52,000, under appeal [S12]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and 2025 B&O and capital gains/estate tax increases; platform calls for asking more from those who can afford it.

spending.basis: Platform calls for more state investment in housing, schools and child care, but she backed cutting Blake legal-aid funding as wasteful during a shortfall.

housing.basis: Voted for EHB 1217 rent and fee increase limits, said rent prices must be stabilized, backs social housing and more public housing investment.

safety.basis: Centers treatment, reentry, root causes and police accountability; voted against I-2113 restoring police pursuits.

climate.basis: Supported the Climate Commitment Act and voted for the 2024 clean-energy transition bill; platform targets major polluters.

experience.basis: Three-term incumbent and Deputy Speaker Pro Tempore with a list of authored laws, running on 'proven leadership'.

immigration.basis: Lead sponsor of HB 2641 to bar police from hiring post-2025 ICE officers; supported immigrant worker protections.

healthcare.basis: Health agenda works within the existing system: insurer prior-authorization rules, charity care, parity and drug costs; no single-payer statement.

social.basis: Pledges to defend gender-affirming care and LGBTQIA+ protections, championed abortion-care protections, endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against I-2081 and co-sponsored and voted for HB 1296, which narrowed its parental rights and added student privacy rights.

candidates.summary: Former strategist for Amazon, Zillow and Expedia, Democratic Party officer and Kitsap nonprofit board member, running on fiscal discipline, affordability and accountability; has not held public office.
highlights: Taxpayer Accountability Standard: five questions any new tax must answer before he votes for it [S8]
Platform calls for audits, performance measures and ending ineffective programs [S6]
Endorsed by AWB, NFIB, Kitsap Builders, Realtors and two police organizations [S7]
Proposes limits on surveillance pricing and a TRUST Act on surplus campaign funds [S9][S10]

taxes.basis: Sets a five-question test before any new tax and says he will not oppose every tax, while calling for tax equity and targeted relief.

spending.basis: Repeatedly calls for audits, performance measures, cutting waste and reviewing existing spending first, while protecting essential services.

housing.basis: Housing plank centers cutting red tape, faster permitting and density; no rent-regulation position.

safety.basis: Pledges law-enforcement staffing and tools, endorsed by WACOPS and Poulsbo police; also backs mental health and addiction services.

climate.basis: Supports transit-oriented growth to cut carbon emissions and environmental protection; no Climate Commitment Act position.

experience.basis: Has not held public office and runs on 'new leadership' and fresh thinking against a three-term incumbent.

reform.basis: Proposes the TRUST Act tightening rules on surplus campaign funds and conflicts of interest.

immigration.basis: Pledges to stand up for immigrant families so they can live without fear.

healthcare.basis: Health plan holds insurers accountable and expands providers within the current system.

social.basis: Pledges to protect LGBTQ+ neighbors and reject intolerance; no statements on sports eligibility or abortion.

tech.basis: Would require disclosure of data-driven pricing and ban use of sensitive personal data to price essential goods.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding, ferries and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Democratic Rep. Greg Nance, in the House since 2023 and focused on ferries and Puget Sound, faces Republican Lance Byrd, an IT program manager who opposes any state income tax and wants to restore parental-rights and natural gas provisions. Nance led the primary about 58% to 30%.

candidates.summary: Bainbridge Island native in the House since 2023, a nonprofit founder and youth mental health advocate whose priorities are ferries, Puget Sound and cost of living.
highlights: Cites $895 million for ferries and $42 million for West Sound Tech [S1]
Voted for the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and for eight failed amendments to narrow it or cut other taxes [S11][S14][S15]
Defended the Climate Commitment Act; voted for the 2024 clean-energy transition bill [S7][S33]
Voted for I-2081 in 2024, then co-sponsored its 2025 rewrite, HB 1296 [S28][S30]

taxes.basis: Voted for ESSB 6346 and 2025 B&O and capital gains/estate increases, but also for amendments to narrow the income tax, cut the sales tax, and for I-2111 in 2024.

spending.basis: Campaigns on securing ferry, school, workforce and local health-care investments.
