housing.basis: Platform favors permit and zoning reform and private-sector incentives, while he voted for EHB 1217 rent-increase limits.

safety.basis: Voted for I-2113 restoring police pursuits, and promotes expanding non-police mental-health response (Poulsbo Fire CARES).

climate.basis: Defended the Climate Commitment Act as making polluters pay and voted for ESHB 1589 on the clean-energy transition.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2023 with committee leadership and a ferry and environment record; shorter tenure than a long-serving member.

reform.basis: Says his campaign takes no corporate money.

healthcare.basis: Health agenda is local capacity within the current system: urgent care, clinics, workforce training.

social.basis: Supports a state constitutional amendment protecting the right to choose; no statements on gender or sports eligibility.

parental-rights.basis: Co-sponsored and voted for HB 1296 narrowing I-2081, after voting for I-2081 itself in 2024.

candidates.summary: Bremerton IT program manager and former restaurant cook running on no state income tax, budget restraint, natural gas access and parental rights; ran for school board in 2023 and State Senate in 2024.
highlights: Opposes any state income tax and would tie budget growth to population and inflation [S2][S3]
Would restore natural gas protections and criticizes the Climate Commitment Act and CETA [S2]
Would restore parental-rights provisions narrowed by HB 1296 [S2]
Wants Growth Management Act reform with fewer state mandates [S3]

taxes.basis: Repeatedly pledges to oppose any state income tax and stop new taxes; called for lowering the gas tax in 2024.

spending.basis: Says the state has a spending problem and would cap budget growth at population plus inflation.

housing.basis: Blames Growth Management Act mandates for limiting supply and wants deregulation to let communities build.

safety.basis: Runs on supporting law enforcement and reducing crime; called for more officers and easing rules that hamper arrests.

climate.basis: Says the CCA and CETA raise energy costs, would restore natural gas protections, and opposed ferry electrification.

experience.basis: Has never held office and pitches himself as 'not a career politician' offering balance against one-party control.

local-control.basis: Wants local communities to decide housing growth 'without one-size-fits-all Olympia rules' under a reformed GMA.

parental-rights.basis: Calls parents the primary decision-makers and would restore I-2081 records access and notification rights removed by HB 1296.

contests.office_does: A State Representative serves a two-year term writing and voting on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Dan Griffey, a retired firefighter first elected in 2014, faces Democrat Jim Pierson, an Army Special Forces veteran and former tech-industry manager. Griffey led the primary with 52%; they split on the income tax, public safety, reproductive rights and immigration.

candidates.summary: Retired Mason County firefighter and former House Republican Whip, in the House since 2014, running on affordability, crime and keeping businesses in the state.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346, the tax on income over $1 million; his amendment to exempt public pensions from it failed [S6][S7]
Campaign site keeps a 'No State Income Tax' plank and calls for a balanced-budget requirement [S5]
'We must put families before felons': tougher penalties and 'applying the law as written' [S5][S2]
Wants a lower gas tax and hydropower counted as renewable energy [S2][S5]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346, ESSB 5813 and ESHB 2081 and yes on I-2111; 'No State Income Tax' platform plank and interview opposition.

spending.basis: Wants budgets based on actual revenues, a balanced-budget requirement and a five-day review period to 'find waste to cut.'

housing.basis: Prioritizes private property rights and land-use freedom; says excessive regulations choke growth.

safety.basis: 'Families before felons' platform with tougher sentences; calls for applying the law as written and ending loopholes that let criminals walk free.

climate.basis: Wants a lower gas tax and hydropower recognized as renewable, citing consumer energy costs.

experience.basis: Elected 2014, former House Republican Whip; campaign cites 141 bills passed.

local-control.basis: Supports housing legislation that 'keeps local decisions local.'

social.basis: Voted against ESSB 5599 and ESHB 1469 (2023 reproductive and gender-affirming care bills); no campaign statements or I-638 position.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for I-2081 and against ESHB 1296, the changes I-1 would repeal; no campaign statement on I-1.

candidates.summary: Army Special Forces veteran and former product and program manager at Apple, Microsoft and GoDaddy, a Democratic precinct officer running on healthcare costs, fair taxes and housing.
highlights: Wants 'the wealthiest individuals and corporations to contribute their share' with property-tax relief for seniors and working families [S2]
Platform: reproductive rights protected, discrimination banned, an expanded path to citizenship [S6]
Wants healthcare to 'move away from a for-profit system' without 'breaking what works' [S6][S1]
Says he does not accept corporate contributions [S5]

taxes.basis: Wants the ultra-wealthy and large corporations to pay more while keeping property taxes low; no statement on the income tax itself.

housing.basis: Pairs renter protections with more supply, faster permitting and condo construction-defect liability reform.

safety.basis: Calls for accountable policing, treatment and recovery access, and prevention investments.

climate.basis: Backs renewable-energy investment and holding polluters accountable, framed as 'practical' climate policy that lowers costs.

healthcare.basis: Wants healthcare moved away from a for-profit system, but 'without breaking what works.'

immigration.basis: Says immigrants deserve 'a fair and expanded path to citizenship.'

social.basis: Platform: live authentically, love who you love, reproductive rights protected and discrimination banned.

reform.basis: Says his campaign does not accept corporate contributions.

experience.basis: Has held no public office beyond precinct committee officer; pitches 'a different perspective' against a 12-year incumbent.

tech.basis: Names AI and data centers among top voter concerns and commits to 'ensuring that new industries pay their fair share of infrastructure costs instead of shifting those costs onto working families,' citing data-center electricity, water and 'who ultimately pays the bill' [S2]. That is data-center cost skepticism, as with Mejia's tech +1, but softer than calling for guardrails, so +1.

contests.office_does: A State Representative serves a two-year term writing and voting on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Travis Couture, the House Republican budget leader since his 2023 arrival, faces first-time Democratic candidate Maria Littlesun, a Shelton social worker and tribal elder-care manager. He campaigns on spending control, public safety and I-1; she campaigns on social housing, special-education funding and reproductive-care access.

candidates.summary: House Republican budget leader since 2023, a Navy submarine veteran and Shelton construction-business owner running on lower costs, public safety and parental rights.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346 and offered amendments to delay the tax and cut a related sales tax on advertising services [S5][S6][S7]
As budget leader, proposes to 'control unsustainable spending' and 'reject unnecessary tax increases' [S2]
Campaigning for I-1: 'Vote yes for parents' rights and vote no for stranger danger' [S4]
Pledges to support law enforcement and 'hold repeat offenders accountable' [S2]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346, ESSB 5813 and ESHB 2081 and yes on I-2111; sponsored amendments to delay the income tax; campaigns for 'less taxes.'

spending.basis: Calls for controlling 'unsustainable spending' and eliminating waste; criticizes 'reckless spending.'

safety.basis: Supports law-enforcement staffing, repeat-offender accountability, restored pursuits and drug penalties, and encampment cleanup.

experience.basis: Incumbent since 2023 and House Republican budget leader; runs on 'experience ... and a record of results.'

social.basis: Voted against ESSB 5599 and ESHB 1469 (2023 reproductive and gender-affirming care bills); no I-638 position.

parental-rights.basis: Campaigns for I-1, says he drafted the current notification language, voted for I-2081 and against ESHB 1296, and supports school choice.

candidates.summary: First-time candidate from Shelton, a social worker and crisis responder who manages Squaxin Island Tribe elder and vulnerable-adult programs, running on affordability, housing, schools and healthcare.
highlights: Supports social housing with wraparound services and tenant protections; says encampment sweeps do not solve root causes [S5]
Would champion full special-education funding and restore dual-language program funding [S5]
Pledges to protect access to contraception and medical abortion [S5]
Wants to protect Apple Health/Medicaid and keep rural clinics open [S5]

spending.basis: Proposes added funding for special education, dual-language programs, rural transit and affordable-housing construction.

housing.basis: Backs social housing, tenant protections and affordable-housing funding, alongside zoning reform for density near transit.

safety.basis: Opposes encampment sweeps and favors social housing with wraparound behavioral-health services.

healthcare.basis: Wants to protect Apple Health and Medicaid access and reform insurance rules within the current system.

social.basis: Pledges to protect contraception and medical-abortion access; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and Stonewall Democrats.

experience.basis: First-time candidate with a social-services and tribal elder-care background.

contests.office_does: A State Senator serves a four-year term writing and voting on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Sen. Drew MacEwen, the Senate Deputy Republican Leader and a 35th District legislator since 2013, faces Democratic Thurston County Commissioner Carolina Mejia. He runs on spending restraint and tax cuts after voting against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million; she runs on cost of living, rural hospitals and infrastructure, and opposes I-1 and I-638.

candidates.summary: Senate Deputy Republican Leader from Shelton, in the Legislature since 2013, a Navy submarine veteran and investment-firm managing partner running on spending restraint and tax relief.
highlights: Voted against ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and against the 2025 capital-gains/estate and B&O increases [S6][S7][S8]
Top priorities: rein in spending, end tax hikes, cut the sales tax and cap property taxes [S2]
Voted for the 2024 parents' bill of rights (I-2081) and against its 2025 rewrite, ESHB 1296 [S10][S11]
Endorsed by the Association of Washington Business and 16 other trade and professional groups [S5][S15]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346, ESSB 5813 and ESHB 2081 and yes on I-2111; campaigns to end tax hikes, cut the sales tax and cap property taxes.

spending.basis: Repeatedly calls for reining in spending and 'responsible budgeting'; says government 'should live within its means.'

experience.basis: In the Legislature since 2013, Senate Deputy Republican Leader; runs on his 'bipartisan track record.'

social.basis: Voted against ESSB 5599 and ESHB 1469 (2023 reproductive and gender-affirming care bills); no campaign statements or I-638 position.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for I-2081 and against ESHB 1296, the changes I-1 would repeal; no campaign statement on I-1.

candidates.summary: Thurston County commissioner since 2021 and county Board of Health chair, who came to the U.S. from Honduras at 11, running on lowering costs, rural hospitals and infrastructure.
highlights: Would cut permitting delays for housing while 'protecting local control over what development looks like' [S4]
Helped found the Regional Housing Authority and the countywide Home Fund as commissioner [S5][S1]
Pledges to keep reproductive health care 'safe, legal, and accessible'; listed as opposing I-1 and I-638 [S4][S7]
Wants 'strict guardrails' so data centers do not pass energy costs to ratepayers [S4]

spending.basis: Calls for dedicated road and bridge funding, broadband, water-system investment and full state funding of public education.

housing.basis: Pairs cutting permitting red tape with a record of founding a regional housing authority and a county housing fund.

local-control.basis: Wants local control over development and says growth should be shaped by residents, 'not dictated from the outside.'

safety.basis: Prioritizes victim services and a treatment-centered addiction response alongside first-responder funding and gun-safety laws.

healthcare.basis: Wants to cap prescription drug prices, protect existing coverage and keep rural hospitals open; no single-payer statement.

social.basis: Pledges to keep reproductive care safe, legal and accessible; listed as opposing I-638; endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance Advocates and Stonewall Democrats.

parental-rights.basis: Listed among elected officials opposing I-1; no other statement on notification, records or opt-outs.

tech.basis: Wants strict guardrails on data centers' energy costs and pollution.

experience.basis: County commissioner since 2021 with no legislative tenure, running on 'It's time the messenger changed.'

contests.office_does: A Court of Appeals judge hears and decides appeals from superior courts.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Judge Erik D. Price, on the Court of Appeals since 2021, is unopposed.

candidates.summary: Court of Appeals judge since 2021 and former Thurston County Superior Court judge, unopposed for a six-year term.
highlights: Court of Appeals judge since 2021; Acting Chief Judge of Division II since 2026 [S1]
Thurston County Superior Court judge 2012-2021, including presiding judge [S1]
Chaired Adult Drug Court and the county's Pre-trial Justice Improvement Team [S1]

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Five-term Rep. Jim Walsh, the state Republican Party chair, faces Aberdeen City Councilmember Kevin Moynihan in the coastal and lower-Columbia 19th District. Walsh led the August primary 55.5% to 44.4%.

candidates.summary: Aberdeen publisher first elected in 2016 and state Republican Party chair since 2023; filed the 2023 parents' bill of rights and anti-income-tax initiatives and opposes the 2026 income tax.
highlights: Voted no on ESSB 6346, the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, and offered amendments to it [S7]
Filed the 2023 initiatives on parents' rights (IL-2081), income taxes (IL-2111), police pursuits and cap-and-trade repeal that were certified to the Legislature [S26]
Offered an amendment to restore parental notification rights in ESHB 1296 and voted against the bill [S8][S9]
Led House floor opposition to letting a state commission remove elected sheriffs [S20]
As party chair, quoted in a release stating WAGOP supports enactment of I-645 [S23]

taxes.basis: Voted against ESSB 6346 and the 2025 tax package, calls the income tax unconstitutional, and filed the 2023 no-income-tax and capital-gains repeal initiatives.

spending.basis: Calls for full audits after reported losses of state dollars, ties the income tax to spending growth, voted against the 2025-27 operating budget, and filed spending-growth-limit initiatives.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent and fee increase limits and the 2026 shelter-siting bill; no affirmative housing plan in the dossier.

safety.basis: Filed police-pursuit and hard-drug initiatives, prefiled a tougher fentanyl-sentencing bill, and opposed state decertification of elected sheriffs.

climate.basis: Voted against the clean fuels program bill and filed initiatives to repeal cap-and-trade.

experience.basis: Five-term incumbent, ranking member on Civil Rights & Judiciary, and state party chair.

local-control.basis: Opposes state removal of elected sheriffs and state limits on local shelter siting; pledges to fight 'unlawful mandates from Olympia.'

immigration.basis: Voted against limits on law enforcement face coverings; session report criticizes pushing sheriffs toward non-cooperation with federal immigration authorities.

parental-rights.basis: Filed the 2023 parents' bill of rights initiative, says parents have a right to notification about school and health information, offered a notification amendment and voted against ESHB 1296.

candidates.summary: Aberdeen City Councilmember, line cook and former HVAC tradesman running on affordability, rent stabilization, rural healthcare and school funding; refuses corporate PAC money.
highlights: Pledges to pass statewide rent stabilization [S1]
Refuses corporate PAC money [S1]
Calls for lower prescription drug costs, affordable childcare and more housing [S4]
Wants more funding for rural and coastal schools and competitive educator pay [S4]
Endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council [S9]

housing.basis: Pledges to pass statewide rent stabilization and lists rent stabilization advocacy; also calls for building more housing.

spending.basis: Calls for public investment in ports, schools, childcare and educator pay; no audit or restraint planks.

healthcare.basis: Would protect rural healthcare infrastructure and lower prescription drug costs within the current system; no single-payer position.

experience.basis: City councilmember without legislative service challenging a five-term incumbent; runs as a worker rather than a career politician.

reform.basis: Refuses corporate PAC money and frames his run against 'powerful interests or political insiders.'

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Three-term Rep. Joel McEntire faces a rematch with labor council president Terry Carlson, who placed first in the four-way primary 43.2% to 41.6%. McEntire was fined by the Legislative Ethics Board and placed under a protection order in September 2026 over Facebook posts.

candidates.summary: Longview timber worker and president of the Cowlitz-Wahkiakum Central Labor Council, running on affordability, infrastructure, rural healthcare and labor protections; supports the millionaires' tax.
highlights: Supports ESSB 6346, the tax on income over $1 million, while pledging to oppose taxes on working families [S4]
Would protect rural hospitals and have the state fill gaps left by federal Medicare and Medicaid cuts [S4]
Calls for cutting costs and delays that make homes more expensive to build [S4]
Endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council [S10]

taxes.basis: Supports the millionaires' income tax and says the wealthy should pay their share, while pledging to oppose taxes on working families.

spending.basis: Calls for state investment in energy, roads, broadband, ports and rural healthcare.

housing.basis: Housing plank is to build more by cutting costs and delays; no tenant-protection or public-housing plank.

climate.basis: Wants environmental protection without raising costs at the gas pump and more power generation.

healthcare.basis: Would protect rural hospitals and backfill federal Medicare and Medicaid cuts within the current system.

experience.basis: Pamphlet lists no public office, only union posts; labor council president and timber worker challenging a three-term incumbent.

candidates.summary: Cathlamet Marine veteran and former teacher first elected in 2020; runs on fiscal restraint and opposition to the 2025-26 tax increases. Fined by the Legislative Ethics Board in 2026 over a Facebook comment.
highlights: Calls ESSB 6346 'blatantly unconstitutional'; roll call records him excused on its final passage [S6][S16]
Says parents have a right to know what is taught in the classroom and supports school choice [S4]
Voted against ESHB 1296 and for all twelve Republican amendments to it [S17]
Sponsored 2025 laws on burrowing-shrimp research and cultural items at graduations [S10]
Fined $500 by the Legislative Ethics Board and placed under a one-year protection order over Facebook posts [S14][S15]

taxes.basis: Opposes the income tax and 2026 tax bills in repeated statements and voted against the 2025 capital gains, services and B&O tax increases.

spending.basis: Calls for living within means and 'right-sizing our government'; voted against the 2025-27 operating budget.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 rent and fee increase limits and the 2026 shelter-siting bill.

safety.basis: Site prioritizes supporting law enforcement; voted against state decertification of sheriffs.

climate.basis: Opposed the Forest Practices Board stream-buffer rule as driven by environmental activism; voted against the clean fuels bill.

experience.basis: Three-term incumbent with enacted bills, seeking a fourth term.

local-control.basis: Says one-size-fits-all state policy does not work; co-signed opposition to state removal of elected sheriffs.

immigration.basis: Co-signed criticism of pushing sheriffs toward non-cooperation with federal immigration authorities; voted against limits on law enforcement face coverings.

parental-rights.basis: Says parents have a right to know what is taught, voted against ESHB 1296 and for all Republican amendments, and offered parents' rights amendments in 2026.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Eight-year incumbent Beth Doglio, who chairs the House Environment & Energy Committee, faces Republican Don Hewett, an Air Force veteran and engineer running for the first time with no stated policy platform and no reported fundraising.

candidates.summary: Eight-year state representative and chair of the House Environment & Energy Committee, formerly a climate and conservation advocate, running on her record on climate, labor, housing and gun legislation.
highlights: Voted for ESSB 6346, the 2026 9.9% tax on income over $1 million, and for the 2025 capital gains and B&O tax bills [S5][S7][S8]
Chairs the House Environment & Energy Committee; cites Clean Buildings standards and sponsors HB 2515 on data centers and other large energy users [S2][S4][S12]
Voted for ESHB 1296, the 2025 amendments to the parental-rights law [S6]
Opposes I-1 and I-638 [S16]
Endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council, Washington Conservation Action and the Alliance for Gun Responsibility [S3]

taxes.basis: Yes on ESSB 6346, ESSB 5813 and ESHB 2081, and prime sponsor of an executive-compensation surcharge (HB 1785).

spending.basis: Pledges to 'continue to invest' and protect a strong social safety net and public employees; voted for the 2025-27 operating budget.

housing.basis: Voted for 2025 rent stabilization (EHB 1217), cites added funding to house the vulnerable, endorsed by the Housing Alliance.

climate.basis: Chairs Environment & Energy, led Clean Buildings standards, voted for clean fuels changes, former Climate Solutions advisor.

experience.basis: Eight years in the House and a standing committee chair.

immigration.basis: Voted for 2SHB 2105 (immigrant worker protections) and SSB 5855 (limits on law-enforcement face coverings).

social.basis: Former Pro-Choice Washington political director, endorsed by Planned Parenthood Alliance and LGBTQ+ Victory Fund, opposes I-638.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 and against Republican amendments to it; opposes I-1.

tech.basis: Prime sponsor of HB 2515 regulating emerging large energy use facilities such as data centers.

candidates.summary: Air Force veteran and engineer running for office for the first time; describes himself as 'not a professional politician' and states no policy platform.
highlights: Former Air Force 96th Bomb Wing police officer and executive engineer [S1]
Pamphlet statement: 'I am not red, I am not blue. I am red, white, and blue.' [S1]
Reports $0 raised and spent with the PDC [S2]

experience.basis: No elected experience; presents himself as a non-politician and regular citizen.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Two Democrats: one-term Rep. Lisa Parshley, a veterinary oncologist and former Olympia councilmember, faces first-time candidate Jamie Keenan-deVargas, a renter and immigrant-rights organizer who refuses corporate money and runs to her left on rent caps, single-payer health care and criminal justice.

candidates.summary: One-term state representative and former Olympia councilmember, a veterinary oncologist, running on affordability, housing supply, renter protections and health care.
highlights: Prime sponsor of HB 1445, the Washington health trust bill for universal public coverage [S15]
Voted for ESSB 6346 and says she 'fought and voted for the Millionaires' Tax' [S3][S6]
Voted for 2025 rent stabilization and supports building 'more homes of every type' [S2][S10]
Voted for ESHB 1296; opposes I-1 and I-638 [S7][S20]
Top contributors include Regence, Genentech, Puget Sound Energy and DaVita [S22]

taxes.basis: Yes on ESSB 6346 and ESSB 5813, says she fought for the millionaires tax, and sponsors a health-insurer premium tax increase.

spending.basis: Pushes expanded childcare subsidies and dedicated affordable-housing funding; voted for the 2025-27 operating budget.

housing.basis: Pairs supply-first 'more homes of every type' with stronger renter protections, a rent-stabilization vote and affordable-housing funding bills.

climate.basis: Voted for clean fuels program changes; endorsed by Washington Conservation Action and Sierra Club.

experience.basis: One House term plus six years on the Olympia City Council, against a first-time candidate.

reform.basis: Accepts contributions of $2,200 to $2,400 from companies and PACs (Regence, Genentech, PSE and Proliance Surgeons PAC at $2,400; DaVita at $2,200).

immigration.basis: Voted for 2SHB 2105 (immigrant worker protections) and SSB 5855 (limits on law-enforcement face coverings).

healthcare.basis: Prime sponsor of the Washington health trust (universal coverage) bill, member of the Universal Health Care Commission.

social.basis: Prime sponsor of an abortion savings program bill, endorsed by Planned Parenthood Votes NW, opposes I-638.

parental-rights.basis: Voted for ESHB 1296 and against Republican amendments to it; opposes I-1.

tech.basis: Sponsors bargaining over AI use by public employers; voted for the data-center energy bill E2SHB 2515.

candidates.summary: Retail worker, renter and founder of immigrant-defense groups running for office for the first time on a volunteer-led, corporate-PAC-free campaign.
highlights: Rejects corporate PAC and lobbying money; top priority is restricting corporate political spending [S2][S5]
Supports inflation-capped rents, repeal of the local rent-control ban and state social housing [S2]
Supports single-payer health care, free childcare and new wealth taxes such as a 2% tax on financial intangibles [S2][S5]
Calls for decriminalizing drug use and removing school resource officers [S4][S5]
Opposes I-1 and I-638 [S7]

taxes.basis: Platform 'heavily reliant on tax restructuring': intangibles tax on $100M+ portfolios, land value tax, windfall-profits tax.

spending.basis: Proposes free childcare, single-payer health care, fare-free transit and state social housing.

housing.basis: Statewide rent caps at inflation, repeal of the rent-control ban, social housing, Housing First and right to counsel.

safety.basis: Divest from prisons, unarmed co-responders, full drug decriminalization, remove school resource officers.

climate.basis: Wants a zero-emission framework and state codification of federal standards, but calls carbon taxes regressive.

experience.basis: First run for office; runs explicitly against 'career politicians'.

local-control.basis: Says state preemption on zoning 'must be massively expanded', while also wanting local authority over rent control restored.

reform.basis: Rejects corporate PAC and lobbying money; proposes corporate political-spending limits and public election vouchers.

immigration.basis: Founded two immigrant-defense groups; wants immigration incarceration abolished and ICE legislated out of Washington.

healthcare.basis: Supports single-payer and the Washington Health Trust 'unequivocally'.

social.basis: Opposes I-638; endorsed by Washington State Stonewall Democrats; no other stated position.

parental-rights.basis: Listed as opposing I-1; no other statement on notification or opt-outs.

tech.basis: Would ban AI rent-pricing software and private police surveillance and impose strict data-center mandates.

contests.office_does: The Assessor sets the market value of all real and personal property in the county, the base used to calculate property taxes; the Assessor does not set tax rates.
contests.race_blurb: Two candidates who both prefer the Democratic Party are running for the open seat. JJ Olson, a decade-long appraiser in the office endorsed by outgoing Assessor Steven Drew, led the primary 55% to 42% over Lynda Nashed Zeman, a county executive administrator and former appointed Lacey councilmember.

candidates.summary: Business Applications Administrator in the Assessor's Office and accredited appraiser who started as a field appraiser about ten years ago; endorsed by the outgoing Assessor and office staff.
highlights: Accredited Washington real property appraiser since 2016; started as a field appraiser and now manages the office's appraisal and tax software [S1]
Says he is leading a technology transformation to make the office more accessible and transparent [S1]
Promises plain-language explanations of how property values are set [S2]
Endorsed by Assessor Steven Drew, 20 current and former office staff, the regional labor council and the county REALTORS association [S3]
Led the certified August primary with 55.10% of the vote [S5]

experience.basis: Continuity candidate: about a decade inside the Assessor's Office, endorsed by the outgoing incumbent and chief deputy; no elected record.

candidates.summary: Executive administrator in the County Commissioners' Office who previously did executive administration in the Assessor's Office for three years; appointed Lacey City Councilmember in 2019.
highlights: Frames the Assessor's job as executive leadership over people, budgets and systems [S1]
Names staff retirements, growing workloads, tight budgets and the systems transition as the office's main challenges [S1]
Would make valuation information easier to understand so owners get answers "before frustration turns into appeals" [S1]
Vice president of the West Puget Sound chapter of the International Association of Assessing Officers [S2]
Endorsed by 22nd LD legislators, two county commissioners and the mayors of Olympia, Tumwater, Yelm and Tenino [S2]

experience.basis: Mixed profile: a county-government insider with a 2019 council appointment, but not the office's continuity pick, running on management change rather than appraisal tenure.

spending.basis: Pledges to "manage resources responsibly" under tight budgets and to run the office with fiscal responsibility; no specific spending proposals.

contests.office_does: The Auditor runs elections, handles vehicle licenses and titles, keeps real estate records, provides passport services, and manages the county's financial operations, including budgeting, accounting and payroll.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Tillie Naputi-Pullar (Prefers Democratic Party) is the only candidate on the ballot. The seat is open: Auditor Mary Hall writes in the same pamphlet that this is her last election as County Auditor.

candidates.summary: Thurston County Elections Manager since 2013, running unopposed for the open Auditor seat as Mary Hall leaves office.
highlights: Elections Manager since 2013; in the Auditor's elections division since 1999 [S1]
Co-chair of the Secretary of State's VoteWA Advisory Board; state Elections Administrator of the Year in 2014 and 2021 [S1]
First-time candidate with no prior elected experience [S1]

contests.office_does: The County Clerk keeps the official records of Superior Court cases and decisions and runs the office where the public files court matters such as protection orders and family-law cases.
contests.race_blurb: Open seat after a county budget cut closed the Clerk's Office public counter for months; limited in-person service resumed September 21. Nicole Miller, a former county Racial Equity Program Manager running on leadership experience, narrowly led Garrett Cady, an independent Clerk's Office employee endorsed by the outgoing clerk, 50.7% to 48.7% in the primary.

candidates.summary: Child-welfare consultant and former Thurston County Racial Equity Program Manager with about 30 years in public service, running from outside the Clerk's Office on leadership and restoring full public access.
highlights: Pledges reliable, full-time in-person access, saying "part-time access is not enough" [S2][S4]
Would take part fully in county budget meetings so "there should be no surprises," and look for ways to increase revenue and reduce costs [S5]
Argues the Clerk is an elected executive and that knowing existing procedures differs from leading an organization [S2][S6]
Endorsed by three county commissioners and the 22nd LD's state senator and representatives [S2]
Narrowly led the certified August primary with 50.72% [S8]

experience.basis: Comes from outside the Clerk's Office and runs on changing how it serves the public, drawing on long public-service management experience rather than office tenure.

spending.basis: Pairs a pledge to restore full-time counter service with examining ways to increase revenue and reduce costs.

candidates.summary: Clerk's Office proceedings specialist and former juvenile court assistant from Yelm, running as an independent with the backing of the outgoing clerk, office leadership and 21 other county clerks.
highlights: Current Clerk's Office employee who has worked the front counter and as a courtroom clerk and trains newer staff [S1][S2]
Calls the commissioners' 2026-2027 budget cut to the office "disproportionate" and pledges to keep all in-person services [S2]
Would restore and expand the Domestic Violence Liaison Program [S1][S2]
Runs as an independent, saying "there is absolutely no place for politics in the Clerk's Office" [S2]
Endorsed by Clerk Linda Myhre Enlow and 21 other county clerks [S2]

experience.basis: Continuity candidate: works inside the Clerk's Office and is endorsed by the outgoing clerk, chief deputy and office staff; no elected record.

reform.basis: Runs as an independent and repeatedly says the clerk must be free of political influence, like nonpartisan judges; no wider structural-reform agenda.

spending.basis: Criticizes the budget cut to the office as disproportionate and pledges to restore and enhance in-person and domestic-violence services.

contests.office_does: A County Commissioner serves as the local government and legislative authority outside city limits; Thurston's five commissioners are nominated by district and elected countywide.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Tye Menser (Prefers Democratic Party), commissioner for District 3 since 2019 and the board's chair, is the only candidate on the ballot. Although nominated by District 3 voters, the commissioner is elected by the whole county in the general.

candidates.summary: District 3 commissioner since 2019 and board chair, a former defense and family-law attorney, running unopposed for another term.
highlights: Commissioner since 2019; chairs the board and the LOTT Clean Water Alliance [S1]
Cites the Regional Housing Council, a countywide Home Fund and supportive housing projects [S1]
Backs jail diversion and the LEAD program, and proposes a countywide regional jail with re-entry programs [S1]

contests.office_does: A Thurston County commissioner sits on the five-member board that is the county's legislative authority outside city limits, adopting the county budget and setting policy for services such as the sheriff and jail, land-use permitting and regional housing funding, for a four-year term.
contests.race_blurb: One-term Commissioner Emily Clouse, a Democrat running on her housing and climate record, faces former Lacey Councilmember Nicolas Martinez-Dunning, who led the District 5 primary 38% to 35% and runs on budget integrity, deputy and jail funding and permit-fee relief. District 5 nominated the two; all county voters decide the seat.

candidates.summary: Gym owner, Marine and National Guard combat veteran and former Lacey City Councilmember (2024-2026), running on budget integrity, public safety funding, recovery-based housing and freezing permit fees.
highlights: Pledges to "protect deputy and jail funding first when budgets get tight"; endorsed by Sheriff Derek Sanders [S2]
Would back recovery-based housing with treatment and freeze the permit fees that rose January 1, 2026 [S2]
Says $20-30 million deficits are forcing cuts and that "Commissioner scandals broke public trust" [S1]
Says his campaign has rejected all PAC and special-interest money [S1]
Led the August District 5 primary with 38.36% to Clouse's 34.68% [S4]

spending.basis: Frames the race around deficits and budget integrity, pledges to report results in plain numbers and tie any fee increase to measured performance, while protecting deputy and jail funding.

housing.basis: Wants the county to welcome builders and would freeze permit fees; homelessness approach is recovery-based housing with treatment rather than a public-housing expansion.

safety.basis: Cites low deputy staffing and rising assaults and would fund deputies and the jail first; endorsed by the sheriff.

experience.basis: Challenger with about two and a half years on Lacey City Council and regional boards but no county-office record.

reform.basis: Runs on rebuilding trust after commissioner scandals, refusing PAC money and moving beyond partisan fighting.

candidates.summary: One-term District 5 commissioner, Army veteran and former DSHS forensic mental health supervisor, running on her record on affordable housing funding, climate programs and budget transparency.
highlights: As Regional Housing Council chair, oversaw approval of $25 million for affordable housing including 186 supportive units [S1]
Cites the Energize Thurston heat-pump program and $7.6 million for Deschutes Estuary restoration; pledges to implement the Comprehensive Plan's climate commitments [S1][S2]
Voted against a county budget process that cut staff and domestic-violence navigation services [S1]
Censured by the board after a 2024 investigation; the Supreme Court affirmed dismissal of a recall petition in February 2026 [S5]
Endorsed by the Thurston County Democrats, labor unions, Washington Conservation Action and Sierra Club [S2]

spending.basis: Opposed a budget that cut staff and domestic-violence services and protected animal services from cuts, alongside "fiscally responsible" and priority-based-spending language.

housing.basis: Record of approving $25 million in public affordable and supportive housing funding; pledges to expand affordable and supportive housing.

safety.basis: Cites data-driven public safety and behavioral health informed by her forensic mental health work; endorsed by gun-safety groups.

climate.basis: Record on heat-pump subsidies, estuary restoration and forest protection, chairs the Climate Mitigation Collaborative, and pledges to implement the county's climate commitments.

experience.basis: One-term incumbent running on her first-term record.

contests.office_does: The Coroner investigates all sudden, violent, suspicious and unusual deaths occurring in the county.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Coroner Gary Warnock (Prefers Democratic Party), in office since 2007, is the only candidate on the ballot.

candidates.summary: Coroner since 2007 and a former deputy coroner and funeral director, running unopposed.
highlights: Coroner since 2007; deputy coroner from 2001 [S1]
Cites state certification and national accreditation of the office in 2025 [S1]
Pledges a fiscally responsible office amid county budget pressures [S1]

contests.office_does: A District Court judge hears civil, small claims, criminal and traffic cases.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Judge Kalo Wilcox, a District Court judge for 16 years, is the only candidate on the ballot.

candidates.summary: District Court judge for 16 years and a former prosecutor, running unopposed.
highlights: District Court judge for 16 years [S1]
Twenty years as a prosecutor, including City of Olympia Prosecuting Attorney [S1]
Highlights the court's Veterans and Mental Health Courts [S1]

contests.office_does: A District Court judge hears civil, small claims, criminal and traffic cases.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Judge Sam Meyer, a District Court judge for 18 years, is the only candidate on the ballot.

candidates.summary: District Court judge for 18 years and a former public defense staff attorney, running unopposed.
highlights: District Court judge for 18 years [S1]
Former staff attorney, Thurston County Office of Assigned Counsel [S1]
Highlights the court's therapeutic courts and expanded municipal court service [S1]

contests.office_does: A District Court judge hears civil, small claims, criminal and traffic cases.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Paul Wohl, a District Court commissioner with no prior elected experience, is the only candidate on the ballot, so the seat will have a new judge.

candidates.summary: District Court commissioner for 12 years and former Olympia city prosecutor, running unopposed for an open judgeship.
highlights: District Court commissioner for 12 years [S1]
Prosecutor and public defender before that, including 14 years as Olympia's prosecutor [S1]
Washington State Judicial College instructor and Associate Dean [S1]

contests.office_does: The Prosecuting Attorney prosecutes criminal actions in superior, district and juvenile courts and provides legal advice to the county.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Christy Peters (Prefers Democratic Party), chief of staff of the Prosecuting Attorney's Office, is the only candidate on the ballot and has no prior elected experience, so the office will change hands.

candidates.summary: Longtime deputy prosecutor and the office's chief of staff since 2011, running unopposed for Prosecuting Attorney.
highlights: Chief of staff of the Prosecuting Attorney's Office since 2011; deputy prosecutor from 1995 [S1]
Would prioritize violent crime and crimes against children and strengthen victim advocacy [S1]
Helped expand therapeutic Drug, Veterans and Mental Health Courts [S1]

contests.office_does: A Thurston PUD commissioner sits on the three-member board of a water utility that runs 271 water systems serving about 25,000 people, adopting its budget and setting rates; this seat is the four-year unexpired remainder of a six-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Appointed Commissioner Jim Campbell, the PUD's former field operations director, is backed by the other two commissioners and his predecessor. Challenger Troy Kirby, a former Lacey parks commissioner, runs on affordability and a critique of the board's fixed charges, PFAS surcharge and emergency bid waivers. All county voters decide the seat.

candidates.summary: Appointed PUD commissioner since October 2025 and former PUD director of field operations, with about 22 years in the water industry after 20 years as an Olympia Brewery foreman.
highlights: Former PUD director of field operations overseeing about 270 water systems; appointed to the board unanimously in September 2025 [S1][S9]
Describes utility management as "infrastructure first, cost second, and safety always" and stresses preventive maintenance [S1]
Recommended a 1.9 percent rate increase for the 2027 budget [S14]
Endorsed by PUD Commissioners Stearns and Olsen and former Commissioner Linda Oosterman [S3]

candidates.summary: State agency communications staffer and seven-year Lacey parks commissioner running on affordable rates, grant and settlement funding for PFAS cleanup, and a critique of the PUD board's fees and bidding.
highlights: Would pay for PFAS cleanup and major projects with state grants, infrastructure funding and polluter settlements [S1]
Fact sheet calls the PUD's $1.78 monthly PFAS surcharge "a tax on the victims, not the polluters" and criticizes fixed charges and emergency bid waivers [S3]
Supports stronger customer assistance programs and open public meetings [S1]
Previously ran for Lacey City Council (2019) and Port of Olympia commissioner (2023) [S5][S6]

contests.office_does: A Thurston PUD commissioner sits on the three-member board of a water utility that runs 271 water systems serving about 25,000 people, adopting its budget and setting rates, for a six-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Commissioner Chris Stearns is not on the ballot, leaving an open seat. State drinking-water loan program manager Chris Pettit, endorsed by all three sitting commissioners, faces small business owner Jeff Curry, a Scott Lake water-district board member running on affordability and solar.

candidates.summary: Small business owner and Scott Lake community water-district board member making his fifth run for office since 2022, on affordability, solar power and a water-quality app.
highlights: Utility experience is a board seat for the Scott Lake community water district [S1]
Pledges to keep rates reasonable and be transparent about utility spending [S1]
Proposes adding solar to the local grid and a public water-quality mobile app [S1]
Ran for county treasurer (2022), Tumwater school board (2023, 2025) and governor (2024) without winning [S4]

candidates.summary: Attorney and state Drinking Water State Revolving Fund program manager, former Washington Conservation Commission director, running for his first elected office on affordability, transparency and conservation.
highlights: Manages the state Drinking Water State Revolving Fund, which lends to the PUD; previously led the Washington State Conservation Commission [S1][S6]
Cites a 25% rise in rates over five years and would pursue cost reductions from a legislative utility-affordability report [S1][S7]
Would expand advisory groups and make rate and budget documents easier to understand [S7]
Endorsed by all three sitting PUD commissioners and by county and city officials [S2]

contests.office_does: The sheriff runs county law enforcement, the county jail, civil process and emergency operations, patrolling the unincorporated county, for a four-year term.
contests.race_blurb: Sheriff Derek Sanders, an independent elected in 2022, won 71% in the primary against Kevin Burton-Crow, a Democrat, special victims detective and president of the deputies' union. Sanders runs on staffing growth and his first-term record; Burton-Crow runs on outside accreditation, published policies and outcome-based accountability.

candidates.summary: One-term sheriff (Prefers Independent Party) with 12 years in law enforcement, running on staffing growth, training and de-escalation and a proposed mental-health wing at the jail.
highlights: Campaign says patrol deputies rose from 33 to 55 and detectives from 8 to 18 during his term [S3]
Proposes a secured jail mental-health wing run by mental health professionals [S4]
Defended vehicle pursuits in 2025, saying pursuits enabled a gang-member arrest [S7]
Asked the Salary Commission to freeze his own salary in 2025 and 2026 [S6]
Won the August primary with 70.69% of the vote [S5]

safety.basis: Emphasizes deputy staffing, recruitment and vehicle pursuits, paired with de-escalation training and a professionally run mental-health wing at the jail.

spending.basis: Pledges investment in employees, facilities and equipment while promising stewardship of taxpayer dollars and freezing his own salary.

experience.basis: Incumbent sheriff since 2023 with 12 years in law enforcement, running on his first-term record.

candidates.summary: Sheriff's Office special victims detective, retired Army sergeant first class and president of the deputies' union (Prefers Democratic Party), running for the first time on accreditation, transparency and prevention-focused policing.
highlights: Would seek outside accreditation through the state sheriffs and police chiefs association and publish office policies [S1][S4]
Says deputies should be judged on community impact "not just by how many stops or arrests they make" [S4]
Pledges victim-centered and harm-reduction training and clear annual budget disclosures [S1]
Endorsed by the Thurston County Democrats, the sheriff's captains' association and the Central Labor Council [S5]
Received 28.99% in the August primary [S7]

safety.basis: Pamphlet and platform measure success by prevention, recovery and community outcomes, with harm-reduction training and an early-intervention abatement team.

spending.basis: Ties spending to measurable outcomes, annual program reports and budget disclosures, and argues accreditation reduces liability costs.

experience.basis: First-time candidate who has not held elected office or command rank, though he has 11 years in the office and a 20-year Army career.

contests.office_does: The Treasurer provides banking, investment, debt and cash management services for the county and all local governments within it except cities.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Incumbent Treasurer Jeff Gadman (Prefers Democratic Party), appointed in 2017, is the only candidate on the ballot.

candidates.summary: Treasurer since 2017, formerly in the Assessor's Office and on the Lacey City Council, running unopposed.
highlights: Treasurer since 2017; 39 years with Thurston County [S1]
Says the county investment pool returned more than $43 million to local governments in 2025 [S1]
Former Lacey City Councilmember (2011-2017) [S1]

contests.office_does: A Court of Appeals judge decides appeals from superior court cases; Division III's District 3 (Chelan, Douglas, Kittitas, Klickitat and Yakima counties) elects two of its five judges for six-year terms.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Judge Megan K. Murphy, appointed to the court in January 2025, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Court of Appeals, Division III judge since her January 2025 appointment; former Yakima County deputy prosecutor and civil litigator; the only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Appointed to Division III in January 2025, replacing Judge Rebecca Pennell [S1][S2]
Yakima County deputy prosecutor for about five years from 2001, then civil litigation in private practice [S1][S2]
Partner at Fox Ballard in Seattle; earlier a Yakima practice in medical-malpractice defense [S2]

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, labor law and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: A 2024 rematch: Republican Rep. Gloria Mendoza, a former Grandview mayor, faces Democrat Chelsea Dimas of Sunnyside. They split on taxes, the Climate Commitment Act, school funding, data centers and state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

candidates.summary: One-term State Representative, former Grandview mayor and founder of a vocational-training business, running on lower taxes, budget restraint and repeal of the Climate Commitment Act.
highlights: Voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 B&O, services and transportation revenue bills [S4][S5][S6][S7]
Would "get rid of the Climate Commitment Act"; voted against the 2025 clean fuels bill [S16][S9]
Voted against the 2025 amendments to the parental-rights law and wrote in support of parents' record-access and notification rights [S8][S18]
Says she is "in the middle" on data centers and wants more study [S15]

taxes.basis: No votes on ESSB 6346, ESHB 2081, ESSB 5814 and ESSB 5801; statements opposing new taxes and calling for eliminating taxes on food and diapers.

spending.basis: Says the state should keep what it has without increasing the budget, voted no on the 2025 operating budget, and pledges to stop runaway government spending.

climate.basis: Calls for repealing the Climate Commitment Act over fuel costs; voted against the 2025 clean fuels program bill.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 limits on rent and fee increases; blames energy policies imposed on developers for home prices.

safety.basis: Called to 'finally fund the police' and for tougher theft and fentanyl penalties; campaigns on safer streets. She voted against the 2025 public safety funding bill, which carried a local option tax (S13).

immigration.basis: Voted twice against the 2026 immigrant worker protections bill; no statement on immigration found.

tech.basis: Undecided on data centers and open to their local benefits; voted against the 2026 bill addressing large energy use facilities.

social.basis: Voted against the 2026 bill improving access to abortion medications; statement says she defends family values.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296 twice and wrote that she fought for parents' access to records, review of materials and notifications.

experience.basis: Incumbent legislator and Assistant Minority Whip with eight prior years as a Grandview council member and mayor.

candidates.summary: Sunnyside nonprofit worker and former state commissioner on human rights and Hispanic affairs, running a second time on affordability, school funding, workers' rights and protection of immigrant families.
highlights: Calls the millionaire's tax "a great path forward" [S5]
"Completely against data centers" until regulations are in place [S4]
Would keep state and local resources out of federal immigration enforcement [S2]
Supports more school funding, universal childcare and collective bargaining for farmworkers [S4][S5]

taxes.basis: Calls the millionaire's tax a great path forward while wanting tax relief for working people.

spending.basis: Fully supports $2 billion more for schools, more mental-health and support staff, and universal childcare.

housing.basis: Would build affordable housing, strengthen renter protections and expand down-payment assistance, while also citing more supply.

safety.basis: Pairs officer recruitment with behavioral-health and crisis response and prevention of violence and addiction.

climate.basis: Supports clean-energy investment and climate preparedness; withdrew support for the 2025 gas tax over costs to working people.

immigration.basis: Would bar state and local resources from federal immigration enforcement and supports labor rights regardless of immigration status.

tech.basis: Completely against data centers; wants a ban until regulations protect water and utility ratepayers.

social.basis: Would protect access to reproductive health care and care regardless of gender identity; no further positions found.

experience.basis: No prior public office beyond precinct committee officer; criticizes 30 years of 'recycled leadership' in the district.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, labor law and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Deb Manjarrez, a Wapato CPA and orchardist, faces Democrat Ezequiel Morfin, a Toppenish electrician and former city council member. They split on taxes and spending, farmworker collective bargaining, data centers and state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

candidates.summary: One-term State Representative, CPA and Wapato orchardist running on limiting state spending, tighter grant audits and redirecting Climate Commitment Act revenue.
highlights: Voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 B&O, services and transportation revenue bills [S5][S6][S7][S8]
Wants tighter grant auditing and accounting standards [S17]
Supports data centers and doubts the Legislature should regulate them [S16]
Voted against the 2025 amendments to the parental-rights law and wrote in support of parents' record-access and notification rights [S9][S19]

taxes.basis: No votes on ESSB 6346, ESHB 2081, ESSB 5814 and ESSB 5801; co-wrote that she stood against 'aggressive new taxes'.

spending.basis: Runs on fighting runaway government spending and tighter grant audits; voted no on the 2025 operating budget.

climate.basis: Blames the 'green agenda' and Climate Commitment Act for utility and fuel costs and voted against the clean fuels bill, but proposes redirecting CCA revenue rather than repeal.

housing.basis: Voted against the 2025 limits on rent and fee increases; attributes homelessness to drugs and mental illness rather than economics.

safety.basis: Frames homelessness as drug and mental illness, wants children kept from drug-addicted parents, and opposed new firearm requirements; she also sponsored an overdose-mapping bill.

immigration.basis: Voted twice against the 2026 immigrant worker protections bill; no statement on immigration found.

tech.basis: Supports data centers, opposes a 'knee-jerk' ban and is not sure the Legislature should act.

social.basis: Voted against the 2026 bill improving access to abortion medications; no statement found.

parental-rights.basis: Voted against ESHB 1296 and co-wrote that she fought for parents' access to records, review of materials and notifications.

experience.basis: One House term, two terms as county Republican chair and 16 years as a precinct committee officer, against a former city council member.

candidates.summary: Toppenish electrician, Yakama Nation electrical inspector and former city council member running on affordability, farmworker collective bargaining and protection of immigrant families.
highlights: Would limit state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement [S3]
Calls farmworker collective bargaining his "largest work" [S5]
Opposes data centers until there is more research [S5]
Supports renter protections, down-payment relief and "fair taxation" [S3][S6]

taxes.basis: Supports 'fair taxation so working people aren't carrying the load alone' and says tax systems favor those at the top; no specific revenue proposal.

spending.basis: Supports $2 billion more for schools and more funding for childcare and preschool.

housing.basis: Would work on renter protections and down-payment relief, alongside tiny homes and expanded city boundaries.

immigration.basis: Supports state protections limiting cooperation with federal immigration enforcement; repeatedly criticizes federal enforcement.

tech.basis: Says no to data centers pending more research and wants oversight and community investment from builders.

experience.basis: Former Toppenish council member and planning commissioner making a first run for the Legislature against an incumbent.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Rep. Chris Corry, the House Republican Deputy Minority Leader, faces Democrat Jack McEntire, a Selah sculptor making his third run for a 15th District House seat. Corry has a long voting record against new taxes and the Climate Commitment Act; McEntire's platform centers on universal health care and need-based access to education.

candidates.summary: Four-term State Representative and House Republican Deputy Minority Leader who campaigns on limited government, lower taxes and parental rights.
highlights: Voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million and the 2025 B&O and services tax bills [S6][S7][S8]
Says an income tax should require a constitutional amendment and a vote of the people [S4]
Voted for 2023 middle-housing legalization and against the 2025 rent-increase cap [S10][S11]
Voted against the Climate Commitment Act (2021) and ESHB 1296 (2025) [S9][S12]

taxes.basis: Voted no on ESSB 6346, EHB 2081 and ESSB 5814, and issued repeated statements opposing the income tax and calling for lower tax burdens.

spending.basis: Repeatedly argues the operating budget has doubled in a decade and the state should manage existing revenue before asking for more.

housing.basis: Voted for middle-housing legalization (supply) and against the 2025 cap on residential rent increases.

safety.basis: Voted against the 2021 police-tactics and use-of-force bills; criticizes the Legislature for not holding repeat offenders accountable.

climate.basis: Voted against the Climate Commitment Act in 2021; no campaign statement on climate.

experience.basis: In the House since 2019 and now Deputy Minority Leader, facing a challenger with no government-office record.

social.basis: Voted against ESHB 1469 on access to reproductive and gender-affirming care; lists Life Choices of Yakima among his community service.

parental-rights.basis: Campaigns on parental rights, voted against ESHB 1296 twice, and criticized the Legislature for not acting on the parental-rights initiative.

immigration.basis: Voted against the 2019 Keep Washington Working Act limiting state cooperation with federal immigration enforcement; one vote, no statement.

candidates.summary: Selah sculptor and Yakima County Democrats vice-chair, in his third run for a 15th District House seat, campaigning on universal health care and need-based access to education.
highlights: Says "We deserve universal health care" [S1]
Says college or vocational education should be based on ability and need, not money [S1]
Called climate change an existential threat in 2020 [S2]
Argues voters have seen "the same faces and ideas" for years [S1]

healthcare.basis: Calls for universal health care and says Washington could provide it, criticizing job-based coverage.

spending.basis: Calls investment the way to transform the region and backs universal education and youth skills programs.

climate.basis: Called climate change an existential threat and urged listening to science (2020); no specific policy stated.

experience.basis: No government-office record; argues voters have seen the same faces and ideas for years.

contests.office_does: A State Representative writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets, covering school funding, tax structure, housing rules, health funding and criminal-justice statutes.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat left by Rep. Jeremie Dufault, who is running for the Senate. Republican Reedy Berg, Yakima's deputy mayor and a middle-school teacher, led the primary with 48%; attorney Liz Hallock, running under a "No Kings" party preference, advanced with 30%.

candidates.summary: Yakima deputy mayor and Toppenish middle-school history teacher running on lower taxes, Climate Commitment Act repeal and parental rights.
highlights: Opposes the state's new income tax and proposes a 0.1% sales-tax cut [S2]
Would repeal the Climate Commitment Act [S2]
Makes parents' right to know what children are taught and what medical decisions are made his first plank [S2]
On the city council, voted against sending a property-tax levy to voters and against a Pride Month proclamation [S6][S7]

taxes.basis: Opposes the income tax and new fees and taxes, proposes a sales-tax cut, and voted against placing a city property-tax levy on the ballot.

spending.basis: Pledges to cut wasteful spending and administrative overhead; says he would have cut more rather than use one-time money on city facilities.

housing.basis: Supports permitting reform to lower housing costs and says the Housing First model is not working.

safety.basis: Backs fully funding police, opposes criminal-justice rollbacks, and would require treatment as a condition of housing assistance.

climate.basis: Would repeal the Climate Commitment Act and reduce fuel taxes and regulations on energy production.

experience.basis: Two years on the Yakima City Council and now deputy mayor, while also presenting himself as 'not a career politician'.

social.basis: Voted against a Pride Month proclamation, stating there are two genders and that science does not support expanding gender identities.

parental-rights.basis: Platform says parents have the right to know what children are taught and what medical decisions are made, and that government has overstepped.

local-control.basis: In the 2026-07-16 Herald-Republic interview he says Olympia's 'excessive taxes, regulations and mandates' stifle local schools and businesses, calls for 'local control over levies and spending priorities' and pledges to block state mandates 'that drain resources' from districts [S3]. This is about state fiscal mandates on local governments (levies, spending priorities), not curricula, notification or opt-outs, so it is local-control evidence under the 2026-10-08 addendum.

candidates.summary: Yakima family and public-disclosure attorney and repeat candidate, running under a "No Kings" party preference on economic inequality, reproductive rights and opposition to President Trump.
highlights: Says "Reproductive rights are being gutted" [S1]
Ran in 2022 to "protect abortion rights and safe abortion access" [S4]
Says Christian teachings are being used "to terrorize immigrants" [S1]
Wants to protect Yakima residents "from the King in the White House" [S1]

social.basis: Says reproductive rights are being gutted; ran in 2022 on protecting abortion rights and access.

immigration.basis: Objects to immigrants being terrorized; no specific enforcement policy stated.

climate.basis: Says the environment and children's futures are being destroyed; worked with Citizens' Climate Lobby (2020).

experience.basis: Has not held government office; runs outside both major parties under a No Kings label.

contests.office_does: A State Senator writes and votes on Washington state law and the operating, capital and transportation budgets for a four-year term, and the Senate confirms the governor's appointments.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Republican State Rep. Jeremie Dufault of Selah is the only candidate for the 15th District Senate seat.

candidates.summary: Republican State Representative for the 15th District, former Selah City Council member and Army Reserve JAG officer; the only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: State Representative, 15th District Position 2; former Selah City Council member [S1][S2]
Voted against the 2026 tax on income over $1 million, saying "these taxes start small and grow" [S3][S5]
Voted against ESHB 1296 (2025), the changes to the parental-rights law that I-1 would undo [S4]
Lieutenant colonel in the U.S. Army Reserve JAG Corps; served in Kuwait and Afghanistan [S1]

contests.office_does: The county assessor sets the market value of every taxable property each year and applies property-tax exemptions; taxing districts, not the assessor, decide how much tax is collected.
contests.race_blurb: Two Republicans: incumbent Jacob Tate, a 30-year veteran of the office seeking a second term, faces first-time candidate Keith Effler, a photographer and developer endorsed by the county Republican Party. Tate stresses accurate, equitable appraisal and modernization; Effler pledges customer service, an online valuation data portal and cutting the tax burden as far as the law allows.

candidates.summary: Incumbent assessor with more than 30 years in the office, including as chief deputy under two predecessors, holding the IAAO Mass Appraisal Specialist designation.
highlights: More than 30 years in the assessor's office; assessor since 2022 [S1][S2]
Says the office shrank from 34 employees to 24 positions through modernization [S2]
Says the assessor's job is accurate, equitable values, not raising or lowering taxes [S2]
Plans online exemption applications for seniors and people with disabilities [S2]

experience.basis: Incumbent assessor with more than 30 years in the office, including as chief deputy.

spending.basis: Cites cutting the office from 34 employees to 24 positions and doing more with fewer people through modernization.

candidates.summary: Commercial photographer, developer and Republican precinct committee officer making a first run for office on a taxpayer-first, customer-service platform.
highlights: Pledges to cut the tax burden 'as far as the law allows' and make the county 'the cheapest tax base in Washington' [S1]
Would launch an online 'data-depot' explaining valuations, comparable sales and parcel tax coefficients [S2][S3]
Would put all forms, including senior exemption forms, online [S2][S4]
Endorsed by the Yakima County Republican Party [S1][S2]

experience.basis: First run for county office from a business background, against a 30-year office veteran; says he won't befriend state officials.

taxes.basis: Statement pledges to 'only collect an absolute minimum,' cut the tax burden as far as the law allows and make the county the cheapest tax base in the state.

contests.office_does: The county auditor runs elections and voter registration, records deeds and other public documents, issues licenses and passports, and keeps the county's accounts and payroll.
contests.race_blurb: Republican Charles Ross, auditor since 2014 and a former state representative, seeks a fourth term against Democrat Maria Cuevas, a retired Yakima Valley College instructor. Ross runs on fair, efficient administration; Cuevas on raising the county's low turnout, Spanish-language service and an independent review of the office.

candidates.summary: Three-term Yakima County Auditor, former 14th District state representative and former Naches mayor.
highlights: Auditor since 2014; state representative 2006-2014; Naches councilman and mayor 1997-2006 [S1]
Says he implements laws he does not always agree with in a fair, professional manner [S1]
Says county plans focus on quality services 'while living within our means' [S3]
Led the August primary with 37.7% [S7]

experience.basis: Three-term incumbent auditor with eight years in the Legislature and nine as a town official.

spending.basis: Describes county planning focused on 'living within our means and being accountable to taxpayers'.

candidates.summary: Retired Yakima Valley College sociology instructor making her first run for office, focused on turnout, bilingual service and public reporting.
highlights: Says the county's turnout is the lowest in the state and would expand outreach to reduce ballot rejections [S1][S2]
Would publish signature challenges and cures by precinct [S2]
Would commission an independent operational review of the office and publish a spending dashboard [S2]
Calls vote-by-mail 'the most democratic way to ensure that everyone participates' [S3]

experience.basis: No prior elected office; runs to 'change the standard' of an office she says has not served the full community.

spending.basis: Proposes a year-one independent operational review, public payroll and expenditure dashboards and internal controls against waste.

contests.office_does: The County Clerk runs the Clerk's Office and is the executive officer of the Superior Court: it processes and keeps court records and exhibits and collects and pays out court fees, fines and restitution.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: incumbent Clerk Billie A. Maggard (Prefers Republican Party), in office since 2023, is the only candidate.

candidates.summary: Yakima County Clerk since January 2023, previously an in-court clerk and a longtime legal assistant; the only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Clerk since January 2023; earlier an in-court clerk for about four years and a legal assistant for almost 20 years [S3]
Named rebuilding relationships within the office and with other departments as her biggest project [S3]
Set electronic filing of court documents as a priority [S3]

contests.office_does: Yakima County's three commissioners adopt the county budget, pass ordinances, set land-use and permitting rules, and oversee roads and the county landfill; District 1 is elected by its own voters.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat between two Republicans: retiring Sheriff Bob Udell, who won 65% in the primary and stresses budget restructuring and partnerships, and contractor Kristoffer Strutner, who would cut regulation and staff and end the county's well-metering program. Coverage of Strutner centers on the Caton Landfill he operated.

candidates.summary: Two-term Yakima County Sheriff with 36 years in the sheriff's office, running on budget restructuring, partnerships and fiscal responsibility.
highlights: 36 years in the sheriff's office, sheriff since his 2018 election [S1][S2]
Says taxes are a last resort; would restructure county operations and seek revenue through growth [S4]
Priorities: public safety, agriculture, water rights and the budget [S3]
Won 65% in the August primary [S5]

experience.basis: 36 years in county law enforcement, eight as the elected sheriff managing one of the county's largest departments.

taxes.basis: Calls taxes 'a last resort' and would rely on growth for new revenue.

spending.basis: Backs the county's hiring freezes and long-term restructuring, and stresses fiscal responsibility, while supporting public money for an animal shelter.

candidates.summary: Heavy civil construction manager and former Caton Landfill operator promising sweeping cuts to county regulation, permitting and staff.
highlights: Would end the county's well-metering Water Resource System and sell its water rights [S1][S4]
Would cut permitting to state minimums, with 30-minute approvals for stamped plans [S2][S3]
Would reduce county staff as regulation is cut [S4]
Operated the Caton Landfill, which lost its permit; disputes misdemeanor tire-dumping charges [S3]

experience.basis: First-time candidate running on 'experience outside the political system' against a 36-year county official.

housing.basis: Would strip permitting to state minimums, speed approvals, allow rural clustering and end water metering to cut the cost to build.

spending.basis: Would reduce county staff, cut infrastructure costs through contracting changes and liquidate water-rights assets into the general fund.

contests.office_does: The County Coroner investigates sudden, unexpected, violent or unnatural deaths in Yakima County, oversees autopsies and may testify in court about a death.
contests.race_blurb: Uncontested: Coroner Marshall Slight (Prefers Republican Party), appointed in 2025 and elected in a 2025 special election, is the only candidate for the full term.

candidates.summary: Yakima County Coroner since his 2025 appointment and chief deputy coroner from 2009; the only candidate on the ballot.
highlights: Chief deputy coroner 2009-2025; appointed coroner in May 2025 after his predecessor resigned [S1][S2]
Won the November 2025 special election with about 70% in election-night returns [S3]
Names aging vehicles and equipment and a tight $600,000 budget as the office's main problems [S2]

contests.office_does: The prosecuting attorney decides which crimes are charged and what plea offers are made in Yakima County, tries criminal cases for the state, and serves as the county government's lawyer.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat between two Republicans who both prosecuted in the office's special assault unit: Tyler Haueter, endorsed by the county Republican Party, pledges no plea-downs for gang violence; Quinn Dalan, endorsed by the Mainstream Republicans, the deputies' guild and retired judges, stresses experience as prosecutor, defender and pro tem judge. The county party ran a months-long campaign against Dalan.

candidates.summary: Kennewick assistant city attorney and former Yakima County special-assault prosecutor running on an enforcement-first platform with the county Republican Party's endorsement.
highlights: Pledges no plea-downs for gang violence and every available sentencing enhancement [S2]
Would end 'soft-on-crime' plea deals for repeat and violent offenders [S2][S3]
Air Force paralegal, defense investigator, then special-assault prosecutor; now prosecutes in Kennewick [S1][S2]
Endorsed by the Yakima County Republican Party [S1]

safety.basis: Repeated explicit pledges: no plea-downs for gang violence, full prosecution of repeat offenders, every sentencing enhancement, 'enforce the law firmly ... without apology'.

experience.basis: Nearly 19 years in the criminal-justice system and current trial work, but a first-time candidate with a shorter career as a lawyer.

candidates.summary: Yakima lawyer since 2008: former deputy prosecutor and unit supervisor, public defender, legal-aid director and current municipal prosecutor for Wapato, Granger and Zillah.
highlights: Former special-assault prosecutor and District Court unit supervisor; cites 65+ trials [S1]
Has also worked as a public defender and pro tem judge [S2][S4]
Endorsed by the Mainstream Republicans, the sheriff's deputies' guild and retired judges [S3]
Target of a months-long county Republican Party campaign questioning her party loyalty [S4]

safety.basis: Prioritizes violent crime and drug trafficking, accountability and law-enforcement partnerships, while citing a balanced view from defense and judicial work.

experience.basis: Eighteen years practicing in Yakima County across prosecution, supervision, defense, civil legal aid, pro tem judging and current municipal prosecution.

contests.office_does: The sheriff runs the Yakima County Sheriff's Office, which patrols unincorporated areas, runs search and rescue, monitors sex offenders and serves civil court papers.
contests.race_blurb: An open seat: retiring Sheriff Bob Udell endorsed his lieutenant Jake Church, who runs on 26 years in law enforcement, against West Richland police officer and business owner Roman Kilinkaridis, who runs as an outsider. Both prefer the Republican Party; they differ on keeping Flock license-plate cameras.

candidates.summary: Yakima County sheriff's lieutenant with 26 years in law enforcement, endorsed by retiring Sheriff Bob Udell.
highlights: Administrative lieutenant handling internal investigations, policy and budgets; 10 years in the sheriff's office after 16 in Toppenish [S1][S4]
Would use analytics to aim limited staff at violent, gang, drug and property crime [S4]
